messages.content: A child aged 16 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, since the POCSO Act defines a 'child' as anyone below 18 years, a 16-year-old victim is fully covered. Penetrative sexual assault carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 10 years, extendable to imprisonment for life, along with a mandatory fine to be used for the victim's medical treatment and rehabilitation. Because the accused is described as a relative, the case may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Sections 5 and 6 if the relative held a position of trust, which raises the minimum sentence to 20 years. Consent is legally immaterial for a child under 18, the offence is non-bailable and cognizable, and the trial takes place before a designated Special Court under the Act.
I was harmed by a mobile phone battery that exploded while charging overnight. Can I claim compensation from the manufacturer under Indian consumer law?

Yes — this falls under the product liability provisions in Chapter VI of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Section 84 makes a product manufacturer liable in a product liability action where, among other grounds, the product has a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from its own manufacturing specifications, doesn't conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions and warnings to prevent harm — your case appears to involve manufacturing defect creating a serious safety hazard. Importantly, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer can be held liable even if they weren't negligent or fraudulent in making an express warranty, which introduces a strict-liability element focused on whether the product caused harm rather than the manufacturer's intent. You can file a complaint before the relevant Consumer Commission (District, State, or National, depending on the claim value), which has the power to order removal of the defect, replacement, refund with interest, compensation including punitive damages for negligence, and even direct withdrawal of the hazardous product from the market. Keep your purchase receipt, photos or medical records of the harm, and any advertising material showing the manufacturer's claims, as this evidence strengthens a product liability claim.
A chemical company's leak was discovered 5 months and 3 weeks ago and villagers are only now organizing to file at the NGT. Are they cutting it too close?

Yes, they should file without any further delay. Under Section 14(3) of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, an application must be made within 6 months from the date the cause of action first arose, which appears to be when the leak was discovered. At 5 months and 3 weeks, the villagers have only about a week of the statutory window left. While the Tribunal can condone a further delay of up to 60 days beyond the 6 months if satisfied there was sufficient cause, relying on that extension is risky and not guaranteed, so they should prepare and file their application as soon as possible rather than waiting even a few more days. Once filed, the Tribunal will also try to dispose of the matter within 6 months, and importantly, ongoing or continuing harm (such as contamination that keeps spreading) may give rise to a fresh, independent cause of action under some NGT rulings, which is worth raising if the leak's effects are still continuing today.
Can you explain what Indian law says about filing an RTI application, for a friend from Chennai?

The RTI Act, 2005 doesn't fix its fee amount directly in the statute itself — Section 27(2)(b) instead empowers the Central and State Governments to prescribe the fee through rules, which is why the exact amount (though commonly Rs 10) can differ slightly between the central government and individual states. In practice, for your friend, if the application is to a central government body, Rs 10 is the correct fee — anything meaningfully higher being demanded is worth double-checking against the applicable RTI Rules.
A friend from Chennai asked me about minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The Companies Act, 2013's oppression-and-mismanagement remedy under Sections 241-242 replaced the earlier Sections 397-409 of the 1956 Act, and expanded the ground beyond just 'oppression' to also cover conduct that is merely 'prejudicial' to the company or its members — a somewhat lower bar than the older law required. In practice, so your friend shouldn't assume this remedy is only for small companies — it's the same legal route that was used in some of India's largest corporate governance disputes.
My elder relative wants to understand a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The 2015 Juvenile Justice Act was the first Indian law to allow trying a 16-18 year old as an adult, but this isn't automatic — the Juvenile Justice Board must first assess, within three months of the child being produced before it, whether the child had the capacity to understand the offence and its consequences, before referring the matter to the Children's Court for a final decision on adult trial. In practice, in your elder relative's case, it's worth confirming through the JJ Board process that a lawyer and child psychologist are actually involved in the preliminary assessment, since the law specifically requires that support.
Can you explain what Indian law says about whether a small business needs to register for GST, for a former employee I used to manage?

The current GST registration thresholds — Rs 40 lakh for goods, Rs 20 lakh for services — have been in place since 1 April 2019, when they were raised from the earlier Rs 20 lakh (goods and services) limit. The Rs 40 lakh goods threshold doesn't apply unconditionally, though — certain categories like ice cream, pan masala, tobacco products, and businesses making inter-state taxable supplies of goods are excluded and must register regardless of turnover. In practice, so the former employee should check which category the business falls into — if it's goods, services, or a mix, since the two thresholds (Rs 40 lakh vs Rs 20 lakh) and the special-category-state exceptions can materially change the answer.
A person i met recently is dealing with a situation involving civil liability for unauthorized computer access. What does Indian law say about this?

Beyond the criminal liability under Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000 for identity theft, unauthorized access to a computer resource can separately attract civil liability for damages by way of compensation under Section 43 of the Act.
A startup founder I'm advising is dealing with a situation involving a daughter's coparcenary rights. What does Indian law say about this?

Since the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 came into force, Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gives a daughter coparcenary rights by birth in Mitakshara joint family property, on the same footing as a son — same rights, same liabilities. The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) clarified that this applies as long as both the father (coparcener) and the daughter were alive on 9 September 2005, regardless of when the daughter was born. In practice, for the founder, this means she can demand her share of the ancestral property and seek partition just as a brother could, regardless of whether she was married at the time or born before or after 2005.
How does Indian law actually treat residence orders and the shared household, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 19 of the PWDV Act, 2005 allows a residence order restraining the respondent from dispossessing the aggrieved person from the shared household, regardless of the respondent's legal interest in it.

A retail application collects continuous background geolocation from users without displaying any privacy disclosure or obtaining consent. What immediate documentation and procedural precautions should be taken first?

Immediate Practical Steps: (1) Preserve evidence: Maintain written logs, physical receipts, electronic records, and timestamps. (2) Review governing terms: Check applicable contracts, statutory notices, or rules of Privacy and Data Protection. (3) Avoid unilateral admissions: Ensure all communications remain factual and accurate without prejudicing legal rights. (4) Consult counsel: Seek professional advice regarding consent and notice under DPDP Act before filing formal pleadings. Note: This information is for general educational and informational purposes under Indian law and does not constitute formal legal advice. For specific disputes or court proceedings, consultation with an advocate is advised.

Review this contract clause: "The founder shall not directly or indirectly engage in or promote any competing business for two years following cessation of employment." Is this enforceable under Indian law, and what are its boundaries?

Regarding the clause "The founder shall not directly or indirectly engage in or promote any competing business for two years following cessation of employment.": This is a post-termination non-compete restriction. Under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, agreements in restraint of trade are void to that extent. Indian courts consistently hold that non-compete covenants extending beyond the term of employment are unenforceable, though non-compete restrictions during active service remain valid. Enforceability depends on statutory compliance, public policy, and whether the restriction is unconscionable or penal.
If my brother is affected by challenging an arbitration award, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The three-month clock under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration Act starts from the date of receipt of the signed award, not from when it was merely delivered or dispatched — a distinction that has actually decided cases, since 'receipt' and 'delivery' aren't treated as automatically the same thing under the Act. In practice, this means your brother should file the Section 34 application well within the window rather than waiting close to the deadline, since even administrative delays (like a court being on vacation) haven't been accepted as grounds for extension beyond the cap.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of National Commission pecuniary jurisdiction isn't handled correctly?

Under the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules, the National Commission has jurisdiction over complaints where consideration exceeds Rs. 2 crore. Jurisdiction is fixed by consideration paid, not compensation claimed, unlike the older 1986 Act.
I run a small consulting outfit in Puducherry with turnover close to ₹1,500,000 a year. Do I cross the GST registration threshold?

Under Section 22 of the CGST Act, 2017, the registration threshold for a supplier of services in Puducherry is ₹2,000,000, and since your turnover of ₹1,500,000 is below that, registration isn't mandatory yet — though you can register voluntarily under Section 25(3) if you want to claim input tax credit or your buyers need GST invoices from you. Keep in mind certain activities trigger compulsory registration under Section 24 regardless of turnover, such as inter-state supply or selling through e-commerce platforms.

I'm Vikram. I have a consumer complaint about an airline that cancelled a flight and won't refund the fare, worth about Rs. 25000000, and the issue arose just over a year ago. Which consumer forum should I approach, and is it too late?

On forum: consumer commissions have pecuniary jurisdiction based on the value of goods or services actually paid as consideration -- District Commission up to Rs. 50 lakh, State Commission above Rs. 50 lakh up to Rs. 2 crore, and National Commission above Rs. 2 crore. Given your amount is around Rs. 25000000, this would fall under the National Commission (above Rs. 2 crore). You can file where you reside or work for gain -- you don't have to file where the seller is located.

On timing: You're within the 2-year limitation period that applies to consumer complaints (counted from when the cause of action arose), so timing shouldn't be a problem here, but it's still best not to delay further.

The Act also allows for mediation as an alternative route under Section 74, through a mediation cell attached to the commission, if you'd prefer to try resolving this without a full hearing.
How does Indian law actually treat District Commission pecuniary jurisdiction, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021, a District Commission has jurisdiction over complaints where the consideration paid does not exceed Rs. 50 lakh.
A friend's mother asked me about maintenance for a wife, child, or parent — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The maintenance provision that used to sit at CrPC Section 125 is now Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023, effective since 1 July 2024, with the substance carried over largely unchanged. Eligible claimants are a wife (including a non-remarried divorced wife), minor children, a disabled adult child, or aged parents; the person ordered to pay must have sufficient means and must have neglected or refused to maintain them. In practice, so if the other side stops paying after an order is passed, your friend's mother can go back to court and the Magistrate has the power to order imprisonment of up to a month for each missed payment.
How does Indian law actually treat the six-month limitation on accident compensation claims, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 166(3), inserted by the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 and in force from 1 April 2022, bars a compensation claim before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal unless filed within six months of the accident; this provision is currently under constitutional challenge before the Supreme Court.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding maintenance for a disabled adult child?

Section 144 BNSS, 2023 is not limited to minor children: it also covers a legitimate or illegitimate major child who is unable to maintain itself because of a physical or mental abnormality or injury, letting such a child claim maintenance from a parent with sufficient means.
A factory worker I spoke with asked me about the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Section 12(1)(c) of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 requires private unaided schools to reserve 25% of entry-level seats (typically Class 1 or pre-primary) for children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups, with the government reimbursing the school for the cost of educating them. In practice, for the worker, the first thing to check is the specific state's income limit and residence radius for RTE admissions, since these details differ from state to state even though the 25% figure itself is set by central law.
A tenant I know is dealing with a situation involving a passport being impounded or seized. What does Indian law say about this?

An order impounding a passport under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967 can be appealed to the Central Passport Organisation (or, depending on which authority passed the order, a designated appellate authority) within 30 days of the order being communicated to the holder. In practice, for the tenant, the key question is which authority actually impounded the passport — if it was just the police holding onto it (as opposed to a formal impounding order from the passport office), that itself may be legally questionable.
Can you explain what Indian law says about the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools, for someone in my apartment complex?

The RTE Act, 2009's 25% reservation for economically weaker and disadvantaged children in private unaided schools was upheld as constitutionally valid by the Supreme Court in 2012. Eligibility is usually tied to family income and residence within a set distance from the school (commonly 1 km for primary classes), though the exact income cut-offs and application process vary by state. In practice, in that person's case, if the school is trying to charge any fee for a seat claimed under this quota, that's not permitted — the seat is meant to be entirely free, with the school reimbursed separately by the government.
I'm Ashok. Lata's cheque for Rs. 120000 bounced, and I sent the legal notice 18 days ago. Lata hasn't responded. What happens now?

Since Lata received the notice 18 days ago, they still have until the 15-day mark to make the payment. If that period passes with no payment, the offence under Section 138 NI Act is treated as complete, and you get 30 days from the end of the 15-day period to file a criminal complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court.

Keep your proof of notice delivery (courier/postal receipt, or acknowledgment) safe, as you'll need it to show the notice was validly served. If payment does come in during the remaining days, that would resolve the matter without needing to go to court.
I run a small trading business in Gujarat with annual turnover around ₹4,500,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of goods in Gujarat, the threshold is ₹40 lakh for goods or ₹20 lakh for services, since Gujarat follows the higher normal-category limit that applies in most Indian states. Since your turnover of ₹4,500,000 is at or above this ₹4,000,000 threshold, you are required to register for GST.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of enforcing a maintenance charge against a transferee isn't handled correctly?
Section 23(2) allows a senior citizen with a right to maintenance out of an estate to enforce that right against a transferee who had notice of it, or where the transfer was gratuitous.
Does a wife lose her right to claim maintenance if she is earning some income herself?

Not automatically. Courts have repeatedly clarified that the test under Section 144 BNSS / Section 125 CrPC is not whether a wife has zero income, but whether her income is sufficient to maintain the standard of living she was accustomed to in the matrimonial home. In Sita Bai (referenced in later maintenance case law), and reaffirmed in Mamta Jaiswal v. Rajesh Jaiswal (2024), courts have held that even an earning wife can claim maintenance if her own income is insufficient to sustain that standard of living. So a modest income on her part doesn't by itself disqualify her -- the Magistrate weighs her income against her needs and the husband's means and both parties' circumstances, rather than applying a strict cut-off.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of expedited reply for life-or-liberty matters isn't handled correctly?
Where a request concerns information relating to the life or liberty of a person, the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires a response within 48 hours.
Review this contract clause: "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement." Is this enforceable under Indian law, and what are its boundaries?

Regarding the clause "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement.": This is an express 'time of the essence' clause. Under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, failure to perform by the agreed deadline renders the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. However, courts evaluate party conduct and extensions to ascertain if time was genuinely intended to be of the essence. Enforceability depends on statutory compliance, public policy, and whether the restriction is unconscionable or penal.
What is the correct legal procedure a colleague at work should follow regarding penalty on a defaulting PIO under Indian law?
Section 20 of the RTI Act, 2005 empowers the Information Commission to impose a per-day penalty on a PIO for unreasonable delay, malafide denial, or destruction of information.
A startup founder I'm advising is dealing with a situation involving whether a small business needs to register for GST. What does Indian law say about this?

GST registration becomes mandatory once a business's aggregate turnover crosses Rs 40 lakh for suppliers of goods, or Rs 20 lakh for suppliers of services, in most states — with lower thresholds of Rs 20 lakh (goods) and Rs 10 lakh (services) applying in special category states in the North East and hill regions. Below these limits, registration is optional (though it can still be done voluntarily to claim input tax credit). In practice, in the founder's case, if the business sells across state lines even occasionally, that can trigger mandatory registration regardless of total turnover, since inter-state taxable supply is one of the categories excluded from the higher threshold.
A shopkeeper in Coimbatore asked me about an unresolved e-commerce or online shopping complaint — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, e-commerce entities are required to acknowledge a consumer's complaint within 48 hours and redress it within one month of receipt. Manufacturers and service providers who run false or misleading advertisements can additionally be penalised under Section 89 — up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of up to Rs 10 lakh for a first offence, rising to five years and Rs 50 lakh for repeat violations. In practice, for the shopkeeper, if the platform hasn't even acknowledged the complaint within 48 hours, that delay itself is a breach of the e-commerce rules, separate from the underlying issue with the product.
If a colleague at work is affected by how a correction request affects the limitation clock, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Where a party makes a genuine request under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (for correction, interpretation, or an additional award), the three-month limitation under Section 34(3) to challenge the award runs from the date the tribunal disposes of that request rather than from the date of the original award — though a request that is, in substance, a disguised attempt to have the tribunal review the award's merits may not get this benefit.
A relative has an overdraft facility secured by property of ₹1,500,000 that's now 90 days overdue and the bank hasn't sent any notice yet. What should they expect?

Once an account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (typically after 90 days of overdue payment under RBI norms), the bank is likely to invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002. The first formal step your relative should expect is a written demand notice under Section 13(2), giving 60 days to repay the outstanding ₹1,500,000 in full. During this 60-day period, the bank cannot take possession of the secured property — your relative can use this time to repay, negotiate a one-time settlement, or file a written representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the notice on factual or legal grounds (though this doesn't pause the clock). If the dues remain unpaid after 60 days, the bank can move to take possession, manage, or sell the property under Section 13(4), if needed seeking the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate's assistance under Section 14. Your relative retains a right to appeal any Section 13(4) action to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
I have a shop that I rent out on a month-to-month basis with no written lease agreement. If I want the tenant to vacate, how much advance notice am I legally required to give?

Under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contract, local law, or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for any purpose other than agriculture or manufacturing (which would include a shop) is deemed to be a lease from month to month. Such a tenancy is terminable by either the lessor or the lessee by giving fifteen days' notice. The notice should be in writing and should be structured to expire with the end of a month of the tenancy, meaning it should align with the monthly rental cycle rather than an arbitrary fifteen-day count. If you accept rent from the tenant after sending the notice, courts have sometimes treated that as a waiver of the notice, so you should be careful about that if you intend to proceed with eviction.
Can you explain what Indian law says about getting married under the Special Marriage Act, for my elder relative?

The 30-day notice period under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 is meant to allow objections strictly on the grounds specified in Section 4 — such as either party already being married, being under the minimum marriageable age, or falling within a prohibited degree of relationship. It is not a general public consultation on the marriage itself, and objections outside these grounds cannot legally block the marriage from proceeding. In practice, so your elder relative needs to plan around the full 30-day notice-and-objection window before the marriage can actually be solemnised, in addition to whatever documentation the Marriage Officer requires.
Under which statutory framework is the notion that 'An FIR can only be registered at the specific police station where the crime physically occurred.' specifically refuted?

Statutory Refutation: The assumption that 'An FIR can only be registered at the specific police station where the crime physically occurred.' is refuted under Criminal Procedure. Substantive Provision: Under the concept of 'Zero FIR' reaffirmed under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), any police station can register an FIR for a cognizable offence irrespective of territorial jurisdiction, and subsequently transfer it to the competent station. Legal Principle: Indian statutes require formal compliance and do not sanction informal evasions.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment, for my sister-in-law?

Any offer or advertisement in a newspaper or other media of money or property as consideration for a person's marriage is itself a punishable offence under Section 4A of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, carrying imprisonment of six months to five years, or a fine, or both — separate from and in addition to the offences of actually giving, taking, or demanding dowry. In practice, for your sister-in-law, it matters whether what happened was an actual exchange of dowry (Section 3) or just a demand for it (Section 4) — both are offences, but they carry different minimum and maximum punishments.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding children are exempt from the reporting-failure penalty?

Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 explicitly states that the penalty for failure to report under Section 21(1) does not apply to a child under the Act, meaning a minor's silence or failure to report abuse (their own or another's) cannot itself be criminally punished.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009, admission under the 25% EWS quota is meant to be free of cost to the family — the school cannot charge tuition or other fees for these seats, and instead claims reimbursement from the government at the rate specified under the rules. In practice, this means your colleague has a right to apply under this quota specifically for admission to Class 1 or the school's designated entry-level class, not for lateral entry into higher grades.
I'm Pooja. As a wife, my husband has a good government job but says he owes me nothing since we're separated. Can I claim maintenance, and how does that work?

This would fall under Section 144 BNSS, which replaced Section 125 CrPC from 1 July 2024, and lets a Magistrate order maintenance for a wife, child, or parent who is neglected despite the other person having sufficient means. Courts treat this as a summary, welfare-oriented remedy meant to prevent destitution, not to punish anyone.

You'd need to file an application before the appropriate Magistrate, along with an affidavit of your income and needs. Maintenance is usually payable from the date you filed the application, not just from the date of the final order, so filing promptly matters. I'd recommend consulting a family-law advocate to help calculate a realistic amount based on the other side's income.
A former employee I used to manage asked me about minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The NCLT's powers once it finds oppression or mismanagement under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are broad — it can order the majority to buy out the minority's shares, set aside prejudicial agreements, remove directors, order forensic audits, or even restructure how the company is managed going forward, though courts have clarified that a director's removal, an isolated bad decision, or simply a breakdown of trust between shareholders doesn't by itself amount to oppression. In practice, this means the former employee can ask the NCLT not just for a declaration that the conduct was wrong, but for concrete relief — like an order forcing the majority to buy out the former employee's shares at a fair price.
What is the correct legal procedure a client I'm helping should follow regarding State Commission pecuniary jurisdiction under Indian law?
Per the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a State Commission has jurisdiction where the consideration paid exceeds Rs. 50 lakh but does not exceed Rs. 2 crore.
A friend from Chennai asked me about a daughter's coparcenary rights — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Since the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 came into force, Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gives a daughter coparcenary rights by birth in Mitakshara joint family property, on the same footing as a son — same rights, same liabilities. The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) clarified that this applies as long as both the father (coparcener) and the daughter were alive on 9 September 2005, regardless of when the daughter was born. In practice, for your friend, this means she can demand her share of the ancestral property and seek partition just as a brother could, regardless of whether she was married at the time or born before or after 2005.
In Tamil Nadu, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Tamil Nadu, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
What is the hierarchy of appeals available to an aggrieved party in Environmental Law?

Appellate Hierarchy: In Environmental Law, initial orders from statutory tribunals or trial courts are subject to structured appeals. Statutory Appeal: First appeals generally lie on questions of fact and law to the immediate appellate authority or District/High Court. Subsequent Review: Second appeals or revisions are typically restricted to substantial questions of law, concluding with discretionary review under Article 136 of the Constitution.
A 17-year-old has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a family friend who often stayed at their home. What punishment applies?

Since the victim is 17, POCSO's protection (covering any child below 18) applies fully. Section 4 of the POCSO Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, prescribes a minimum sentence of 10 years' rigorous imprisonment, extendable to life, plus a mandatory fine for penetrative sexual assault. Whether this rises to aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Sections 5 and 6 — carrying a higher minimum of 20 years — depends on whether the family friend can be shown to have been in a position of trust or authority over the child, which courts have interpreted broadly where someone had regular access to and influence over a child's household and routine. Consent is legally immaterial given the victim's age, and the matter is tried by a designated Special Court under the Act.
If a person I met recently is affected by 60-day timeline for interim maintenance, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Once a maintenance application is made under Section 144 BNSS, 2023, the Magistrate is expected, as far as possible, to dispose of the application for interim maintenance and proceeding expenses within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the person from whom maintenance is claimed.
I was harmed by a water purifier that was advertised to remove 99% of contaminants but tested at far lower removal rates. Can I claim compensation from the manufacturer under Indian consumer law?

Yes — this falls under the product liability provisions in Chapter VI of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Section 84 makes a product manufacturer liable in a product liability action where, among other grounds, the product has a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from its own manufacturing specifications, doesn't conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions and warnings to prevent harm — your case appears to involve non-conformity with an express warranty made about the product. Importantly, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer can be held liable even if they weren't negligent or fraudulent in making an express warranty, which introduces a strict-liability element focused on whether the product caused harm rather than the manufacturer's intent. You can file a complaint before the relevant Consumer Commission (District, State, or National, depending on the claim value), which has the power to order removal of the defect, replacement, refund with interest, compensation including punitive damages for negligence, and even direct withdrawal of the hazardous product from the market. Keep your purchase receipt, photos or medical records of the harm, and any advertising material showing the manufacturer's claims, as this evidence strengthens a product liability claim.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding wife's maintenance claim?

Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the successor to Section 125 CrPC, lets a wife unable to maintain herself — including a divorced wife who has not remarried — claim a monthly allowance from a husband with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain her, on application before a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
What does the law say if a factory worker I spoke with is facing hit-and-run accident compensation?

Under the Compensation to Victims of Hit and Run Motor Accidents Scheme, 2022, notified under the Motor Vehicles Act, victims (or their families) are entitled to Rs 2 lakh for death and Rs 50,000 for grievous injury from the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund, regardless of whether the offending vehicle or driver is ever traced, with payment meant to be made within about three months. In practice, for the worker, the key step is filing the claim through the police/insurance council process for the hit-and-run scheme promptly, since it's a fixed statutory amount rather than something to negotiate.
Someone I met recently is dealing with a situation involving a builder delaying possession of a flat. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) gives a homebuyer an unqualified right to act when a builder fails to hand over possession by the date agreed in the sale agreement: either withdraw from the project and get a full refund with interest, or stay in the project and receive monthly interest compensation for every month of the delay until possession. This right exists regardless of what the builder-buyer agreement itself says. In practice, for this person, the first practical step is to check whether the project was registered with the state RERA authority — this remedy runs through that authority, not a civil court.
Can you explain what Indian law says about anticipatory bail in a case under the SC/ST Atrocities Act, for a shopkeeper in Coimbatore?

The bar on anticipatory bail under Section 18 of the SC/ST Act, 1989 excludes the ordinary pre-arrest bail provision (now BNSS Section 482, earlier CrPC Section 438) in cases registered under the Act. But courts must still conduct a preliminary examination of whether the FIR and complaint actually disclose the ingredients of an SC/ST Act offence before applying that bar — a mere allegation isn't automatically enough. In practice, in the shopkeeper's case, this means the strategy isn't just to argue for bail on general grounds, but specifically to show the court that the complaint doesn't make out a prima facie case under the Act.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of filing a domestic violence complaint isn't handled correctly?
Under Section 12 of the PWDV Act, 2005, an aggrieved person, a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf can file an application before a Magistrate.
My cousin who works in chennai is dealing with a situation involving expedited reply for life-or-liberty matters. What does Indian law say about this?

Where an RTI request concerns information relating to the life or liberty of a person, the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires a response within 48 hours of receipt of the request, rather than the usual 30 days.
How does Indian law actually treat enforcing a maintenance charge against a transferee, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 23(2) allows a senior citizen with a right to maintenance out of an estate to enforce that right against a transferee who had notice of it, or where the transfer was gratuitous.
A tenant I know wants to understand how long you have to file a civil suit. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The Limitation Act, 1963 doesn't erase the underlying right — it only bars going to court to enforce it after the deadline. So a debt that's become time-barred (typically after three years) still technically exists, and if the debtor voluntarily repays it later, that payment is valid; the debtor just can't be dragged to court to force that repayment. In practice, in the tenant's case, if there's any written acknowledgment of the debt — even something informal like an email — that can reset the limitation period under Section 18, so it's worth checking for that before assuming the claim is time-barred.
I heard something about drawer's payment window after notice that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?

After receiving a Section 138 demand notice under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the drawer of a dishonoured cheque has 15 days to pay the cheque amount; only if payment is not made within that window does the cause of action to file a criminal complaint arise, on the 16th day.
I lent money to a friend and the ₹55,000 repayment cheque they gave bounced with 'funds insufficient' as the reason. Does the reason for bounce matter legally?

Not much, as long as the cheque was issued toward a legally enforceable debt or liability. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 applies when a cheque is dishonoured because the account has insufficient funds, or because the amount exceeds what's arranged to be paid from that account under an agreement with the bank — 'funds insufficient' is the classic and most common trigger for this section. Your process is the same regardless: send a legal demand notice within 30 days of learning of the bounce, asking for the ₹55,000; if a friend doesn't pay within 15 days of receiving it, you can file a criminal complaint within about a month after that. On conviction, the punishment is imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹110,000), or both, and courts frequently use the fine or compensation route to make you whole rather than imposing jail time, especially if a friend is willing to settle.
A shopkeeper in coimbatore is dealing with a situation involving charging both identity theft and online cheating together. What does Indian law say about this?

Where a stolen password or credential (an offence under Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000) is then used to impersonate the victim and deceive a third party, both Section 66C for the identity theft and Section 66D for the resulting cheating by personation can be invoked together for the same course of conduct.
I was stopped in Uttar Pradesh and my breathalyser reading was above the limit for the first time. What's the penalty?

Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), driving with a blood alcohol concentration above 30 mg per 100 ml of blood is an offence regardless of which state you're in, since this is a central enactment applied uniformly, including in Uttar Pradesh. For a first-time offence, the punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Your driving licence can also be suspended, and traffic police are empowered to seize the vehicle. If the case goes to court, you'll be tried in the local Traffic Court or Judicial Magistrate's court, and if an accident causing injury or death resulted, you could separately face charges under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 as well.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman?

The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 initially appeared to limit a husband's maintenance obligation to just the iddat period (roughly three months), but the Supreme Court in Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) interpreted the Act to mean the husband must make a 'reasonable and fair provision' within the iddat period that is sufficient to sustain the divorced wife for her entire future, not just those three months — effectively extending real protection well beyond the iddat window while keeping the Act's text intact.
Under which statutory framework is the notion that 'A contract is legally valid only if it is typed on judicial stamp paper and signed before a notary.' specifically refuted?

Statutory Refutation: The assumption that 'A contract is legally valid only if it is typed on judicial stamp paper and signed before a notary.' is refuted under Contract Law. Substantive Provision: Under the Indian Contract Act, oral agreements and un-notarized written agreements are valid contracts if made with free consent of competent parties for lawful consideration and object. Stamp duty affects evidentiary admissibility, but is not an element of contract formation. Legal Principle: Indian statutes require formal compliance and do not sanction informal evasions.
In Odisha, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Odisha, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding State Commission pecuniary jurisdiction?
Per the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules made under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a State Commission has jurisdiction where the consideration paid exceeds Rs. 50 lakh but does not exceed Rs. 2 crore.
What does the law say if my neighbour is facing maternity leave entitlement?

The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid maternity leave under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children, of which up to 8 weeks can be taken before the expected delivery date. For a third or subsequent child, the entitlement drops to 12 weeks, and adoptive or commissioning mothers get 12 weeks from the date of adoption or the child's birth. The Act applies to establishments with 10 or more employees. In practice, for your neighbour, the key eligibility check is the 80-days-worked-in-12-months requirement — if that's satisfied, the 26-week entitlement applies regardless of whether she's on a permanent or contract role.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of consequence of not challenging an award in time isn't handled correctly?
If an award is not challenged within the Section 34(3) limitation period, it attains finality under Section 35 and becomes enforceable as a decree under Section 36.
If a client I'm helping is affected by maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Despite the existence of the 1986 Act specific to Muslim women, courts (including the Allahabad High Court in several recent rulings) have reaffirmed that a divorced Muslim woman retains the right to seek ongoing maintenance under the secular maintenance provision (now BNSS Section 144, earlier CrPC Section 125) as long as she hasn't remarried — the 1986 Act doesn't bar her from that route, since Parliament never explicitly excluded it. In practice, this means your client should know that if her former husband genuinely cannot pay, the law does provide a further fallback — first to relatives who'd inherit from her, and only then to the State Waqf Board.
My builder was supposed to hand over possession of my flat 18 months ago and keeps pushing the date. What can I actually claim under RERA?

Under Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA), once a builder fails to give possession by the date committed to in the agreement for sale, you have two options, entirely your choice: (1) withdraw from the project and claim a full refund of every rupee you've paid, plus interest, and compensation; or (2) stay in the project and claim interest for every month of delay until you actually get possession. This right exists regardless of what fine print in your builder-buyer agreement might say (courts and RERA authorities have consistently held that a builder can't contract out of Section 18 by inserting a token, low, fixed 'delay penalty' clause). The interest rate is prescribed by your specific state's RERA rules, not left to the builder to decide -- most states use the State Bank of India's highest Marginal Cost of Lending Rate (MCLR) plus 2%. You file the complaint with your State Real Estate Regulatory Authority (for refund/interest) or before the Adjudicating Officer (for additional compensation claims) -- you may need separate applications for each. There's generally no strict limitation period barring such claims, but don't delay unnecessarily. This is general information; the exact interest rate and procedure vary by state, so check your specific State RERA's rules and consider consulting a lawyer for the complaint drafting.
A 17-year-old has disclosed being sexually assaulted by their tuition teacher. What punishment applies?

Since POCSO defines a 'child' as anyone under 18, a 17-year-old is fully protected under the Act. Under Section 4, penetrative sexual assault carries a minimum sentence of 10 years' rigorous imprisonment, extendable to life, plus a mandatory fine. But because the accused is a tuition teacher — a person in a position of trust and authority over the child — this is very likely to be charged as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Sections 5 and 6, which carries a higher minimum sentence of 20 years, extendable to life imprisonment, or the death penalty in the gravest cases. Consent is legally immaterial given the victim is under 18, and the matter is tried before a Special Court set up under the Act.
What is the correct legal procedure my cousin who works in Chennai should follow regarding expedited reply for life-or-liberty matters under Indian law?
Where a request concerns information relating to the life or liberty of a person, the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires a response within 48 hours.

How does the principle of consent and notice under DPDP Act protect rights and govern legal relations in India?

The doctrine of consent and notice under DPDP Act serves as an important safeguard under Privacy and Data Protection. The foundational statutory principle under digital personal data legislation requiring data fiduciaries to obtain clear, unbundled, and informed consent accompanied by an itemized privacy notice specifying processing purposes. Its invocation is subject to good faith, statutory limits, and reasonable restrictions. Parties relying on this principle must demonstrate compliance with relevant legal rules.
Is there a Section 166A in the Motor Vehicles Act that lets insurance companies deny all claims if the six-month filing window under Section 166(3) is missed by even one day?

I'm not able to verify a Section 166A in the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 with that specific automatic-denial rule. What I can confirm is that Section 166(3), in force since 1 April 2022, requires claims to be filed within six months of the accident, and that this provision is currently under constitutional challenge before the Supreme Court, with courts at times directing that claims not be dismissed as time-barred while that challenge is pending — so an automatic, unconditional denial for even a one-day delay doesn't match the current, actively evolving legal position. Please verify the current status with a lawyer before assuming any claim is barred.
My relative took an education loan secured by property of about ₹2,000,000 and has missed EMIs for 5 months. The bank has now classified it as NPA. What can the bank do under SARFAESI?

Once the loan account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset under RBI norms, the bank (as a secured creditor) can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Under Section 13(2), it must first issue a written demand notice giving your relative 60 days to repay the entire outstanding dues on the ₹2,000,000 loan. During this 60-day window, the bank cannot take possession — your relative can repay in full, negotiate a one-time settlement, or file a written representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the notice, which the bank must respond to with reasons within 15 days (though filing a representation does not pause the 60-day clock). If the dues remain unpaid after 60 days, the bank can proceed under Section 13(4) to take possession, manage, or sell the secured property, if necessary seeking assistance from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate under Section 14 to physically take possession. Your relative retains the right to appeal any action taken under Section 13(4) to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of eligibility for mutual consent divorce isn't handled correctly?

Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows a joint divorce petition where spouses have lived separately for at least one year, cannot live together, and mutually agree to dissolve the marriage.
How do the missing details in 'A factory operating near a residential layout emits pungent smoke and unverified effluent.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Environmental Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) Whether the industrial unit holds valid Consent to Establish (CTE) and Consent to Operate (CTO); (2) Whether local zoning laws designate the area as industrial or mixed residential; (3) Specific lab test reports or environmental monitoring records. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
How is the actual maintenance amount decided by the court? Is there a fixed formula?

There's no fixed formula under Section 144 BNSS -- the amount is left to the Magistrate's discretion, based on the facts of each case. Courts typically look at the paying party's income and financial capacity, the claimant's reasonable needs and standard of living, and any dependents on either side. The Supreme Court's guidelines in Rajnesh v. Neha (2021) require both parties to file standardised affidavits disclosing their income and assets, specifically so the court has real numbers to work with rather than estimates. Because there's no set formula, outcomes can vary quite a bit case to case, which is also why having accurate financial documentation on your side matters.
A small business owner I know is dealing with a situation involving gratuity owed after leaving a job. What does Indian law say about this?

Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employee becomes eligible for gratuity after completing five years of continuous service (courts have accepted 240 days worked in the fifth year as satisfying this), except where employment ends due to death or disablement, in which case the five-year requirement doesn't apply at all. Gratuity is calculated as (last drawn salary × 15 × number of years of service) ÷ 26, and the maximum payable under the Act is capped at Rs 20 lakh, following the 2018 amendment that raised it from Rs 10 lakh. In practice, in the business owner's case, since gratuity is calculated on the *last drawn* salary, any recent increment actually raises the gratuity amount, so it's worth confirming the employer used the most recent basic + DA figure.
Can you explain what Indian law says about anticipatory bail, for a factory worker I spoke with?

The BNSS, 2023 shifted anticipatory bail from CrPC Section 438 to its own Section 482. The substance of the remedy is unchanged: someone who reasonably apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence can ask the Sessions Court or High Court to direct that they be released on bail if arrested. One statutory exception under Section 482(4) blocks this route in cases of rape of a girl under sixteen or gang rape of a woman under eighteen. In practice, practically, this gives the worker a legal route to avoid arrest altogether while the case proceeds, provided the underlying offence isn't one of those excluded under Section 482(4).
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding anticipatory bail in a case under the SC/ST Atrocities Act?

Under Section 18 read with Section 18A of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, no preliminary inquiry is required before registering an FIR, and anticipatory bail is barred once the Act applies — but the Supreme Court's more recent rulings have insisted that this bar only kicks in when a prima facie offence under the Act is genuinely disclosed, not for every complaint that merely invokes the Act's sections.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on an unresolved e-commerce or online shopping complaint?

Liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 runs across the supply chain — manufacturers, sellers, and e-commerce marketplaces can all be held responsible when goods are defective or services deficient, under the Act's product liability chapter. E-commerce platforms specifically must acknowledge a complaint within 48 hours and resolve it within one month, and consumers can escalate unresolved matters to the District, State, or National Consumer Commission depending on the value involved.

Despite the existence of the 1986 Act specific to Muslim women, courts (including the Allahabad High Court in several recent rulings) have reaffirmed that a divorced Muslim woman retains the right to seek ongoing maintenance under the secular maintenance provision (now BNSS Section 144, earlier CrPC Section 125) as long as she hasn't remarried — the 1986 Act doesn't bar her from that route, since Parliament never explicitly excluded it.
