Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding 60-day timeline for interim maintenance?

Once a maintenance application is made under Section 144 BNSS, 2023, the Magistrate is expected, as far as possible, to dispose of the application for interim maintenance and proceeding expenses within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the person from whom maintenance is claimed.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on how long copyright protection lasts?

Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended), copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work generally lasts for the lifetime of the author plus 60 years, counted from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death. For works of joint authorship, the 60-year period runs from the death of whichever author dies last.
A factory worker I spoke with asked me about a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Once a loan account is classified as a non-performing asset, Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 requires the secured creditor (usually a bank or NBFC) to issue a demand notice giving the borrower 60 days to repay the outstanding dues before the lender can move to take possession of the mortgaged property under Section 13(4). In practice, for the worker, the 60-day period isn't just a waiting period — it's the window to either repay, negotiate a settlement, or file a written objection under Section 13(3A) challenging the notice.
If a colleague at work is affected by hit-and-run accident compensation, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The Motor Vehicles Act's hit-and-run compensation scheme, in force since April 2022, guarantees Rs 2 lakh to the family in case of death and Rs 50,000 for grievous injury, paid out of the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund even if the driver responsible is never identified. Accepting this payout, however, closes the door on separately approaching the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal for a higher amount. In practice, your colleague should be aware that accepting the Rs 2 lakh or Rs 50,000 payout under this scheme generally means giving up the right to separately claim a larger amount before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal.
If a colleague at work is affected by filing a domestic violence complaint, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, an aggrieved person, a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf can file an application before a Magistrate seeking relief for domestic violence.
A friend from Chennai is dealing with a situation involving whether a small business needs to register for GST. What does Indian law say about this?

The current GST registration thresholds — Rs 40 lakh for goods, Rs 20 lakh for services — have been in place since 1 April 2019, when they were raised from the earlier Rs 20 lakh (goods and services) limit. The Rs 40 lakh goods threshold doesn't apply unconditionally, though — certain categories like ice cream, pan masala, tobacco products, and businesses making inter-state taxable supplies of goods are excluded and must register regardless of turnover. In practice, so your friend should check which category the business falls into — if it's goods, services, or a mix, since the two thresholds (Rs 40 lakh vs Rs 20 lakh) and the special-category-state exceptions can materially change the answer.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of retrospective effect of the 2005 amendment isn't handled correctly?

The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) held that a daughter's coparcenary right under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 arises by birth and applies retrospectively, regardless of whether her father was alive on 9 September 2005 when the amendment came into force.
A scammer is using my old resume's email signature to pose as me while contacting recruiters for fake job offers. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers cheating by personation through email, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
If someone in my family is affected by phishing versus direct password theft, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 66D of the IT Act, 2000 covers deception through personation, such as phishing using a spoofed identity to trick a victim, which is analytically distinct from Section 66C's identity theft (which criminalizes actually stealing and using someone's password or credential) — the two sections often apply together when phishing leads to actual credential theft.
If a cheque bounces because the signature on it doesn't match the bank's records rather than because of insufficient funds, does Section 138 of the NI Act still apply?

Yes, it can still apply. Courts have held that Section 138 covers not only dishonour for insufficiency of funds but also cases where the amount exceeds the arrangement made with the bank, and technical reasons such as a signature mismatch have also been held to attract the section, as in Lakshmi Dyechem v. State of Gujarat (2012). The same procedural requirements apply: a written notice within 30 days of learning of the dishonour, and 15 days for the drawer to pay before a complaint can be filed. If the cheque was issued for something other than a legally enforceable debt or liability, such as a gift, Section 138 will not apply.
I run a small trading business in Kerala with annual turnover around ₹3,800,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of goods in Kerala, the threshold is ₹40 lakh for goods or ₹20 lakh for services, since Kerala follows the higher normal-category limit that applies in most Indian states. Since your turnover of ₹3,800,000 is below this ₹4,000,000 threshold, registration isn't mandatory yet, though you can opt for voluntary registration under Section 25(3) if you want to claim input tax credit or issue GST invoices. Note that certain categories — like inter-state suppliers, e-commerce sellers, or those under compulsory registration in Section 24 — must register regardless of turnover.
A cheque for ₹220,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹220,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹440,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding enhanced punishment for institutional heads?

Section 21(2) of the POCSO Act, 2012 prescribes a more severe punishment — imprisonment of up to one year and a fine — for a person in charge of a company or institution who fails to report an offence under Section 19(1) committed by a subordinate under their control.
I'm Meena. I filed an RTI application with the state electricity board 32 days ago and haven't received a reply. What are my options?

Since it's been 32 days with no reply, the PIO has crossed the standard 30-day deadline under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act (add 5 more days if your request went through an Assistant PIO or was transferred under Section 6(3)). At this point, you can file a First Appeal to the First Appellate Authority of the state electricity board within 30 days of the missed deadline. The Appellate Authority is expected to decide the appeal within 30 days, extendable to a total of 45 days.

If you're still not satisfied after the First Appeal (or it isn't decided in time), you can file a Second Appeal to the Central or State Information Commission, generally within 90 days of the First Appellate Authority's order.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools?

The RTE Act's Section 12(1)(c) reservation applies to private unaided non-minority schools, requiring 25% of Class 1 (or equivalent entry-level) seats to go to children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups. Implementation has varied significantly by state, and courts have repeatedly had to direct governments to frame clearer rules to ensure the quota is actually filled rather than left as seats on paper.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on filing an RTI application?

Under Section 7(6) of the RTI Act, 2005, if the Public Information Officer fails to respond within the mandated 30-day period (or 48 hours where the information concerns someone's life or liberty), the information must then be provided to the applicant free of cost, regardless of any fee ordinarily applicable.
My neighbour is dealing with a situation involving PIO's ordinary reply deadline. What does Indian law say about this?
Under Section 7(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, a Public Information Officer must respond to an RTI application within 30 days of receipt.
What is the correct legal procedure someone from my hometown should follow regarding District Commission pecuniary jurisdiction under Indian law?
Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021, a District Commission has jurisdiction over complaints where the consideration paid does not exceed Rs. 50 lakh.
If someone refuses to take a breathalyser test when stopped by police in Jammu and Kashmir, is that treated the same as failing it?

Yes. Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as applied uniformly across India including in Jammu and Kashmir since this is a central law, refusal to undergo a breath test is generally treated as a positive reading for the purpose of prosecution — courts and traffic police treat refusal as an aggravating factor rather than a way to avoid the charge. If prosecuted and convicted for a first offence, the punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to ₹10,000, or both, with a subsequent offence attracting up to 2 years' imprisonment and a fine up to ₹15,000. The legal limit remains 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood, and beyond the breathalyser, police can rely on a blood test under Section 204 of the Act if a breath test is refused or inconclusive.
How does Indian law actually treat repeat conviction for theft, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 303(2) of the BNS, 2023 provides enhanced punishment for a second or subsequent conviction for theft: rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than one year, extendable to five years, along with a fine.
I am Rajesh from Guwahati. I gave Pooja a cheque of Rs. 380000 as repayment for a personal loan, but the cheque bounced due to insufficient funds. What should I do next?

Since the cheque bounced for insufficient funds, this falls under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Your first step is to send Pooja a written legal (demand) notice, and you must do this within 30 days of receiving the bank's cheque-return memo -- don't let that window lapse, as it can affect your ability to prosecute later.

After the notice is served, Pooja gets 15 days to pay the Rs. 380000 back. Only if that 15-day period passes without payment does the cause of action for a criminal complaint arise, and you'd then have 30 days from the end of that period to file the complaint in court. The trial procedure itself is now governed by the BNSS rather than the old CrPC.

I'd suggest consulting a local advocate to draft the notice correctly, since defects in the notice (wrong amount, wrong dates) are a common reason these cases get dismissed.
What are the stamp duty and registration requirements for documents executed in Alternative Dispute Resolution?

Under the Indian Stamp Act and Registration Act, instruments in Alternative Dispute Resolution must be stamped with adequate state-specific stamp duty prior to or at execution. Failure to stamp properly renders the document inadmissible in evidence.
I'm Ashok. Deepa's cheque for Rs. 120000 bounced, and I sent the legal notice 5 days ago. Deepa hasn't responded. What happens now?

Since Deepa received the notice 5 days ago, they still have until the 15-day mark to make the payment. If that period passes with no payment, the offence under Section 138 NI Act is treated as complete, and you get 30 days from the end of the 15-day period to file a criminal complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court.

Keep your proof of notice delivery (courier/postal receipt, or acknowledgment) safe, as you'll need it to show the notice was validly served. If payment does come in during the remaining days, that would resolve the matter without needing to go to court.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving how long you have to file a civil suit. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires a court to dismiss any suit, appeal, or application filed after the prescribed limitation period, even if the other side doesn't raise the delay as a defence. For most suits to recover money or a debt, that period is three years from when the cause of action arose; for recovering possession of immovable property, it's generally twelve years. In practice, for your colleague, the critical date to pin down is exactly when the debt or claim first became due, since the three-year clock (for most money claims) starts running from that point, not from when the dispute escalated.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of theft after preparation to cause hurt isn't handled correctly?

Where a person makes preparation for causing death, hurt, or restraint in order to commit a theft, to escape after committing it, or to retain the stolen property, Section 307 of the BNS, 2023 applies, prescribing rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years plus a fine.
What is the hierarchy of appeals available to an aggrieved party in Alternative Dispute Resolution?

Appellate Hierarchy: In Alternative Dispute Resolution, initial orders from statutory tribunals or trial courts are subject to structured appeals. Statutory Appeal: First appeals generally lie on questions of fact and law to the immediate appellate authority or District/High Court. Subsequent Review: Second appeals or revisions are typically restricted to substantial questions of law, concluding with discretionary review under Article 136 of the Constitution.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of children are exempt from the reporting-failure penalty isn't handled correctly?
Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 exempts a child from the penalty for failure to report under Section 21(1).
A party claims: 'Parents who gifted property to children can never revoke the gift even if children abandon them.' What is the correct legal response to this assertion?

Legal Response: This assertion has no legal standing in Indian jurisprudence. Explanation: Under Section 23 of the Senior Citizens Act, if property was transferred on condition of providing basic care, failure to do so allows the Maintenance Tribunal to declare the transfer void. Advise: Reject the assertion in formal correspondence citing the applicable legal rules. Note: Courts are not fully aligned on whether the maintenance condition must be expressly recorded in the transfer document (Madras High Court) or can be inferred (Bombay High Court, 2026) -- so document the maintenance condition explicitly wherever possible to avoid this dispute.
If my cousin who works in Chennai is affected by waiver of the cooling-off period, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, the Supreme Court held that the six-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is directory, not mandatory, and family courts have discretion to waive it where reconciliation is impossible and disputes such as alimony and custody are genuinely settled.
A cheque for ₹250,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹250,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹500,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
A tenant I know brought up challenging an arbitration award recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The three-month clock under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration Act starts from the date of receipt of the signed award, not from when it was merely delivered or dispatched — a distinction that has actually decided cases, since 'receipt' and 'delivery' aren't treated as automatically the same thing under the Act. In practice, this means the tenant should file the Section 34 application well within the window rather than waiting close to the deadline, since even administrative delays (like a court being on vacation) haven't been accepted as grounds for extension beyond the cap.
What does the law say if a tenant I know is facing how long copyright protection lasts?

Once a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work's copyright term expires — 60 years after the author's death under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — the work enters the public domain and can be freely copied, adapted, or republished without permission, unlike a trademark, which can in principle be renewed forever. In practice, for the tenant, the calculation starts from the beginning of the calendar year *after* the author's death, not the exact death date itself, so it's worth getting that starting point right.
A friend from Chennai is dealing with a situation involving how long copyright protection lasts. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended), copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work generally lasts for the lifetime of the author plus 60 years, counted from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death. For works of joint authorship, the 60-year period runs from the death of whichever author dies last. In practice, in your friend's case, if the work was written by more than one author, the 60-year clock only starts running once the last surviving co-author has passed away, not the first.
What does the law say if a relative going through a difficult time is facing how long a trademark registration lasts?

Under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a trademark registration is valid for 10 years from the date of the original application (not the date the certificate is actually issued), and can be renewed indefinitely for further 10-year periods by filing Form TM-R and paying the prescribed fee before expiry. In practice, in your relative's case, if the renewal deadline has already passed, there's still a one-year window (six months grace plus a further six months) to apply for restoration, but after that the mark can be picked up by someone else.
A friend's mother wants to understand a company's exposure to insolvency proceedings. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The minimum default amount needed to trigger insolvency proceedings against a company under IBC Section 7 is Rs 1 crore, following the increase notified in March 2020 (it was Rs 1 lakh before that). The NCLT is expected to decide, within 14 days of receiving the application, whether the default actually exists based on records or other evidence submitted. In practice, in your friend's mother's case, it's worth knowing that even if the Rs 1 crore threshold is met, the NCLT isn't obligated to admit the case automatically — it can weigh whether the company is otherwise viable.
Someone set up a fake customer-support Twitter handle impersonating my company to collect users' bank details. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers cheating by personation targeting the public through a computer resource, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
Why have Indian courts consistently rejected the premise that 'A domestic violence complaint can only be filed against the husband, not in-laws or other relatives.'?

Judicial Rationale: Courts reject this premise because it undermines public policy and statutory intent in Women and Child Protection. Legal Reasoning: Under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, a domestic incident can be filed against any adult male or female relative who has lived in a shared household with the aggrieved woman. Precedent: Judicial orders hold that statutory mandates cannot be bypassed by customary assumptions.
How does Indian law actually treat enhanced punishment for institutional heads, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 21(2) of the POCSO Act, 2012 prescribes imprisonment up to one year and a fine for a person in charge of an institution who fails to report a subordinate's offence.

What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of notice must align with the tenancy cycle isn't handled correctly?
A 15-day Section 106 notice for a month-to-month tenancy should expire with the end of a month of the tenancy, aligned with the monthly rental cycle.
A factory worker I spoke with asked me about how long you have to file a civil suit — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Missing the limitation period is fatal under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 — courts are bound to dismiss a late suit even without anyone raising the objection. That said, Section 18 allows a written, signed acknowledgment of the debt by the debtor to reset the limitation clock, and Section 5 (for appeals and applications, not fresh suits) lets courts condone delay if there's sufficient cause. In practice, this means the worker can't rely on the court to dismiss an obviously late claim on its own volition if it's actually an appeal or application rather than a fresh suit — the court still has to be asked to apply the bar.
If a client I'm helping is affected by cheating by personation online, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device — pretending to be someone else online to deceive a third party — with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine of up to Rs. 1 lakh, the same punishment prescribed under Section 66C.
In a civil suit where I'm claiming my neighbour built a wall on my land, who has to prove that in court?

Under Section 104 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024, replacing Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872), the general rule is that whoever desires the court to give a judgment as to a legal right dependent on certain facts must prove those facts -- in other words, the burden of proof lies on the person asserting the claim. In your scenario, since you are the one asserting that the wall encroaches on your land, the initial burden of proof lies on you to establish that fact (through survey records, title documents, boundary demarcation, etc.), not on your neighbour to disprove it. This is the same 'he who asserts must prove' principle that existed under the old Evidence Act's Section 101, simply carried forward with renumbering into the BSA -- the substance of the rule hasn't changed.
A shopkeeper in Coimbatore is dealing with a situation involving hit-and-run accident compensation. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 161 of the Motor Vehicles Act, along with the 2022 hit-and-run compensation scheme, entitles victims to Rs 2 lakh (death) or Rs 50,000 (grievous injury) from a dedicated government fund, untraced-driver cases included. This is separate from the criminal side — under BNS Section 106(2), a driver who causes death by rash driving and flees without reporting can face up to 10 years' imprisonment. In practice, in the shopkeeper's situation, it's worth checking whether the driver was ever identified later, since if so, the higher compensation route through the regular insurer/MACT process becomes available instead.

Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding eligibility for mutual consent divorce?

Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows both spouses to file a joint petition for divorce by mutual consent if they have lived separately for at least one year, cannot live together, and mutually agree the marriage should be dissolved.

How can this clause be negotiated or amended to be fair and balanced: "Neither party shall be liable for failure or delay in performance resulting from acts of God, war, pandemic, or events beyond reasonable control."?

Negotiation Strategy: To balance the clause "Neither party shall be liable for failure or delay in performance resulting from acts of God, war, pandemic, or events beyond reasonable control.": This is a force majeure clause governed contractually under Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act. If an unforeseen event falls within the clause, performance is excused. Without an express clause, frustration of contract requires satisfying the stringent impossibility test of Section 56. Proposed Revision: Introduce mutual notice requirements, proportionality to actual damages, and exceptions for force majeure or innocent non-performance.
Regarding 'A commercial client withheld cloud access keys after an invoice dispute.', how do the legal consequences differ depending on the underlying facts?

Branching Legal Outcomes: In Information Technology Law, the legal path diverges significantly based on key variables: (1) The ownership clauses governing proprietary data hosted on the servers; (2) Whether the withholding constitutes unauthorized denial of access under the IT Act; (3) The dispute resolution and suspension clauses in the master services agreement. Comparative Scenarios: If formal documentation and statutory notice exist, summary or expedited remedies may be available. Conversely, if transactions were informal or dispute arises over core facts, comprehensive evidentiary trials are required.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over filing a summary suit for recovery of debt under Order 37 CPC, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for filing a summary suit for recovery of debt under Order 37 CPC is determined by statutory rules under Civil Law. Initial Filing: Ensure claim arises from a bill of exchange, promissory note, or written liquidated contract. Followed by: Draft plaint with specific endorsement under Order 37 CPC. Adjudication Route: Serve summons for judgment on defendant. Concluding with: Defendant must obtain leave to defend from court by showing substantial triable defense. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
The Tribunal gave me a compensation award, but the insurance company hasn't paid yet. What can I do?

Under the Motor Vehicles Act, once the Tribunal makes an award, the insurer is generally required to comply with it within 30 days. If payment isn't made, you can approach the Tribunal for execution of the award, similar to executing a civil court decree -- this can include attaching the insurer's or owner's assets to recover the amount. If the insurer is disputing the award itself rather than simply delaying payment, they would need to have filed an appeal in the High Court within 90 days of the award; if they didn't do that, the award should generally be treated as final and enforceable. I'd recommend going back to the same advocate who handled your claim to file for execution.
A tenant I know asked me about a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Under Section 3(2) read with the rest of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, presents given to the bride or bridegroom at the time of marriage are not treated as 'dowry' as long as they aren't demanded as a consideration for the marriage and are of a customary nature reasonable given the financial status of the person giving them — though these gifts must still be listed in a signed list with descriptions and approximate value, under the Rules made under the Act. In practice, so if the tenant saw or received something like a newspaper notice offering money in exchange for marriage, that itself is a separate punishable offence under Section 4A, independent of whether any dowry was actually exchanged.
How does the principle of direct vs indirect tax protect rights and govern legal relations in India?

The doctrine of direct vs indirect tax serves as an important safeguard under Tax-related legal concepts. Direct taxes like income tax are levied directly on income/wealth of a person, while indirect taxes like GST are levied on the supply of goods and services and generally passed on to the consumer. Its invocation is subject to good faith, statutory limits, and reasonable restrictions. Parties relying on this principle must demonstrate compliance with relevant legal rules.
A shopkeeper in Coimbatore brought up how long copyright protection lasts recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

Anonymous or pseudonymous works, and works first published after an author's death, are treated a bit differently under the Copyright Act, 1957: protection generally runs for 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following first publication, rather than from the date of death, since the date of death may not even be known. In practice, so if the shopkeeper is dealing with an anonymous or posthumously published work, the relevant 60-year clock runs from first publication instead of from any date of death.
Can you explain what Indian law says about the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools, for a small business owner I know?

The RTE Act's Section 12(1)(c) reservation applies to private unaided non-minority schools, requiring 25% of Class 1 (or equivalent entry-level) seats to go to children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups. Implementation has varied significantly by state, and courts have repeatedly had to direct governments to frame clearer rules to ensure the quota is actually filled rather than left as seats on paper. In practice, so if the business owner's application is refused without valid reason despite meeting the eligibility criteria, that refusal can be challenged, since the Supreme Court has upheld this reservation as a constitutionally valid, enforceable right.
If someone in my family is affected by notice period after cheque dishonour, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, once a cheque is dishonoured for insufficiency of funds against a legally enforceable debt, the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the bank's dishonour information.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of compounding a cheque dishonour offence isn't handled correctly?
Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes Section 138 offences compoundable notwithstanding the CrPC, so the parties can settle at any stage and the accused stands acquitted.
Villagers near a proposed mining site want to challenge the environmental clearance granted just 3 weeks ago before construction begins. Is the NGT the right forum?

Yes. Under Section 14 of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, the NGT has jurisdiction over civil cases involving a substantial question relating to the environment arising under the enactments in Schedule I, which includes environmental clearance decisions under environmental protection laws. Since the clearance was granted only 3 weeks ago, the villagers are well within the 6-month limitation period under Section 14(3), so there's no urgency risk from a limitation standpoint — though acting sooner is still wise if they want to seek a stay before construction advances significantly, since the Tribunal can grant interim relief while the main challenge is pending. The NGT is meant to dispose of matters within 6 months and follows principles of natural justice rather than the strict Code of Civil Procedure, making it faster than an ordinary civil suit.
If my brother is affected by whether a small business needs to register for GST, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The turnover figure that matters for GST registration is 'aggregate turnover' — which is broader than just taxable sales, and includes exempt supplies, exports, and inter-state supplies too, all computed PAN-India across every branch of the business, not per state. So a business might look like it's under the Rs 40 lakh goods threshold on taxable sales alone but actually be over it once exempt and export turnover is added in. In practice, this means your brother isn't required to register below the applicable threshold, but doing so voluntarily can still make sense if your brother wants to claim input tax credit on purchases.
A classmate studying law is dealing with a situation involving the second-motion cooling-off period. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 requires a second motion to be moved not before six months and not later than eighteen months after the first motion for mutual consent divorce, during which the court checks that consent remains genuine and the petition has not been withdrawn.
Can a company director be personally prosecuted if a company cheque bounces?

It depends on their role. Under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (which extends liability under Section 138 to companies), every person who was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the company's business at the time the offence was committed can be held liable along with the company -- but liability isn't automatic just from being a director. Courts have held that a complaint must specifically show how a particular director was responsible for the day-to-day affairs of the company; a non-executive or nominee director with no role in the relevant transaction generally cannot be roped in merely by virtue of holding the title of director. Also note: if insolvency proceedings against the company are underway, the Supreme Court has held that the moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code applies to Section 138 proceedings against the corporate debtor itself, though not against the individual directors or signatories personally. This is a fact-specific area, so a company facing this situation should get specific legal advice on which individuals are actually exposed.
A factory worker I spoke with wants to understand a builder delaying possession of a flat. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Under RERA Section 18, a delayed possession doesn't have to be simply absorbed by the buyer — they can choose to exit and claim a full refund plus interest (commonly around 10% per annum), or remain in the project and receive ongoing monthly interest until the flat is actually delivered. The interest rate for staying on is typically tied to the SBI's lending benchmark (MCLR) plus a couple of percentage points, and is fixed by the respective state's RERA authority. In practice, in the worker's case, it's worth comparing the numbers: staying in the project and taking monthly delay-interest may work out differently than withdrawing for a full refund, so it's a real financial choice, not just a formality.
Someone in my apartment complex is dealing with a situation involving maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman. What does Indian law say about this?

The starting point of this entire body of law was the 1985 Shah Bano case, where the Supreme Court held a Muslim husband liable to pay maintenance to his divorced wife under Section 125 CrPC beyond the iddat period; Parliament's response — the 1986 Act — was itself read down by the Court in Danial Latifi (2001) so that it doesn't actually leave a divorced Muslim woman worse off than women of other religions. In practice, for that person, this means the 'reasonable and fair provision' isn't legally limited to three months' worth of support — courts have read it to require enough to sustain her going forward, so it's worth asking for a realistic lump-sum figure rather than a token amount.
What is the correct legal procedure a small business owner I know should follow regarding bond to prevent further violence under Indian law?
Under Section 19(3) of the PWDV Act, 2005, the Magistrate may require the respondent to execute a bond to prevent further domestic violence, treated as an order under Chapter VIII CrPC.
If my cousin in Pune is affected by snatching as a standalone offence, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

As of the new criminal code (BNS, 2023), snatching is dealt with under its own Section 304, separately from ordinary theft. Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding punishment for an ordinary person's failure to report?

Failure to report an offence under Section 19 or Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012 (or failure to record such an offence) is punishable under Section 21(1) with imprisonment of either description for up to six months, a fine, or both.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a daughter's coparcenary rights?

Prior to 2005, daughters had no birthright share in ancestral Mitakshara property; the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 changed that by rewriting Section 6 so daughters become coparceners by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as sons. This is not retrospective in the sense of unwinding partitions completed before 20 December 2004, but the Supreme Court's 2020 ruling in Vineeta Sharma confirmed the right doesn't depend on the father being alive in 2005.
A person i met recently is dealing with a situation involving children are exempt from the reporting-failure penalty. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 explicitly states that the penalty for failure to report under Section 21(1) does not apply to a child under the Act, meaning a minor's silence or failure to report abuse (their own or another's) cannot itself be criminally punished.
A factory worker I spoke with asked me about setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The POSH Act, 2013 requires an Internal Committee wherever an employer has 10 or more employees (Section 4), and where an organisation doesn't cross that threshold, complaints instead go to the Local Committee set up by the District Officer. The Internal Committee's inquiry into a complaint must conclude within 90 days, and non-constitution of the committee is penalised under Section 26. In practice, this means the worker can point the employer to Section 4 of the POSH Act as the legal basis for demanding the committee be set up, rather than this being a discretionary HR policy.
A tenant I know asked me about a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Offences under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 are split into petty (up to 3 years), serious (3 to 7 years), and heinous (7 years or more) categories. Only the heinous category, and only for children between 16 and 18, opens the door to trial as an adult, following a preliminary capacity assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board — a child below 16, regardless of the offence, cannot be tried as an adult under this Act. In practice, this means the tenant shouldn't assume adult trial is automatic just because the offence sounds serious — the specific offence has to carry a real statutory minimum of seven years, not just a high maximum.
I heard something about who can file a consumer complaint that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?

Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows a complaint before a District Commission to be filed not only by the affected consumer but also by a recognised consumer association on their behalf, by one or more consumers representing numerous consumers with the same interest (with the Commission's permission), or by the Central Government, Central Authority, or a State Government; complaints can also be filed electronically.
This clause appears in an agreement I was given: "Goods once sold will not be returned, exchanged, or refunded under any circumstances." What does it mean in practical terms?

Plain Meaning: The clause states: "Goods once sold will not be returned, exchanged, or refunded under any circumstances." Explanation: This is a common retail boilerplate disclaimer. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, such unilateral disclaimers cannot override consumer statutory rights against defective goods, deficiency in service, or unfair trade practices, and are classified as unfair contract terms. Practical Advice: Read this in the context of the entire document, especially definitions, cure periods, and exception clauses.
If a colleague at work is affected by theft after preparation to cause hurt, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Where a person makes preparation for causing death, hurt, or restraint in order to commit a theft, to escape after committing it, or to retain the stolen property, Section 307 of the BNS, 2023 applies, prescribing rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years plus a fine — the most severe of the BNS theft provisions (Sections 303-307).
Does Section 33-B of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act allow either party to unilaterally extend the 3-month limitation under Section 34(3) by simply issuing a legal notice?

Next Step: Consult an advocate and rely exclusively on formal registered documentation and statutory procedures.
What does the law say if a relative going through a difficult time is facing whether a small business needs to register for GST?

Certain categories of suppliers must register for GST from day one, irrespective of turnover — this includes anyone making inter-state taxable supplies, e-commerce operators, and casual taxable persons, among others. For everyone else, the general goods/services turnover thresholds (currently Rs 40 lakh / Rs 20 lakh in most states) determine when registration becomes compulsory. In practice, for your relative, the calculation needs to include all supplies — even exempt sales and any inter-state supply — not just the obviously taxable revenue, since 'aggregate turnover' is defined more broadly than that.
What are the sequential procedural steps for recovering unpaid gratuity from an employer in India?

The process for recovering unpaid gratuity from an employer under Labour and Employment Law requires compliance with established steps: Step 1: Verify 5 years of continuous service in an establishment with 10+ employees. Step 2: Submit Form I in writing to the employer within 30 days of leaving. Step 3: If unpaid or disputed, file Form N before the Controlling Authority. Step 4: Obtain an order and recover dues with statutory simple interest. Formats, fee schedules, and limitation periods must be verified with the official forum rules.
Which court do I approach to file a cheque bounce case against Ashok in Chennai, and is there a time limit?

A Section 138 complaint is filed before the Judicial Magistrate having jurisdiction, typically where the cheque was presented for collection or where the bank branch is located, subject to the specific territorial rules that apply after the 2015 amendment to the NI Act. In practice, this usually means the court within whose jurisdiction Chennai's relevant bank branch falls.

On timing: you must send the demand notice within 30 days of the cheque-return memo, wait 15 days for payment, and then file the complaint within 30 days after that 15-day period ends. Missing these windows can be fatal to the complaint, so it's worth confirming the exact dates with a lawyer before filing.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan?

SARFAESI Section 13 lays out enforcement of security interest in two steps: first, a 60-day demand notice under Section 13(2) once the account is an NPA; then, if unpaid, possession action under Section 13(4). If the bank takes only symbolic possession, the borrower may still occupy the property, but the lender can proceed to auction; physical possession, if needed, is obtained with the help of the District Magistrate under Section 14.
A tenant i spoke with is dealing with a situation involving how a correction request affects the limitation clock. What does Indian law say about this?

Where a party makes a genuine request under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (for correction, interpretation, or an additional award), the three-month limitation under Section 34(3) to challenge the award runs from the date the tribunal disposes of that request rather than from the date of the original award — though a request that is, in substance, a disguised attempt to have the tribunal review the award's merits may not get this benefit.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving being laid off or retrenched from a job. What does Indian law say about this?

Where a business is transferred (Section 25FF) or an undertaking closes down (Section 25FFF), workmen who've completed at least a year of continuous service are entitled to the same notice-and-compensation protection as under Section 25F, treated as if they had been retrenched — unless, in the case of a transfer, the new employer offers continued service on terms no less favourable than before. In practice, for your colleague, the first thing to verify is whether all three Section 25F conditions were actually met — a retrenchment missing even the government notice can be challenged as legally invalid, separate from any dispute about the reason for the layoff.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman?

The starting point of this entire body of law was the 1985 Shah Bano case, where the Supreme Court held a Muslim husband liable to pay maintenance to his divorced wife under Section 125 CrPC beyond the iddat period; Parliament's response — the 1986 Act — was itself read down by the Court in Danial Latifi (2001) so that it doesn't actually leave a divorced Muslim woman worse off than women of other religions.
Someone I met recently wants to understand a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking, or abetting the giving or taking of dowry is punishable with a minimum of five years' imprisonment and a fine of at least Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is higher (courts can impose a lesser sentence only for adequate and special reasons recorded in writing). Section 4 separately punishes merely demanding dowry, directly or indirectly, from the bride's or groom's family, with imprisonment of six months to two years and/or a fine. In practice, in this person's case, if dowry was given only because of pressure or coercion from the other side, the law has been read to shield the giver from being treated as equally culpable as an abettor.
What is the correct legal procedure someone in my family should follow regarding residence orders and the shared household under Indian law?

Section 19 of the PWDV Act, 2005 allows a residence order restraining the respondent from dispossessing the aggrieved person from the shared household, regardless of the respondent's legal interest in it.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on snatching as a standalone offence?

Section 304 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines snatching as theft committed by suddenly, quickly, or forcibly grabbing movable property from a person or their possession. It is a new addition — the IPC had no equivalent section — and the punishment prescribed is imprisonment up to three years, plus a fine.
What does Indian law currently say about a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment?

The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 makes both giving and taking dowry equally punishable — there's no exemption for the party who was pressured into giving it — though in practice, Section 7(3) has been read to protect a person who was compelled to give dowry from being treated as an abettor of the offence. Any agreement to give or take dowry is void under Section 5 and legally unenforceable.
A client I'm helping is dealing with a situation involving whether a small business needs to register for GST. What does Indian law say about this?

Certain categories of suppliers must register for GST from day one, irrespective of turnover — this includes anyone making inter-state taxable supplies, e-commerce operators, and casual taxable persons, among others. For everyone else, the general goods/services turnover thresholds (currently Rs 40 lakh / Rs 20 lakh in most states) determine when registration becomes compulsory. In practice, for your client, the calculation needs to include all supplies — even exempt sales and any inter-state supply — not just the obviously taxable revenue, since 'aggregate turnover' is defined more broadly than that.
How does Indian law actually treat maintenance for elderly parents, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Under Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023, a father or mother unable to maintain themselves can claim a monthly allowance from a child who has sufficient means but neglects or refuses to maintain them.
What does the law say if a client I'm helping is facing anticipatory bail in a case under the SC/ST Atrocities Act?

Section 18 of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 bars anticipatory bail for someone accused of an offence under the Act. However, the Supreme Court clarified in Shajan Skaria v. State of Kerala (2025) that this bar isn't absolute — it applies only where a prima facie case under the Act is actually made out from the complaint and materials on record; if the essential ingredients of the offence aren't disclosed, courts remain free to consider anticipatory bail on its merits. In practice, for your client, the key question a court will ask first is whether the complaint, on its face, actually discloses the elements of an SC/ST Act offence — if it doesn't, the Section 18 bar on anticipatory bail may not apply at all.
What is the correct legal procedure my neighbour should follow regarding waiver of a termination notice by accepting rent under Indian law?
A landlord who serves a Section 106 notice but then accepts rent afterward risks that conduct being treated as a waiver of the notice.
My cousin in Pune asked me about an unresolved e-commerce or online shopping complaint — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines unfair trade practice broadly enough to include disclosing a consumer's personal data without consent, refusing to take back defective goods within the stated period, or not issuing a proper bill — all of which a consumer can complain about, with e-commerce platforms specifically required to acknowledge such complaints within 48 hours. In practice, this means your cousin doesn't have to accept the platform's own dispute-resolution process as final — a formal consumer complaint remains available if the issue isn't resolved within the statutory month.
A tenant i spoke with is dealing with a situation involving compounding a cheque dishonour offence. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes offences under Section 138, including cheque dishonour, compoundable notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure, meaning the complainant and accused can settle at any stage and the accused stands acquitted once the matter is compounded.
If a small business owner I know is affected by police assistance in implementing an order, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 19(5) of the PWDV Act, 2005 allows the Magistrate, while passing a residence or protection order, to direct the officer-in-charge of the nearest police station to give protection to the aggrieved person or assist in implementing the order.
What does the law say if a factory worker I spoke with is facing a company's exposure to insolvency proceedings?

Under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, a financial creditor can apply to the National Company Law Tribunal to start Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor only where the default is at least Rs 1 crore — a threshold that was raised from the original Rs 1 lakh by a government notification in March 2020. In practice, for the worker, the practical checkpoint is whether the outstanding default actually crosses Rs 1 crore — below that, the Section 7 route to the NCLT simply isn't available, though other recovery options may be.
Someone hacked into my friend's Instagram account using her old password and sent scam messages to her contacts pretending to be her. What cybercrime provisions would apply to this in India?

This would likely attract both Section 66C and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's password, electronic signature, or other unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to three years and a fine that may extend to Rs. 1 lakh. Since the person also used that stolen access to pretend to be your friend and deceive her contacts, Section 66D, which punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, would also apply, carrying the same punishment: imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh. In practice, both sections are commonly invoked together in cases where identity theft is used as the means to commit an online impersonation-based fraud.
How does the principle of statutory prospective application protect rights and govern legal relations in India?

The doctrine of statutory prospective application serves as an important safeguard under Criminal Law. Under India's criminal justice framework, substantive offences committed on or after 1 July 2024 are governed prospectively by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and procedural steps by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), ensuring full protection against retrospective criminal liability as guaranteed under Article 20(1) of the Constitution. Its invocation is subject to good faith, statutory limits, and reasonable restrictions. Parties relying on this principle must demonstrate compliance with relevant legal rules.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a builder delaying possession of a flat, for a relative going through a difficult time?

Under RERA Section 18, a delayed possession doesn't have to be simply absorbed by the buyer — they can choose to exit and claim a full refund plus interest (commonly around 10% per annum), or remain in the project and receive ongoing monthly interest until the flat is actually delivered. The interest rate for staying on is typically tied to the SBI's lending benchmark (MCLR) plus a couple of percentage points, and is fixed by the respective state's RERA authority. In practice, in your relative's case, it's worth comparing the numbers: staying in the project and taking monthly delay-interest may work out differently than withdrawing for a full refund, so it's a real financial choice, not just a formality.
A 17-year-old girl has been accused of a heinous assault. Does her gender make any difference to how the preliminary assessment under the Juvenile Justice Act works?

No, gender makes no difference to the Section 15 process. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 applies the preliminary assessment requirement uniformly to any child who has completed 16 years and is accused of a heinous offence, regardless of whether the child is a boy or a girl. The Juvenile Justice Board must assess her mental and physical capacity to have committed the offence, her ability to understand the consequences, and the circumstances of the alleged offence, with expert assistance if required, within 3 months of her first production before the Board. Only if the Board finds she should be tried as an adult under Section 18(3) does the case move to the Children's Court; the rest of the statutory framework, including safeguards during detention and the option of being placed in a place of safety rather than adult prison, also applies without any gender-based distinction.
What is the correct legal procedure an acquaintance from college should follow regarding the 3-month limitation to challenge an award under Indian law?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a challenge to an arbitral award must be made within three months of receiving it, or of a Section 33 correction request being disposed of.
If my neighbour is affected by a daughter's coparcenary rights, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted by the 2005 amendment, makes a daughter a coparcener in her own right by birth — with an equal claim to partition of ancestral property as any son in the family. This position, once disputed across conflicting Supreme Court rulings, was finally settled in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020). In practice, this gives your neighbour standing to file a partition suit in respect of ancestral Mitakshara property, with the same rights her brothers would have.
I received an arbitral award in a shareholder dispute 5 months ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 5 months have passed since you received the award, you are very likely already outside both the initial 3-month window and the extra 30-day condonable period, meaning a Section 34 challenge may no longer be maintainable regardless of the merits of your objection — courts have consistently held there is no scope to condone delay beyond 3 months plus 30 days. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
How does Indian law actually treat punishment for cheque dishonour, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes cheque dishonour punishable with imprisonment of up to two years, a fine that may extend to twice the cheque amount, or both.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding maintenance for a wife, child, or parent?

Under BNSS Section 144 (the successor to CrPC Section 125), a Magistrate can order a person with sufficient income to pay maintenance to a wife, children, or parents who cannot support themselves. This is a secular remedy, applicable regardless of religion, and courts can also grant interim maintenance while the case is pending; if the payer defaults, the law allows for imprisonment of up to a month for each unpaid instalment.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding residence orders and the shared household?

Section 19 of the PWDV Act, 2005 allows the Magistrate to pass a residence order restraining the respondent from dispossessing the aggrieved person from the shared household or otherwise disturbing her possession of it, regardless of whether the respondent has a legal or equitable interest in that household.
What is the correct legal procedure an acquaintance from college should follow regarding filing a second appeal under Indian law?
A Second Appeal to the Central or State Information Commission can be filed under Section 19(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, within 90 days of the FAA's order or the expiry of its decision period.
Does the 15-day notice rule under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act apply to farmland leased out to a tenant farmer as well, or is there a different notice period for agricultural land?

No, a different, longer period applies to agricultural leases. Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 draws a distinction based on the purpose of the lease: a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes is deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable by either the lessor or the lessee by giving six months' notice, whereas a lease for any other purpose (such as residential or commercial use) is on a month-to-month basis, terminable by fifteen days' notice. Since farmland fits the agricultural-purpose category, the six-month notice requirement would apply rather than the fifteen-day one. Keep in mind that Section 106 only applies in the absence of a contrary written contract or local law or usage, and many states have their own tenancy or land reform laws that can override this default rule for agricultural land specifically.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving filing a first appeal. What does Indian law say about this?

If a Public Information Officer fails to respond within the time limit under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, or gives an unsatisfactory decision, the applicant can file a First Appeal to the First Appellate Authority within the same public authority under Section 19(1).
If a classmate studying law is affected by identity theft using stolen credentials, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 punishes fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or other unique identification feature, with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine that may extend to Rs. 1 lakh.
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹35,000/month non-residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 6 months' rent for non-residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹35,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹210,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
If my elder relative is affected by notice period for a month-to-month tenancy, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contrary contract, local law, or usage, a lease for any purpose other than agriculture or manufacturing (such as residential or commercial use) is deemed a month-to-month tenancy, terminable by either party giving 15 days' notice.
Can you explain what Indian law says about anticipatory bail in a case under the SC/ST Atrocities Act, for someone I met recently?

The SC/ST Act's Section 18 bar on anticipatory bail exists to protect complainants from intimidation, but courts scrutinise whether the alleged conduct was actually connected to the victim's caste or tribal identity — knowing someone's SC/ST status while insulting them isn't, by itself, enough; the insult has to be intended to humiliate them because of that identity for the Act's offences, and its bail bar, to apply. In practice, this gives this person's lawyer a specific legal argument to raise at the first hearing: that the alleged remarks or conduct weren't shown to be linked to the complainant's caste identity, which is a requirement for the Act to apply.
What legal traps or risks arise if someone relies on the assumption that 'A contract is legally valid only if it is typed on judicial stamp paper and signed before a notary.'?

Risk Overview: Relying on 'A contract is legally valid only if it is typed on judicial stamp paper and signed before a notary.' exposes individuals to serious legal vulnerabilities in Contract Law. Correct Principle: Under the Indian Contract Act, oral agreements and un-notarized written agreements are valid contracts if made with free consent of competent parties for lawful consideration and object. Stamp duty affects evidentiary admissibility, but is not an element of contract formation. How does Indian law actually treat PIO's ordinary reply deadline, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, a Public Information Officer must respond to an application within 30 days of receipt.
A cheque for ₹45,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹45,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹90,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
What happened to old Section 438 CrPC? I keep seeing 'Section 482' now and I'm confused because I thought 482 was about the High Court's inherent powers.

You're right to be confused -- this is one of the most commonly mixed-up renumbering points in the BNSS. Under the old Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973: Section 438 CrPC dealt with anticipatory bail, and Section 482 CrPC dealt with the High Court's inherent powers (used for quashing FIRs, preventing abuse of court process, etc.). Under the new Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (effective 1 July 2024), the numbers have swapped roles: anticipatory bail is now Section 482 BNSS, and the High Court's inherent powers provision is now Section 528 BNSS. So 'Section 482' today means anticipatory bail, not inherent powers -- but if you're reading anything written or decided before July 2024, 'Section 482' there almost certainly means inherent powers under the old CrPC. Always check which code (CrPC or BNSS) a document is referring to before relying on a section number.
What risks or one-sided obligations does this clause impose: "The property is conveyed on an 'as-is, where-is' basis without any representation or warranty regarding encumbrances or title defects."?

The clause "The property is conveyed on an 'as-is, where-is' basis without any representation or warranty regarding encumbrances or title defects." presents specific commercial and legal risks: This is an 'as-is' disclaimer. While it puts the buyer on notice to conduct due diligence, Indian law under the Transfer of Property Act imposes a statutory duty on the seller to disclose latent material title defects of which the seller is aware and the buyer could not easily discover. The signing party should seek mutual obligations, reasonable liability caps, or specific carve-outs.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding penalty on a defaulting PIO?

Section 20 of the RTI Act, 2005 empowers the Information Commission to impose a penalty on a Public Information Officer for unreasonable delay, malafide denial, or destruction of information, calculated per day of delay, subject to a prescribed maximum.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on being laid off or retrenched from a job?

Before an employer can lawfully retrench a workman under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, three things have to happen together — notice or pay in lieu of notice, compensation at 15 days' average pay per completed year of service, and intimation to the government. Skipping any of these makes the retrenchment procedurally invalid, giving the workman grounds to challenge it, quite apart from whether the underlying reason for the layoff was itself justified.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding expedited reply for life-or-liberty matters?

Where an RTI request concerns information relating to the life or liberty of a person, the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires a response within 48 hours of receipt of the request, rather than the usual 30 days.
Someone in my family is dealing with a situation involving residence orders and the shared household. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 19 of the PWDV Act, 2005 allows the Magistrate to pass a residence order restraining the respondent from dispossessing the aggrieved person from the shared household or otherwise disturbing her possession of it, regardless of whether the respondent has a legal or equitable interest in that household.
What is the hierarchy of appeals available to an aggrieved party in Senior Citizen-related law?

Appellate Hierarchy: In Senior Citizen-related law, initial orders from statutory tribunals or trial courts are subject to structured appeals. Statutory Appeal: First appeals generally lie on questions of fact and law to the immediate appellate authority or District/High Court. Subsequent Review: Second appeals or revisions are typically restricted to substantial questions of law, concluding with discretionary review under Article 136 of the Constitution.
My relative took a business loan of about ₹4,500,000 and has missed EMIs for 5 months. The bank has now classified it as NPA. What can the bank do under SARFAESI?

Once the loan account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset under RBI norms, the bank (as a secured creditor) can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Under Section 13(2), it must first issue a written demand notice giving your relative 60 days to repay the entire outstanding dues on the ₹4,500,000 loan. During this 60-day window, the bank cannot take possession — your relative can repay in full, negotiate a one-time settlement, or file a written representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the notice, which the bank must respond to with reasons within 15 days (though filing a representation does not pause the 60-day clock). If the dues remain unpaid after 60 days, the bank can proceed under Section 13(4) to take possession, manage, or sell the secured property, if necessary seeking assistance from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate under Section 14 to physically take possession. Your relative retains the right to appeal any action taken under Section 13(4) to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on challenging an arbitration award?

Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 sets a strict three-month limitation period to apply to set aside an arbitral award, running from the date the party actually received the award. Courts can extend this by a further 30 days if satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay — but the Supreme Court has held this extra 30-day window is an absolute outer limit, with the words 'but not thereafter' meaning no application can be entertained beyond three months plus 30 days, no matter how compelling the excuse.
