Where a business is transferred (Section 25FF) or an undertaking closes down (Section 25FFF), workmen who've completed at least a year of continuous service are entitled to the same notice-and-compensation protection as under Section 25F, treated as if they had been retrenched — unless, in the case of a transfer, the new employer offers continued service on terms no less favourable than before. In practice, for your client, the first thing to verify is whether all three Section 25F conditions were actually met — a retrenchment missing even the government notice can be challenged as legally invalid, separate from any dispute about the reason for the layoff.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding theft in a dwelling house or place of worship?

Theft committed inside a dwelling house, place of worship, or means of transport is punished more severely under Section 305 of the BNS, 2023, carrying imprisonment of up to seven years plus a fine, rather than the up-to-three-year term under ordinary Section 303 theft.
A factory worker I spoke with is dealing with a situation involving maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman. What does Indian law say about this?

The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 initially appeared to limit a husband's maintenance obligation to just the iddat period (roughly three months), but the Supreme Court in Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) interpreted the Act to mean the husband must make a 'reasonable and fair provision' within the iddat period that is sufficient to sustain the divorced wife for her entire future, not just those three months — effectively extending real protection well beyond the iddat window while keeping the Act's text intact. In practice, in the worker's case, if the amount offered under the 1986 Act seems inadequate, she isn't locked out of also applying under the regular maintenance provision (BNSS Section 144) as long as she hasn't remarried.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over filing an environmental application before the National Green Tribunal (NGT), and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for filing an environmental application before the National Green Tribunal (NGT) is determined by statutory rules under Environmental Law. Initial Filing: Identify substantial question relating to environment arising from implementation of specified enactments. Followed by: Draft application setting out environmental damage and relief sought within 6 months limitation. Adjudication Route: Submit petition before the appropriate Zonal Bench of the NGT. Concluding with: Participate in expert committee inspections and hearings. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
How does Indian law actually treat the pre-2022 position on claim timelines, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Before Section 166(3) came into force on 1 April 2022, the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 did not itself prescribe a strict limitation period for compensation claims, and courts generally took a liberal, claimant-friendly approach to delayed filings given the beneficial nature of the provision.
If a client I'm helping is affected by maintenance for a wife, child, or parent, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 144 BNSS lets a Judicial Magistrate order maintenance for a wife, children, or parents from a person of sufficient means who has neglected or refused to support them. A wife can lose this right if she is living in adultery, unreasonably refuses to live with her husband, or the couple is separated by mutual consent — otherwise the remedy, including interim maintenance, remains available while the case is being decided. In practice, this remedy is available to your client regardless of religion, since maintenance under this section has consistently been treated by courts as a secular right.
If my elder relative is affected by maintenance for a disabled adult child, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 144 BNSS, 2023 is not limited to minor children: it also covers a legitimate or illegitimate major child who is unable to maintain itself because of a physical or mental abnormality or injury, letting such a child claim maintenance from a parent with sufficient means.
My colleague wants to know if compensation awarded here affects her right to separately sue for damages. What does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provide?

No, it doesn't bar a separate civil suit. Under Section 12(2), any compensation or damages ordered by the Magistrate is without prejudice to her right to file a separate suit for compensation or damages. If a civil court later passes a decree for damages in her favour, the amount already paid under the Magistrate's order gets set off against that decree, so she isn't compensated twice for the same harm but also isn't prevented from pursuing a larger civil claim.
A relative going through a difficult time wants to understand gratuity owed after leaving a job. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to any factory, shop, or establishment with 10 or more employees — and once it applies, it keeps applying even if headcount later drops below 10. Gratuity is payable at 15 days' wages for every completed year of service (or any part of a year beyond six months), calculated on the last drawn basic salary plus dearness allowance, with a statutory ceiling of Rs 20 lakh. In practice, so if your relative's employer is delaying payment, the law doesn't require your relative to wait passively — an application in Form I to the employer, and if unresolved, to the Controlling Authority, can push the payment along, with interest accruing on delayed amounts.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a builder delaying possession of a flat?

A homebuyer's remedy for delayed possession sits in Section 18 of RERA, 2016 — it isn't something that has to be separately negotiated into the sale agreement, since it's a statutory right. The choice between a refund-with-interest and monthly delay-interest belongs to the buyer, and the claim is filed before the State Real Estate Regulatory Authority, which is meant to dispose of such complaints within a set timeframe.
What is the correct legal procedure a tenant I spoke with should follow regarding notice must align with the tenancy cycle under Indian law?
A 15-day Section 106 notice for a month-to-month tenancy should expire with the end of a month of the tenancy, aligned with the monthly rental cycle.
My ex created a fake dating profile with my pictures and is chatting with strangers pretending to be me. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers identity theft through unauthorized use of your photos and persona online, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
Under the Domestic Violence Act, can a woman file a case against her mother-in-law or sister-in-law, or only against her husband?

She can file against more than just her husband in certain circumstances. The Act defines "respondent" as any adult male person who is or has been in a domestic relationship with the aggrieved person, but there is a specific proviso: an aggrieved wife or a woman in a relationship in the nature of marriage may also file a complaint against a relative of the husband or male partner. So while the primary respondent contemplated by the definition is an adult male, female relatives of the husband can be brought in as respondents in a complaint alongside him under this proviso, particularly where they are implicated in the acts of domestic violence or in denying her the shared household.
What legal traps or risks arise if someone relies on the assumption that 'Signing an 'as-is' purchase receipt waives all consumer protection rights against defective products.'?

Risk Overview: Relying on 'Signing an 'as-is' purchase receipt waives all consumer protection rights against defective products.' exposes individuals to serious legal vulnerabilities in Consumer Protection. Correct Principle: Boilerplate waivers and disclaimers cannot override statutory consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Sellers remain liable for manufacturing defects, misleading advertisements, and unfair trade practices. Can you explain what Indian law says about hit-and-run accident compensation, for a small business owner I know?

Where the driver in an accident can't be traced, Indian law still provides for compensation: the 2022 scheme under the Motor Vehicles Act sets Rs 2 lakh for a death and Rs 50,000 for grievous injury, paid from the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund. If the vehicle and driver are traced, the compensation figures are different and higher, and the victim can alternatively pursue a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. In practice, so the business owner doesn't need to wait for the police to trace the driver — the hit-and-run scheme exists precisely for cases where the vehicle is never identified.
How does Indian law actually treat National Commission pecuniary jurisdiction, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Under the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules, the National Commission has jurisdiction over complaints where consideration exceeds Rs. 2 crore. Jurisdiction is fixed by consideration paid, not compensation claimed, unlike the older 1986 Act.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of obtaining a protection order isn't handled correctly?

Once satisfied domestic violence occurred, a Magistrate can pass a protection order under Section 18 of the PWDV Act, 2005, restraining the respondent from further violence, aiding it, or contacting the aggrieved person.
What does the law say if someone I met recently is facing maintenance for a wife, child, or parent?

Maintenance claims by a wife, child, or parent are now governed by Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, which replaced CrPC Section 125 from 1 July 2024. It covers a wife (including a divorced wife who hasn't remarried), a minor child, an adult child unable to maintain itself due to disability, and parents unable to maintain themselves — payable by anyone with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to support them. There is no statutory ceiling on the amount, interim maintenance is available during the case, and failure to pay can mean imprisonment of up to one month per default. In practice, for this person, the practical route is to file the maintenance application before a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class, and to ask specifically for interim maintenance so support isn't delayed until the case concludes.
How does Indian law actually treat who can file a consumer complaint, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows a complaint before a District Commission to be filed by the affected consumer, a recognised consumer association on their behalf, consumers representing numerous others with the same interest, or the Central/State Government.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over registering a conveyance or sale deed for immovable property, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for registering a conveyance or sale deed for immovable property is determined by statutory rules under Property Law. Initial Filing: Conduct title due diligence and verify encumbrance certificates for 13 to 30 years. Followed by: Draft the sale deed incorporating complete property boundaries and consideration details. Adjudication Route: Pay prescribed state stamp duty and registration fees. Concluding with: Present deed with two witnesses before the Sub-Registrar of Assurances. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
How does Indian law actually treat notice period for a month-to-month tenancy, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease for any purpose other than agriculture or manufacturing is deemed month-to-month, terminable by 15 days' notice.
A factory worker I spoke with is dealing with a situation involving snatching as a standalone offence. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 304 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines snatching as theft committed by suddenly, quickly, or forcibly grabbing movable property from a person or their possession. It is a new addition — the IPC had no equivalent section — and the punishment prescribed is imprisonment up to three years, plus a fine. In practice, if the case is still pending investigation, the worker should check whether the chargesheet correctly cites Section 304 BNS rather than an old IPC theft section, since the two carry different maximum punishments.
For my health insurance policy: I want to know what interest I'm owed if my claim is paid late. What are my rights under IRDAI rules?

Under IRDAI's regulations, once a claim is delayed beyond the mandated settlement window (typically 30 days from the date the insurer receives the last necessary document, or up to 45 days for certain categories), the insurer is liable to pay you interest on the claim amount at 2% above the applicable bank rate for every day of the delay, without you needing to make a separate application for it — it is meant to be paid automatically along with the settled claim.
What does the law say if my neighbour is facing a builder delaying possession of a flat?

Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) gives a homebuyer an unqualified right to act when a builder fails to hand over possession by the date agreed in the sale agreement: either withdraw from the project and get a full refund with interest, or stay in the project and receive monthly interest compensation for every month of the delay until possession. This right exists regardless of what the builder-buyer agreement itself says. In practice, for your neighbour, the first practical step is to check whether the project was registered with the state RERA authority — this remedy runs through that authority, not a civil court.
My friend's father passed away without a will, and now her brothers are saying she has no claim over the ancestral family property because she is married. Is that correct under Hindu law?

No, that is not correct. Under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as amended by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, a daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son, with the same rights in coparcenary (ancestral) property and subject to the same liabilities. Her marital status makes no difference to this right. The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) confirmed that this right accrues by birth and applies retrospectively — a daughter's coparcenary right does not depend on whether her father was alive on 9 September 2005, the date the amendment came into force. So your friend, as a daughter, has an equal share as a coparcener in the ancestral property, on par with her brothers.
An artist friend of mine is dealing with a situation involving how long a trademark registration lasts. What does Indian law say about this?

The 10-year validity clock for an Indian trademark under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 runs from the original filing date, even if the actual registration certificate takes a couple of years to be issued due to examination or opposition — so a mark filed in 2020 that gets registered only in 2022 is still due for renewal in 2030, not 2032. In practice, so if your artist friend registered the mark but hasn't actually been using it in business for five years since registration, that's a separate vulnerability the Registrar can act on, quite apart from the renewal question.
I was stopped in Karnataka and my breathalyser reading was above the limit for the first time. What's the penalty?

Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), driving with a blood alcohol concentration above 30 mg per 100 ml of blood is an offence regardless of which state you're in, since this is a central enactment applied uniformly, including in Karnataka. For a first-time offence, the punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Your driving licence can also be suspended, and traffic police are empowered to seize the vehicle. If the case goes to court, you'll be tried in the local Traffic Court or Judicial Magistrate's court, and if an accident causing injury or death resulted, you could separately face charges under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 as well.
A salaried individual wants to understand why certain deductions were disallowed. Is there any limitation period or time sensitivity that must be kept in mind here?

Indian law establishes strict statutory limitation periods for initiating legal actions in Tax-related legal concepts. This issue is governed by rules relating to direct vs indirect tax. Direct taxes like income tax are levied directly on income/wealth of a person, while indirect taxes like GST are levied on the supply of goods and services and generally passed on to the consumer. Procedural Rule: Delay in serving statutory notices or filing petitions within the prescribed window can cause the claim to become time-barred. Prompt action and calculation of limitation from the date of cause of action is essential.
What is the key difference between direct vs indirect tax and tax assessment and appeal under Indian law?

direct vs indirect tax and tax assessment and appeal are distinct legal concepts in Tax-related legal concepts. direct vs indirect tax: Direct taxes like income tax are levied directly on income/wealth of a person, while indirect taxes like GST are levied on the supply of goods and services and generally passed on to the consumer. tax assessment and appeal: Taxpayers who disagree with a tax assessment generally have a structured appellate process available to challenge it. The difference lies primarily in the legal threshold, statutory conditions, and consequences. Selecting the proper legal characterization depends on the specific facts and remedies sought.
I'm Ramesh. I filed an RTI application with the district collector's office 32 days ago and haven't received a reply. What are my options?

Since it's been 32 days with no reply, the PIO has crossed the standard 30-day deadline under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act (add 5 more days if your request went through an Assistant PIO or was transferred under Section 6(3)). At this point, you can file a First Appeal to the First Appellate Authority of the district collector's office within 30 days of the missed deadline. The Appellate Authority is expected to decide the appeal within 30 days, extendable to a total of 45 days.

If you're still not satisfied after the First Appeal (or it isn't decided in time), you can file a Second Appeal to the Central or State Information Commission, generally within 90 days of the First Appellate Authority's order.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on maintenance for a wife, child, or parent?

The maintenance provision that used to sit at CrPC Section 125 is now Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023, effective since 1 July 2024, with the substance carried over largely unchanged. Eligible claimants are a wife (including a non-remarried divorced wife), minor children, a disabled adult child, or aged parents; the person ordered to pay must have sufficient means and must have neglected or refused to maintain them.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding compounding a cheque dishonour offence?

Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes offences under Section 138, including cheque dishonour, compoundable notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure, meaning the complainant and accused can settle at any stage and the accused stands acquitted once the matter is compounded.
A relative going through a difficult time is dealing with a situation involving getting married under the Special Marriage Act. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 5 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 requires the couple to file notice with the Marriage Officer of a district where either party has resided for at least 30 days immediately before giving the notice. This residency-and-notice requirement, and the subsequent 30-day public objection window, has been criticised by courts (including remarks by the Supreme Court) as invasive of privacy, though it remains the current legal position. In practice, this means your relative should know objections can only succeed if they fall within Section 4's specific grounds — family disapproval on its own isn't a valid legal objection under this Act.
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹50,000/month non-residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 6 months' rent for non-residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹50,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹300,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
A child aged 14 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, penetrative sexual assault on a child below 16 years of age — which covers a 14-year-old victim — carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 20 years, extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's natural life, along with a mandatory fine. The 2019 amendment specifically raised this minimum from 10 to 20 years for victims under 16 to reflect the heightened severity. Since the accused is described as a relative, the offence may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5/6 if the relative was in a position of trust or authority, in which case the minimum sentence rises further to 20 years up to life, or even the death penalty in the most extreme cases where the court considers it warranted. Since a child under 18 is involved, consent is legally irrelevant, and the case will be tried by a Special POCSO Court, with the trial conducted in a manner sensitive to the child.
My elder relative wants to understand minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 let a member (or members) of a company approach the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for relief where the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner oppressive to some members or prejudicial to the company's or public interest. To even file the petition, Section 244 requires either at least 100 members (or one-tenth of the total membership, whichever is less) or members holding at least one-tenth of the issued share capital, with all calls on their shares paid up. In practice, in your elder relative's case, it's worth documenting the specific conduct carefully, since courts have made clear that mere loss of confidence between shareholders or a single bad business decision doesn't, on its own, count as oppression.
A woman wants to know if she can withdraw her Section 12 application later if she reconciles with her husband.

Yes, she generally can. Since proceedings under Section 12 are civil in nature and initiated at her instance (or on her behalf), she retains the ability to withdraw the application if she chooses to reconcile, similar to how a complainant can withdraw many civil proceedings. In practice, courts will usually record her statement confirming the withdrawal is voluntary before closing the matter. It's worth noting that if reconciliation later breaks down again, she isn't permanently barred from approaching the Magistrate afresh under Section 12 for renewed protection or relief if fresh incidents of domestic violence occur.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding snatching as a standalone offence?

The BNS, which came into force on 1 July 2024 and replaced the IPC, created a new, separate offence of snatching under Section 304. Earlier, a chain- or phone-snatching incident would just be charged as ordinary theft; now it has its own provision, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment and a fine.
I run a small consulting business in Manipur with annual turnover around ₹1,100,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of services in Manipur, the threshold is ₹10 lakh, since these are notified special category states with the lowest limit for both goods and services. Since your turnover of ₹1,100,000 is at or above this ₹1,000,000 threshold, you are required to register for GST.
A temple trust wants to challenge illegal construction encroaching on a protected lakebed, discovered 5 months ago. Which forum should they approach and is there a time limit?

Yes, the National Green Tribunal is the right forum, since encroachment on a protected water body raises a substantial question relating to the environment under Section 14 of the NGT Act, 2010, covering enactments listed in Schedule I such as water and environment protection laws. Under Section 14(3), the application must be filed within 6 months of the cause of action arising — here, roughly the discovery of the encroachment 5 months ago — so the trust still has about a month left, but should file well before that margin closes given how quickly delays can eat into the remaining time. The Tribunal aims to dispose of matters within 6 months of filing and can grant interim orders to halt further construction while the case is pending.
I paid ₹500,000 to a builder in Bhopal for a flat and possession is now 14 months overdue. What does RERA say I'm entitled to?

Under Section 18(1) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, if a promoter fails to hand over possession by the date agreed in the agreement for sale, an allottee has two options. First, the allottee may withdraw from the project and claim a full refund of the amount paid, along with interest. Second, the allottee may choose to remain in the project, in which case the promoter must pay interest for every month of delay until possession is handed over. The exact rate of interest is not fixed by Section 18 itself -- it is prescribed by the rules framed by the relevant State's Real Estate Regulatory Authority, so the applicable state rules should be checked for the precise figure. This is separate from Section 31, which deals with the filing of complaints before the Authority or the Adjudicating Officer, not with penalties or imprisonment.
If my cousin who works in Chennai is affected by enforcing a maintenance charge against a transferee, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 23(2) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 allows a senior citizen with a right to receive maintenance out of an estate to enforce that right against a transferee of the estate who had notice of the right, or where the transfer was gratuitous — though not against a transferee for consideration without notice of the right.
What is the correct legal procedure a tenant I spoke with should follow regarding damages for breach of contract under Indian law?

Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 entitles a party who suffers a breach to compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things, or that both parties knew at the time of contracting was likely to result from the breach — but excludes remote or indirect loss.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of consequence of failing to register a compulsorily registrable document isn't handled correctly?

Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 provides that a document required to be registered under Section 17 but left unregistered cannot be admitted as evidence of the transaction affecting the immovable property, though it may sometimes be used for limited collateral purposes.
I received an arbitral award in an employment severance dispute 11 weeks ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 11 weeks have passed since you received the award, you should still be within, or close to, the permissible window, so you should file your Section 34 application without further delay to be safe, especially since if you're past the initial 3 months you would need to show sufficient cause for the extension and delay itself weakens that showing. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
What is the correct legal procedure an acquaintance from college should follow regarding 60-day timeline for interim maintenance under Indian law?

Once a maintenance application is made under Section 144 BNSS, 2023, the Magistrate is expected, as far as possible, to dispose of the application for interim maintenance within sixty days from the date of service of notice.
If my elder relative is affected by challenging an arbitration award, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 sets a strict three-month limitation period to apply to set aside an arbitral award, running from the date the party actually received the award. Courts can extend this by a further 30 days if satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay — but the Supreme Court has held this extra 30-day window is an absolute outer limit, with the words 'but not thereafter' meaning no application can be entertained beyond three months plus 30 days, no matter how compelling the excuse. In practice, in your elder relative's case, given how strictly courts have enforced the 3-month-plus-30-day cap, it's worth treating that deadline as truly final rather than assuming a court will show flexibility for a good reason.

Review this contract clause: "The party committing breach agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the other party against all third-party losses, costs, and attorney fees." Is this enforceable under Indian law, and what are its boundaries?

Regarding the clause "The party committing breach agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the other party against all third-party losses, costs, and attorney fees.": This is an indemnity clause. Under Indian law, indemnity protects the promisee from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or any third party. Unlike ordinary damages under Section 73 which require proof of actual foreseeable loss, an indemnity obligation is triggered upon accrual of liability. Enforceability depends on statutory compliance, public policy, and whether the restriction is unconscionable or penal.
A child aged 9 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, penetrative sexual assault on a child below 16 years of age — which covers a 9-year-old victim — carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 20 years, extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's natural life, along with a mandatory fine. The 2019 amendment specifically raised this minimum from 10 to 20 years for victims under 16 to reflect the heightened severity. Since the accused is described as a relative, the offence may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5/6 if the relative was in a position of trust or authority, in which case the minimum sentence rises further to 20 years up to life, or even the death penalty in the most extreme cases where the court considers it warranted. Since a child under 18 is involved, consent is legally irrelevant, and the case will be tried by a Special POCSO Court, with the trial conducted in a manner sensitive to the child.
Does Section 80 of the Registration Act require every sale deed to be registered within 24 hours of signing, regardless of value?

I'm not able to verify a Section 80 in the Registration Act, 1908 imposing a 24-hour registration deadline. What I can confirm is that Section 23 of the Act generally requires a document to be presented for registration within four months of its execution, and Section 17 sets out which documents must be registered at all (based on the type of instrument and, for some clauses, a Rs. 100 value threshold) — a strict 24-hour deadline regardless of value doesn't match what I can verify. Please check the current bare act before relying on this.
What does the law say if a relative going through a difficult time is facing filing an RTI application?

The RTI Act, 2005 doesn't fix its fee amount directly in the statute itself — Section 27(2)(b) instead empowers the Central and State Governments to prescribe the fee through rules, which is why the exact amount (though commonly Rs 10) can differ slightly between the central government and individual states. In practice, for your relative, if the application is to a central government body, Rs 10 is the correct fee — anything meaningfully higher being demanded is worth double-checking against the applicable RTI Rules.
This clause appears in an agreement I was given: "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement." What does it mean in practical terms?

Plain Meaning: The clause states: "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement." Explanation: This is an express 'time of the essence' clause. Under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, failure to perform by the agreed deadline renders the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. However, courts evaluate party conduct and extensions to ascertain if time was genuinely intended to be of the essence. Practical Advice: Read this in the context of the entire document, especially definitions, cure periods, and exception clauses.
What does Indian law currently say about maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman?

Despite the existence of the 1986 Act specific to Muslim women, courts (including the Allahabad High Court in several recent rulings) have reaffirmed that a divorced Muslim woman retains the right to seek ongoing maintenance under the secular maintenance provision (now BNSS Section 144, earlier CrPC Section 125) as long as she hasn't remarried — the 1986 Act doesn't bar her from that route, since Parliament never explicitly excluded it.
What is the correct legal procedure a classmate studying law should follow regarding cheque dishonoured due to signature mismatch under Indian law?
Section 138 is not limited to dishonour for insufficient funds; dishonour for signature mismatch has also been held to attract the section, as in Lakshmi Dyechem v. State of Gujarat (2012).
Can agreements and documentation under Property Law be validly executed using electronic or digital signatures in India?

Electronic Signatures: Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, electronic agreements and digital signatures are legally recognized, except for specified excluded instruments such as wills, negotiable instruments, and immovable property conveyances.
What is the correct legal procedure a friend of mine should follow regarding filing a first appeal under Indian law?
If a PIO fails to respond in time under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, or gives an unsatisfactory decision, the applicant can file a First Appeal under Section 19(1).
What risks or one-sided obligations does this clause impose: "Goods once sold will not be returned, exchanged, or refunded under any circumstances."?

The clause "Goods once sold will not be returned, exchanged, or refunded under any circumstances." presents specific commercial and legal risks: This is a common retail boilerplate disclaimer. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, such unilateral disclaimers cannot override consumer statutory rights against defective goods, deficiency in service, or unfair trade practices, and are classified as unfair contract terms. The signing party should seek mutual obligations, reasonable liability caps, or specific carve-outs.
A builder in Amritsar changed my flat's possession date without my consent, and I paid ₹600,000 so far. Can I get out of the deal?

Yes. Under Section 18(1) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, if the builder unilaterally changes the agreed possession date, you have the right to withdraw from the project. You must exercise this within 45 days of the changed date being communicated (or of the original committed date passing without possession), and on withdrawal, the builder is required to refund the full ₹600,000 you've paid, along with interest at the rate notified by the Amritsar state's RERA authority. Alternatively, instead of withdrawing, you can choose to remain in the project and claim monthly interest compensation for the delay until possession is actually handed over. Either way, you should file your complaint with the relevant state RERA authority to enforce this right, since the builder is unlikely to volunteer the refund without a formal demand or complaint.
What is the correct legal procedure a colleague at work should follow regarding retrospective effect of the 2005 amendment under Indian law?

The Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) held that a daughter's coparcenary right under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 arises by birth and applies retrospectively, regardless of whether her father was alive on 9 September 2005 when the amendment came into force.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of maintenance for a disabled adult child isn't handled correctly?

Section 144 BNSS, 2023 also covers a legitimate or illegitimate major child who is unable to maintain itself because of a physical or mental abnormality or injury, letting such a child claim maintenance from a parent with sufficient means.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of the second-motion cooling-off period isn't handled correctly?
Section 13B(2) requires the second motion to be moved between six and eighteen months after the first, so the court can confirm consent remains genuine.
What is the correct legal procedure my elder relative should follow regarding repeat conviction for theft under Indian law?

Section 303(2) of the BNS, 2023 provides enhanced punishment for a second or subsequent conviction for theft: rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than one year, extendable to five years, along with a fine.
If someone in my family is affected by transfers other than gifts covered by Section 23, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 is not limited to gifts — the phrase "transferred by way of gift or otherwise" has been read by courts to also cover release deeds, settlements, and sales made on the understanding that the senior citizen would be looked after, so such transfers can equally be challenged if the condition is breached.
If a child who was sexually abused tells a friend about it but the friend, also a minor, doesn't report it to anyone out of fear, can the friend be punished under the POCSO Act for not reporting?

No. Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 expressly states that the punishment for failure to report under Section 21(1) shall not apply to a child under the Act. Since the friend who stayed silent is also a minor, they are exempted from the penal consequences of not reporting, even though Section 19 technically imposes the reporting obligation on "any person." This carve-out reflects the recognition that children may lack the capacity, safety, or understanding to report such incidents themselves, and the law does not want to criminalize a child's silence or fear.
What does the law say if a startup founder I'm advising is facing gratuity owed after leaving a job?

Continuous service for gratuity purposes under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 isn't broken by sanctioned leave, sickness, accident, strike, or a lock-out not caused by the employee's own fault — all of that still counts toward the five-year threshold. Once eligibility is established, the employer must determine and pay the gratuity amount on its own, without the employee having to demand it, though in practice an application in Form I is commonly filed if there's a delay. In practice, for the founder, the key number to check first is total continuous service — if it's just short of five years, it's worth seeing whether the employer counted paid leave, sick leave, or authorised absence correctly, since those shouldn't break continuity.
A company keeps sending me marketing emails even after I asked them to stop and delete my data. What are my rights under Indian data protection law?

Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act), consent is the primary legal basis a company (a 'Data Fiduciary') needs to process your personal data, and that consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous. Critically, you have the right to withdraw consent at any time, and withdrawal is supposed to be as easy as giving consent was in the first place -- once you withdraw, the company must stop processing your data for that purpose within a reasonable time, unless the processing is required for a legal obligation independent of your consent. If they continue anyway, you can file a complaint with the company's Grievance Officer first (a company processing personal data is required to designate one and publish their contact details), and if unresolved, escalate it to the Data Protection Board of India once it's operational for your case. Note that as of the DPDP Rules 2025 (notified 13 November 2025), businesses have a compliance deadline of 13 May 2027 to fully implement the operational requirements, so enforcement mechanisms and Board processes are still being phased in -- but the underlying consent and withdrawal rights under the Act itself apply from commencement. This is general information; if this is a larger unresolved grievance, check the Ministry of Electronics and IT's current guidance for the exact complaint process available at the time you're reading this, since implementation details are still evolving.
I need legal help: A client gave me a cheque that bounced, and I want to recover the money. What should I do next?

Factual Assessment Required: While Banking and Financial Law provides remedies, your inquiry omits critical facts necessary to determine your exact legal rights: (1) The date on the bank return memo; (2) Whether statutory demand notice was dispatched within 30 days of receiving the memo; (3) Whether 15 days elapsed without payment. Legal Impact: Outcomes under Indian law turn heavily on these specific thresholds. Clarifying these details and reviewing documentary evidence with an advocate is the essential first step.
A cheque for ₹480,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹480,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹960,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
If a client I'm helping is affected by the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The RTE Act, 2009's 25% reservation for economically weaker and disadvantaged children in private unaided schools was upheld as constitutionally valid by the Supreme Court in 2012. Eligibility is usually tied to family income and residence within a set distance from the school (commonly 1 km for primary classes), though the exact income cut-offs and application process vary by state. In practice, in your client's case, if the school is trying to charge any fee for a seat claimed under this quota, that's not permitted — the seat is meant to be entirely free, with the school reimbursed separately by the government.
Can a child who doesn't report their own sexual abuse be punished under POCSO for failing to report it?

No. Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 expressly states that the mandatory reporting penalty under Section 21(1) does not apply to a child (defined under the Act as anyone below 18) -- so a child victim, or a child who witnesses abuse of another child, cannot be prosecuted for failing to report it themselves. The reporting obligation and its penalty for non-compliance are aimed at adults -- family members, teachers, doctors, neighbours, or anyone else who becomes aware of the abuse -- not at the child.
What is the correct legal procedure a person I met recently should follow regarding PIO's ordinary reply deadline under Indian law?
Under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, a Public Information Officer must respond to an application within 30 days of receipt.
My relative took a loan taken by his late father, now inherited of about ₹4,000,000 and has missed EMIs for 5 months. The bank has now classified it as NPA. What can the bank do under SARFAESI?

Once the loan account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset under RBI norms, the bank (as a secured creditor) can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Under Section 13(2), it must first issue a written demand notice giving your relative 60 days to repay the entire outstanding dues on the ₹4,000,000 loan. During this 60-day window, the bank cannot take possession — your relative can repay in full, negotiate a one-time settlement, or file a written representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the notice, which the bank must respond to with reasons within 15 days (though filing a representation does not pause the 60-day clock). If the dues remain unpaid after 60 days, the bank can proceed under Section 13(4) to take possession, manage, or sell the secured property, if necessary seeking assistance from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate under Section 14 to physically take possession. Your relative retains the right to appeal any action taken under Section 13(4) to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding filing against relatives of the husband?

While the PWDV Act, 2005 primarily defines a "respondent" as an adult male in a domestic relationship with the aggrieved person, a specific proviso allows an aggrieved wife or a woman in a relationship in the nature of marriage to also file a complaint against a relative of the husband or male partner, so female in-laws can be named as respondents alongside the husband.
How do the missing details in 'A woman is being harassed for dowry demands and threatened with expulsion from home.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Women and Child Protection statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) The date of marriage and whether offences under dowry prohibition laws occurred within seven years; (2) Whether formal complaints have been lodged with the local women's cell or protection officer; (3) Documentary evidence of bank transfers, text messages, or domestic incidents. A salaried individual wants to understand why certain deductions were disallowed. What conflicting legal principles arise in this situation, and how are such tensions reconciled under Indian law?

This scenario presents a tension between party autonomy and statutory protection under Tax-related legal concepts. While parties have the freedom to contract and conduct business, statutory rules governing direct vs indirect tax impose mandatory public policy safeguards: Direct taxes like income tax are levied directly on income/wealth of a person, while indirect taxes like GST are levied on the supply of goods and services and generally passed on to the consumer. Indian courts reconcile these interests by upholding reasonable contractual expectations while strictly refusing to enforce terms that violate statutory mandates or natural justice.
A person i met recently is dealing with a situation involving revoking a conditional gift for failure to maintain. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 23(1) of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 provides that where a senior citizen transfers property by gift or otherwise on condition that the transferee provide basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee fails or refuses to do so, the transfer is deemed made by fraud, coercion, or undue influence and can be declared void by the Maintenance Tribunal at the transferor's option.
If my neighbour is affected by the second-motion cooling-off period, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 requires a second motion to be moved not before six months and not later than eighteen months after the first motion for mutual consent divorce, during which the court checks that consent remains genuine and the petition has not been withdrawn.
How do the missing details in 'A vendor failed to deliver components on time, causing our firm major financial losses.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Contract Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) Whether time was expressly made of the essence in the contract; (2) Whether indirect or consequential losses were within mutual contemplation when contracting; (3) Whether notice of breach and cure opportunity was provided. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of the six-month limitation on accident compensation claims isn't handled correctly?

Section 166(3), inserted by the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 and in force from 1 April 2022, bars a compensation claim before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal unless filed within six months of the accident; this provision is currently under constitutional challenge before the Supreme Court.
A shopkeeper in Coimbatore is dealing with a situation involving gratuity owed after leaving a job. What does Indian law say about this?

Continuous service for gratuity purposes under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 isn't broken by sanctioned leave, sickness, accident, strike, or a lock-out not caused by the employee's own fault — all of that still counts toward the five-year threshold. Once eligibility is established, the employer must determine and pay the gratuity amount on its own, without the employee having to demand it, though in practice an application in Form I is commonly filed if there's a delay. In practice, for the shopkeeper, the key number to check first is total continuous service — if it's just short of five years, it's worth seeing whether the employer counted paid leave, sick leave, or authorised absence correctly, since those shouldn't break continuity.
A shopkeeper in coimbatore is dealing with a situation involving enhanced punishment for institutional heads. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 21(2) of the POCSO Act, 2012 prescribes a more severe punishment — imprisonment of up to one year and a fine — for a person in charge of a company or institution who fails to report an offence under Section 19(1) committed by a subordinate under their control.
If my sister-in-law is affected by hit-and-run accident compensation, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Where the driver in an accident can't be traced, Indian law still provides for compensation: the 2022 scheme under the Motor Vehicles Act sets Rs 2 lakh for a death and Rs 50,000 for grievous injury, paid from the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund. If the vehicle and driver are traced, the compensation figures are different and higher, and the victim can alternatively pursue a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. In practice, so your sister-in-law doesn't need to wait for the police to trace the driver — the hit-and-run scheme exists precisely for cases where the vehicle is never identified.
Can you explain what Indian law says about how long copyright protection lasts, for a former employee I used to manage?

Anonymous or pseudonymous works, and works first published after an author's death, are treated a bit differently under the Copyright Act, 1957: protection generally runs for 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following first publication, rather than from the date of death, since the date of death may not even be known. In practice, so if the former employee is dealing with an anonymous or posthumously published work, the relevant 60-year clock runs from first publication instead of from any date of death.
A factory worker I spoke with asked me about anticipatory bail in a case under the SC/ST Atrocities Act — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Under Section 18 read with Section 18A of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, no preliminary inquiry is required before registering an FIR, and anticipatory bail is barred once the Act applies — but the Supreme Court's more recent rulings have insisted that this bar only kicks in when a prima facie offence under the Act is genuinely disclosed, not for every complaint that merely invokes the Act's sections. In practice, so the worker should be aware that even where an FIR cites the SC/ST Act, that alone doesn't automatically shut the door on anticipatory bail — recent Supreme Court rulings require the court to look closer first.
A party claims: 'A domestic violence complaint can only be filed against the husband, not in-laws or other relatives.' What is the correct legal response to this assertion?

Legal Response: This assertion has no legal standing in Indian jurisprudence. Explanation: Under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, a domestic incident can be filed against any adult male or female relative who has lived in a shared household with the aggrieved woman. Advise: Reject the assertion in formal correspondence citing the applicable legal rules.
What is the correct legal procedure a friend of mine should follow regarding waiver of the cooling-off period under Indian law?

In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, the Supreme Court held the six-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is directory, not mandatory, and can be waived in appropriate cases.
What are the stamp duty and registration requirements for documents executed in Women and Child Protection?

Under the Indian Stamp Act and Registration Act, instruments in Women and Child Protection must be stamped with adequate state-specific stamp duty prior to or at execution. Failure to stamp properly renders the document inadmissible in evidence.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding a company's exposure to insolvency proceedings?

The minimum default amount needed to trigger insolvency proceedings against a company under IBC Section 7 is Rs 1 crore, following the increase notified in March 2020 (it was Rs 1 lakh before that). The NCLT is expected to decide, within 14 days of receiving the application, whether the default actually exists based on records or other evidence submitted.
A 16-year-old has been accused of a serious offence that carries a maximum sentence of 5 years. Does the preliminary assessment under Section 15 of the Juvenile Justice Act apply to him?

No, not necessarily. Section 15 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 applies specifically to 'heinous offences,' which under Section 2(33) of the Act are defined as offences for which the minimum punishment under the Indian Penal Code (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) or any other law is imprisonment of 7 years or more. An offence carrying a maximum sentence of 5 years does not meet this threshold — it would typically fall under the category of a 'serious offence' (punishable with imprisonment between 3 and 7 years) rather than a 'heinous offence.' As a result, the Section 15 preliminary assessment process (which can lead to trial as an adult) would not apply to him for this charge, and his case would proceed through the ordinary Juvenile Justice Board process applicable to children in conflict with law, which focuses on rehabilitation rather than adult-style trial and sentencing.
How does Indian law actually treat filing a domestic violence complaint, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Under Section 12 of the PWDV Act, 2005, an aggrieved person, a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf can file an application before a Magistrate.

How can this clause be negotiated or amended to be fair and balanced: "The property is conveyed on an 'as-is, where-is' basis without any representation or warranty regarding encumbrances or title defects."?

Negotiation Strategy: To balance the clause "The property is conveyed on an 'as-is, where-is' basis without any representation or warranty regarding encumbrances or title defects.": This is an 'as-is' disclaimer. While it puts the buyer on notice to conduct due diligence, Indian law under the Transfer of Property Act imposes a statutory duty on the seller to disclose latent material title defects of which the seller is aware and the buyer could not easily discover. Proposed Revision: Introduce mutual notice requirements, proportionality to actual damages, and exceptions for force majeure or innocent non-performance.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding enforcing a maintenance charge against a transferee?

Section 23(2) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 allows a senior citizen with a right to receive maintenance out of an estate to enforce that right against a transferee of the estate who had notice of the right, or where the transfer was gratuitous — though not against a transferee for consideration without notice of the right.
How do the missing details in 'Someone accused me of cheating in a business deal and threatened to get me arrested.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Criminal Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) Whether there was fraudulent intention at inception or merely a breach of contract; (2) Whether an FIR or private complaint has actually been registered; (3) The documentary evidence of payments and communications. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
A small business owner i know is dealing with a situation involving eligibility for mutual consent divorce. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows both spouses to file a joint petition for divorce by mutual consent if they have lived separately for at least one year, cannot live together, and mutually agree the marriage should be dissolved.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan?

The 60-day window in a SARFAESI demand notice under Section 13(2) is not a formality — the Supreme Court has held that a bank's failure to properly respond to a borrower's written objection during this period is a fatal procedural flaw that can void the entire subsequent possession or sale action. The borrower can also approach the Debt Recovery Tribunal to challenge steps taken under Section 13(4).
A small business owner i know is dealing with a situation involving transfers other than gifts covered by Section 23. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 is not limited to gifts — the phrase "transferred by way of gift or otherwise" has been read by courts to also cover release deeds, settlements, and sales made on the understanding that the senior citizen would be looked after, so such transfers can equally be challenged if the condition is breached.
I heard something about District Commission pecuniary jurisdiction that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?

Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021, a District Commission has jurisdiction over complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed Rs. 50 lakh.
My brother brought up minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The NCLT's powers once it finds oppression or mismanagement under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are broad — it can order the majority to buy out the minority's shares, set aside prejudicial agreements, remove directors, order forensic audits, or even restructure how the company is managed going forward, though courts have clarified that a director's removal, an isolated bad decision, or simply a breakdown of trust between shareholders doesn't by itself amount to oppression. In practice, this means your brother can ask the NCLT not just for a declaration that the conduct was wrong, but for concrete relief — like an order forcing the majority to buy out your brother's shares at a fair price.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment?

Any offer or advertisement in a newspaper or other media of money or property as consideration for a person's marriage is itself a punishable offence under Section 4A of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, carrying imprisonment of six months to five years, or a fine, or both — separate from and in addition to the offences of actually giving, taking, or demanding dowry.
A woman wants to know if this Act covers live-in relationships or only married couples. What does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provide?

Yes — the Act is not limited to legally married couples. It defines a 'domestic relationship' broadly to include relationships 'in the nature of marriage,' which courts have interpreted to cover many live-in relationships meeting certain criteria (such as a reasonable period of cohabitation and a shared household). A woman in such a relationship can file an application under Section 12 just as a married woman can, seeking protection orders, residence orders, or monetary relief.
How should a citizen prepare to handle initiating statutory action for cheque dishonour smoothly?

Practical Guide: Handling initiating statutory action for cheque dishonour in Banking and Financial Law involves: Step 1: Present cheque within 3 months validity and obtain bank return memo. Step 2: Dispatch formal statutory demand notice within 30 days of receiving return memo. Step 3: Grant the drawer 15 days from receipt of notice to make payment. Step 4: If unpaid, file criminal complaint before Judicial Magistrate within 30 days thereafter. Can either spouse simply withdraw their consent after the first motion for mutual consent divorce has already been filed, or is the couple bound to go through with the divorce at that point?

Either party can withdraw their consent at any point before the divorce decree is actually passed by the court. Under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, on the second motion the court must be satisfied that the parties have not withdrawn their consent, and if either party does withdraw consent before the decree is granted, the court cannot pass a decree of mutual consent divorce. This is a well-recognized feature of the mutual consent route: unlike other fault-based grounds for divorce, mutual consent divorce requires the consent of both spouses to remain intact right up until the final decree, and its withdrawal at any stage before that will halt the proceedings under this specific provision (though the other spouse may then need to pursue divorce on other statutory grounds if they still wish to separate).
A 17-year-old accused of a heinous offence has no family able to afford a lawyer for the preliminary assessment stage. Is legal representation guaranteed?

Yes — the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 guarantees legal aid throughout proceedings, including during the Section 15 preliminary assessment. The child is entitled to free legal assistance through the Legal Services Authority, and the Board must ensure the child's family, along with legal counsel, receive a copy of the assessment order once passed. The preliminary assessment itself is not a trial but a capacity evaluation — examining the child's mental and physical ability to have committed the offence, understanding of consequences, and surrounding circumstances — to be completed within 3 months of the child's first production before the Board, before any decision is made on whether to try him as an adult under Section 18(3).
A friend's mother brought up a passport being impounded or seized recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The Supreme Court has clarified that only the passport authority under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967 has the power to impound a passport — the police, by contrast, can only seize a passport as a document or property under general criminal procedure powers, but cannot themselves impound it, since the Passports Act is a specific law that overrides the general provision. In practice, this means your friend's mother has a 30-day window to appeal the impounding order to the appropriate appellate authority, so that deadline shouldn't be missed while gathering other paperwork.
What risks or one-sided obligations does this clause impose: "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement."?

The clause "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement." presents specific commercial and legal risks: This is an express 'time of the essence' clause. Under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, failure to perform by the agreed deadline renders the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. However, courts evaluate party conduct and extensions to ascertain if time was genuinely intended to be of the essence. The signing party should seek mutual obligations, reasonable liability caps, or specific carve-outs.
A colleague at work wants to understand anticipatory bail. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Since 1 July 2024, pre-arrest (anticipatory) bail applications are filed under BNSS Section 482, not the earlier CrPC Section 438. The core protection is the same — a person apprehending arrest in a non-bailable case can approach the Sessions Court or High Court in advance — but Section 482(4) carves out an exception, denying this relief to those accused of raping a girl under sixteen or of gang-raping a woman under eighteen. In practice, so if your colleague is filing this application now, it should specifically cite BNSS Section 482, since courts have been rejecting applications that are still worded under the repealed CrPC Section 438.
A startup founder I'm advising brought up how long a trademark registration lasts recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The 10-year validity clock for an Indian trademark under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 runs from the original filing date, even if the actual registration certificate takes a couple of years to be issued due to examination or opposition — so a mark filed in 2020 that gets registered only in 2022 is still due for renewal in 2030, not 2032. In practice, so if the founder registered the mark but hasn't actually been using it in business for five years since registration, that's a separate vulnerability the Registrar can act on, quite apart from the renewal question.

Depending on the exact conduct, relevant provisions could include Section 66C (identity theft, up to 3 years plus fine) or Section 66 (computer-related offences), but I don't want to state a specific section number or punishment I haven't confirmed.
