A friend's mother brought up a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 makes both giving and taking dowry equally punishable — there's no exemption for the party who was pressured into giving it — though in practice, Section 7(3) has been read to protect a person who was compelled to give dowry from being treated as an abettor of the offence. Any agreement to give or take dowry is void under Section 5 and legally unenforceable. In practice, this means your friend's mother should keep any list of wedding gifts that were genuinely voluntary and customary, since properly documented gifts (not demanded as a marriage condition) fall outside the definition of dowry.
If a factory worker I spoke with is affected by being laid off or retrenched from a job, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Where a business is transferred (Section 25FF) or an undertaking closes down (Section 25FFF), workmen who've completed at least a year of continuous service are entitled to the same notice-and-compensation protection as under Section 25F, treated as if they had been retrenched — unless, in the case of a transfer, the new employer offers continued service on terms no less favourable than before. In practice, for the worker, the first thing to verify is whether all three Section 25F conditions were actually met — a retrenchment missing even the government notice can be challenged as legally invalid, separate from any dispute about the reason for the layoff.
Is there a Section 45 in the POCSO Act, 2012 that requires a child victim to formally file a written complaint before any investigation can begin?

I can't verify a Section 45 in the POCSO Act, 2012 imposing that requirement, and this doesn't match the framework I can confirm. Section 19 of the Act instead places the reporting duty on any adult who has knowledge of or apprehends an offence, and Section 21(3) specifically exempts a child from penalty for not reporting — the Act is generally structured to lower barriers to reporting on a child's behalf, not to require a formal written complaint from the child before action can be taken. A residents' welfare association wants to stop a builder from cutting down a protected grove for a parking lot, work that started 5 months ago. Should they go to the NGT or a regular civil court?

The National Green Tribunal is the appropriate forum. Under Section 14 of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, the NGT has jurisdiction over civil cases involving substantial environmental questions arising under the enactments in Schedule I, including matters relating to forest and tree protection. Since the felling started 5 months ago, they are still within the 6-month limitation period under Section 14(3), though with limited time to spare, so they should file promptly, ideally seeking interim relief to halt further felling while the matter is pending, since Tribunal proceedings aren't bound by the ordinary Code of Civil Procedure and can move faster than a regular civil suit.
Someone used my Aadhaar-linked digital signature without my knowledge to sign an online loan application. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers unauthorized use of your unique identification feature, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
Are there mandatory pre-litigation steps or notices required before approaching a court under Women and Child Protection?

In Women and Child Protection, several statutory frameworks mandate pre-litigation steps. For government bodies or statutory claims, advance notice of 30 to 60 days is frequently mandatory. Commercial disputes and certain family matters require attempting pre-litigation mediation unless urgent interim relief is claimed.

I filed an RTI application two months ago and never received a reply from the Public Information Officer. What is the legally prescribed timeline I should have received a response in, and what can I do now?

Under Section 7(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, a Public Information Officer is required to respond to an RTI application within 30 days of receipt (this extends to 48 hours where information concerns the life or liberty of a person). Since more than 30 days have passed without a reply, Section 7(2) deems this a refusal, and you can file a First Appeal under Section 19(1) to the First Appellate Authority within the same public authority. There is no strict limitation period fixed in the Act itself for the first appeal, though the customary practice followed by most public authorities is 30 days from when the reply was due, with the FAA empowered to condone delay for sufficient cause. The FAA must decide the appeal within 30 days, extendable to a maximum of 45 days with recorded reasons, under Section 19(6).
My friend endured abuse two years ago but only recently found the strength to consider filing. Is she too late to use Section 12?

No, she isn't too late. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 does not impose a strict limitation period on when a Section 12 application must be filed relative to when the abuse occurred — this is different from many other laws that have fixed filing deadlines. She can file even years after the incidents, particularly if the domestic relationship or its effects are ongoing or relevant to her present circumstances. Once she does file, the Magistrate is required under Section 12(5) to endeavour to dispose of the application within 60 days from the first hearing, so while there's no bar on when she starts, the process itself is meant to move quickly once she does.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of filing a second appeal isn't handled correctly?
A Second Appeal to the Central or State Information Commission can be filed under Section 19(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, within 90 days of the FAA's order or the expiry of its decision period.
A cheque for ₹1,500,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹1,500,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹3,000,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of charging both identity theft and online cheating together isn't handled correctly?
Where stolen credentials (Section 66C) are used to impersonate the victim and deceive a third party, both Section 66C and Section 66D of the IT Act, 2000 can be invoked together for the same conduct.
Can you explain what Indian law says about anticipatory bail, for my cousin in Pune?

Since 1 July 2024, pre-arrest (anticipatory) bail applications are filed under BNSS Section 482, not the earlier CrPC Section 438. The core protection is the same — a person apprehending arrest in a non-bailable case can approach the Sessions Court or High Court in advance — but Section 482(4) carves out an exception, denying this relief to those accused of raping a girl under sixteen or of gang-raping a woman under eighteen. In practice, so if your cousin is filing this application now, it should specifically cite BNSS Section 482, since courts have been rejecting applications that are still worded under the repealed CrPC Section 438.
If my cousin in Pune is affected by a company's exposure to insolvency proceedings, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The Rs 1 crore default threshold for Section 7 IBC applications applies specifically to corporate debtors, and where multiple financial creditors are owed money that collectively crosses the threshold, the default of one creditor can, in certain cases, be aggregated with others owed by the same corporate debtor to meet the minimum. In practice, so if your cousin's claim alone falls short of Rs 1 crore, checking whether it can be combined with other creditors owed by the same company is worth exploring.
I run a small consulting business in Delhi with annual turnover around ₹2,100,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of services in Delhi, the threshold is ₹40 lakh for goods or ₹20 lakh for services, since Delhi follows the higher normal-category limit that applies in most Indian states. Since your turnover of ₹2,100,000 is at or above this ₹2,000,000 threshold, you are required to register for GST.
For the matter 'A commercial client withheld cloud access keys after an invoice dispute.', what specific documentary checklist must be prepared to resolve the factual ambiguity?

Documentary Checklist: To resolve ambiguity in this Information Technology Law issue, compile: (1) The ownership clauses governing proprietary data hosted on the servers; (2) Whether the withholding constitutes unauthorized denial of access under the IT Act; (3) The dispute resolution and suspension clauses in the master services agreement. Next Step: Cross-reference these documents with relevant statutory timelines before issuing formal communications.

I'm Meena. I noticed an online purchase made using my debit card details without my knowledge for Rs. 90000, and I reported it to my bank about 150 hours after I got the bank's SMS alert (a bit later than I'd have liked). Will I get the full amount back?

Reporting after roughly 6.2 days puts you past the 3-working-day zero-liability window (note: this is 3 WORKING days, not a flat 72 hours -- the two aren't the same measure). You may still fall in the 'limited liability' category if you reported within 4-7 working days, where your liability is capped -- typically Rs. 5,000, Rs. 10,000, or Rs. 25,000 depending on your account/card type, rather than the full Rs. 90000.

Beyond 7 working days, liability depends on the bank's own board-approved policy, so it can vary. File your complaint in writing regardless, since even outside these windows banks are required to investigate and can still credit some or all of the amount depending on the facts.
What prerequisites and documentation are essential before initiating initiating statutory action for cheque dishonour?

Prerequisites & Jurisdiction: In Banking and Financial Law, before undertaking initiating statutory action for cheque dishonour, applicants must ensure: (1) Mandatory preparation: Present cheque within 3 months validity and obtain bank return memo. (2) Initial compliance: Dispatch formal statutory demand notice within 30 days of receiving return memo. Subsequent procedure: Grant the drawer 15 days from receipt of notice to make payment. If unpaid, file criminal complaint before Judicial Magistrate within 30 days thereafter. Careful preparation of documentary evidence avoids summary dismissal.
A shopkeeper in Coimbatore asked me about anticipatory bail — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Anticipatory bail is now governed by Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, which replaced Section 438 of the old CrPC from 1 July 2024. It lets a person who reasonably fears arrest for a non-bailable offence apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for a direction that, if arrested, they be released on bail. Under Section 482(4), this remedy is barred for anyone accused of raping a woman under sixteen, or of gang rape of a woman under eighteen. In practice, for the shopkeeper, the first thing to confirm is which offence is alleged — if it falls under the Section 482(4) exception, anticipatory bail simply isn't available and a different strategy is needed.
A friend's mother wants to understand getting married under the Special Marriage Act. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The Special Marriage Act, 1954's 30-day notice-and-objection process, under Sections 5 to 8, applies to civil marriages performed outside religious rites — commonly used for inter-faith or inter-caste couples. The notice is entered in the Marriage Notice Book and displayed publicly; objections can only be raised on the grounds set out in Section 4 of the Act (such as an existing marriage or being below the minimum age of 21 for the groom and 18 for the bride), not on unrelated personal grounds. In practice, in your friend's mother's case, since courts have flagged privacy concerns about the public 30-day notice, it's worth checking with the local Marriage Officer whether any recent court directions in that state limit how the notice is displayed.
What does the law say if my elder relative is facing maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman?

The starting point of this entire body of law was the 1985 Shah Bano case, where the Supreme Court held a Muslim husband liable to pay maintenance to his divorced wife under Section 125 CrPC beyond the iddat period; Parliament's response — the 1986 Act — was itself read down by the Court in Danial Latifi (2001) so that it doesn't actually leave a divorced Muslim woman worse off than women of other religions. In practice, for your elder relative, this means the 'reasonable and fair provision' isn't legally limited to three months' worth of support — courts have read it to require enough to sustain her going forward, so it's worth asking for a realistic lump-sum figure rather than a token amount.
A colleague at work wants to understand a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Under the SARFAESI Act, a bank cannot simply seize mortgaged property the moment a loan goes into default — Section 13(2) requires a formal 60-day demand notice first, and only if the borrower fails to pay within that window can the lender proceed to symbolic or physical possession under Section 13(4). Within those 60 days, the borrower can also file a written objection under Section 13(3A), which the bank is legally required to consider and respond to with reasons. In practice, in your colleague's case, it's worth checking whether the bank actually responded in writing to any objection raised, since courts have voided possession actions where the bank simply ignored the borrower's reply.
I received an arbitral award in an IT services contract 3 months and 10 days ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 3 months and 10 days have passed since you received the award, you should still be within, or close to, the permissible window, so you should file your Section 34 application without further delay to be safe, especially since if you're past the initial 3 months you would need to show sufficient cause for the extension and delay itself weakens that showing. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
A small business owner I know asked me about getting married under the Special Marriage Act — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Section 5 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 requires the couple to file notice with the Marriage Officer of a district where either party has resided for at least 30 days immediately before giving the notice. This residency-and-notice requirement, and the subsequent 30-day public objection window, has been criticised by courts (including remarks by the Supreme Court) as invasive of privacy, though it remains the current legal position. In practice, this means the business owner should know objections can only succeed if they fall within Section 4's specific grounds — family disapproval on its own isn't a valid legal objection under this Act.
What is the correct legal procedure someone in my family should follow regarding liquidated damages versus proving actual loss under Indian law?

Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs liquidated damages where a contract itself fixes a sum payable on breach; courts can award reasonable compensation up to that stipulated amount, and unlike a claim under Section 73, strict proof of actual loss is not required to invoke Section 74.
What is the correct legal procedure my elder relative should follow regarding compounding a cheque dishonour offence under Indian law?
Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes Section 138 offences compoundable notwithstanding the CrPC, so the parties can settle at any stage and the accused stands acquitted.
Someone created a fake Instagram profile using my photos and is messaging my relatives asking for money in my name. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers impersonation to extract money from your relatives, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
How can this clause be negotiated or amended to be fair and balanced: "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement."?

Negotiation Strategy: To balance the clause "Time is of the essence with respect to all performance obligations under this agreement.": This is an express 'time of the essence' clause. Under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, failure to perform by the agreed deadline renders the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. However, courts evaluate party conduct and extensions to ascertain if time was genuinely intended to be of the essence. Proposed Revision: Introduce mutual notice requirements, proportionality to actual damages, and exceptions for force majeure or innocent non-performance.
A small business owner I know wants to understand a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 makes both giving and taking dowry equally punishable — there's no exemption for the party who was pressured into giving it — though in practice, Section 7(3) has been read to protect a person who was compelled to give dowry from being treated as an abettor of the offence. Any agreement to give or take dowry is void under Section 5 and legally unenforceable. In practice, this means the business owner should keep any list of wedding gifts that were genuinely voluntary and customary, since properly documented gifts (not demanded as a marriage condition) fall outside the definition of dowry.
A tenant i spoke with is dealing with a situation involving withdrawing consent before the decree. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, either spouse can withdraw their consent to a mutual consent divorce at any point before the decree is actually passed; if consent is withdrawn, the court cannot grant the mutual consent divorce and the case cannot proceed on that basis.
A friend from Chennai asked me about hit-and-run accident compensation — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Section 161 of the Motor Vehicles Act, along with the 2022 hit-and-run compensation scheme, entitles victims to Rs 2 lakh (death) or Rs 50,000 (grievous injury) from a dedicated government fund, untraced-driver cases included. This is separate from the criminal side — under BNS Section 106(2), a driver who causes death by rash driving and flees without reporting can face up to 10 years' imprisonment. In practice, in your friend's situation, it's worth checking whether the driver was ever identified later, since if so, the higher compensation route through the regular insurer/MACT process becomes available instead.
A tenant I know brought up how long a trademark registration lasts recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

A lapsed trademark isn't necessarily gone forever — Section 25(4) allows an application for restoration within one year of expiry (after a six-month grace period from the expiry date itself), on payment of a restoration fee, though this window is strict and missing it means the mark goes back into the pool for anyone else to register. In practice, this means the tenant should file the renewal well before expiry — Form TM-R with the fee — since the process is described as far less involved than the original registration itself.
What's the difference between 'coparcenary property' and 'self-acquired property' when it comes to a daughter's inheritance rights?

This distinction matters a lot in practice. Coparcenary (or ancestral) property is property inherited up to four generations of male lineage in an undivided Hindu family under Mitakshara law, in which a coparcener acquires a right by birth -- this is what Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act (as amended in 2005) gives daughters equal rights in, alongside sons. Self-acquired property, by contrast, is property a person has earned or bought themselves (or inherited from someone other than through the coparcenary line, and treated as their separate property). A person is free to will away their self-acquired property to anyone they choose; a daughter's statutory coparcenary right under Section 6 doesn't apply to it. If the self-acquired property owner dies without a will (intestate), Section 8 and the Class I heirs schedule of the Hindu Succession Act apply instead, under which sons and daughters (along with the widow and mother) inherit equally as Class I heirs regardless of the coparcenary rules. So depending on whether a specific property is ancestral/coparcenary or self-acquired, a different provision of the Act governs a daughter's share.
How does Indian law actually treat State Commission pecuniary jurisdiction, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Per the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a State Commission has jurisdiction where the consideration paid exceeds Rs. 50 lakh but does not exceed Rs. 2 crore.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of identity theft using stolen credentials isn't handled correctly?

Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000 punishes fraudulently using another's electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature, with imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding how long you have to file a civil suit?

Missing the limitation period is fatal under Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 — courts are bound to dismiss a late suit even without anyone raising the objection. That said, Section 18 allows a written, signed acknowledgment of the debt by the debtor to reset the limitation clock, and Section 5 (for appeals and applications, not fresh suits) lets courts condone delay if there's sufficient cause.
My coworker logged into my company email using a password he guessed and sent messages pretending to be me to a client. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers unauthorized use of your password combined with impersonation to deceive a client, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
I received an arbitral award in a partnership dissolution matter 6 weeks ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 6 weeks have passed since you received the award, you should still be within, or close to, the permissible window, so you should file your Section 34 application without further delay to be safe, especially since if you're past the initial 3 months you would need to show sufficient cause for the extension and delay itself weakens that showing. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.

Review this contract clause: "Neither party shall be liable for failure or delay in performance resulting from acts of God, war, pandemic, or events beyond reasonable control." Is this enforceable under Indian law, and what are its boundaries?

Regarding the clause "Neither party shall be liable for failure or delay in performance resulting from acts of God, war, pandemic, or events beyond reasonable control.": This is a force majeure clause governed contractually under Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act. If an unforeseen event falls within the clause, performance is excused. Without an express clause, frustration of contract requires satisfying the stringent impossibility test of Section 56. Enforceability depends on statutory compliance, public policy, and whether the restriction is unconscionable or penal.
How does Indian law actually treat timeline for deciding a first appeal, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
The First Appellate Authority must dispose of a first appeal within 30 days, extendable to a maximum of 45 days with recorded reasons, under Section 19(6) of the RTI Act, 2005.
A community group wants compensation for a chemical spill that happened 8 months ago. Can this be taken to the National Green Tribunal, and is there a time limit?

Yes, environmental matters like this fall within the National Green Tribunal's civil jurisdiction under Section 14 of the NGT Act, 2010, covering substantial questions relating to the environment arising under the enactments listed in Schedule I. However, Section 14(3) requires that the application be made within 6 months from the date the cause of action first arose. Since your situation is already close to or has crossed this window, you should act promptly — the Tribunal does have limited power to condone a further delay of up to 60 days beyond the 6 months if you can show sufficient cause for the delay, but there's no guarantee of that extension being granted, so filing without further delay is advisable. The Tribunal is also mandated to try to dispose of applications within 6 months of filing.
Can agreements and documentation under Family Law be validly executed using electronic or digital signatures in India?

Electronic Signatures: Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, electronic agreements and digital signatures are legally recognized, except for specified excluded instruments such as wills, negotiable instruments, and immovable property conveyances.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of timeline for deciding a first appeal isn't handled correctly?
The First Appellate Authority must dispose of a first appeal within 30 days, extendable to a maximum of 45 days with recorded reasons, under Section 19(6) of the RTI Act, 2005.
What does the law say if a relative going through a difficult time is facing snatching as a standalone offence?

Under Section 304 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, "snatching" is now a standalone offence — it did not exist as a separate crime under the old Indian Penal Code, where it was prosecuted simply as theft. It covers suddenly, quickly, or forcibly seizing movable property from a person or their possession, and it carries imprisonment of up to three years along with a fine. In practice, since the offence didn't exist as a distinct crime before July 2024, it matters whether your relative's incident happened before or after that date, as that decides which law and which FIR section applies.
My brother is dealing with a situation involving gratuity owed after leaving a job. What does Indian law say about this?

Five years of continuous service is the general eligibility threshold for gratuity under the 1972 Act, but this bar disappears entirely if the employee's service ends because of death or disablement — their nominee or they themselves become entitled regardless of tenure. The formula for full-time employees is last drawn wages divided by 26, multiplied by 15, multiplied by the number of completed years of service, subject to the Rs 20 lakh statutory cap. In practice, this means your brother doesn't need five years of service at all if the separation was due to death or disablement — that eligibility bar is waived entirely in those situations.
What does the law say if a client I'm helping is facing a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment?

Under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking, or abetting the giving or taking of dowry is punishable with a minimum of five years' imprisonment and a fine of at least Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is higher (courts can impose a lesser sentence only for adequate and special reasons recorded in writing). Section 4 separately punishes merely demanding dowry, directly or indirectly, from the bride's or groom's family, with imprisonment of six months to two years and/or a fine. In practice, in your client's case, if dowry was given only because of pressure or coercion from the other side, the law has been read to shield the giver from being treated as equally culpable as an abettor.
My elder relative is dealing with a situation involving punishment for an ordinary person's failure to report. What does Indian law say about this?

Failure to report an offence under Section 19 or Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012 (or failure to record such an offence) is punishable under Section 21(1) with imprisonment of either description for up to six months, a fine, or both.
A tenant I know is dealing with a situation involving getting married under the Special Marriage Act. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Sections 5 to 7 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954, a couple wanting a civil marriage must first give written notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one of them has lived for the preceding 30 days. The Marriage Officer then publishes this notice for 30 days, during which anyone can object on specific statutory grounds (such as bigamy or a prohibited relationship); if no valid objection is raised, the marriage can be solemnised after that period. In practice, for the tenant, the residency requirement means the notice has to be filed with the Marriage Officer of a district where one of them has actually lived for the preceding 30 days — not just anywhere convenient.
My relative took a personal loan secured against a flat of about ₹3,200,000 and has missed EMIs for 5 months. The bank has now classified it as NPA. What can the bank do under SARFAESI?

Once the loan account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset under RBI norms, the bank (as a secured creditor) can invoke the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Under Section 13(2), it must first issue a written demand notice giving your relative 60 days to repay the entire outstanding dues on the ₹3,200,000 loan. During this 60-day window, the bank cannot take possession — your relative can repay in full, negotiate a one-time settlement, or file a written representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the notice, which the bank must respond to with reasons within 15 days (though filing a representation does not pause the 60-day clock). If the dues remain unpaid after 60 days, the bank can proceed under Section 13(4) to take possession, manage, or sell the secured property, if necessary seeking assistance from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate under Section 14 to physically take possession. Your relative retains the right to appeal any action taken under Section 13(4) to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
I'm a schoolteacher and I suspect a student is being sexually abused by a family member, but I'm not 100% sure and I'm worried about the consequences of being wrong. What does the law require of me?

Under Section 19(1) of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, 'any person' who has apprehension that an offence under the Act is likely to be committed, or has knowledge that such an offence has been committed, is legally required to report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police -- the standard is apprehension or knowledge, not certainty or proof. You do not need to be sure; the law is built around the idea that early reporting protects the child, and investigation/verification is the police's job, not yours. If you fail to report, Section 21(1) POCSO makes that a punishable offence with imprisonment up to six months, a fine, or both -- and if you're in charge of an institution (like a school), failing to report an offence by someone under your control can attract up to one year's imprisonment plus a fine under Section 21(2). On the flip side, Section 22 protects people who report in good faith even if the complaint later turns out to be unfounded, so you won't be penalised for a genuine, good-faith report that doesn't pan out. Given what you're describing, the legally required step is to report your suspicion to the police or SJPU -- you're not expected to investigate or confirm it yourself first.
A person used my old Aadhaar photo to open a fraudulent SIM card in my name. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers unauthorized use of your unique identification feature to obtain a SIM, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
If my elder relative is affected by cheque dishonoured due to signature mismatch, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Courts have held that Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is not limited to dishonour for insufficiency of funds; a dishonour for signature mismatch has also been held to attract the section, as in Lakshmi Dyechem v. State of Gujarat (2012), provided the other statutory conditions (notice, payment window, existing debt) are met.

If I file an application under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act asking the tribunal to correct a computational error in the award, does that pause or restart the three-month clock for filing a Section 34 challenge?

It can shift when the clock starts, but there is some nuance here. Section 34(3) provides two alternative starting points for the three-month limitation period: ordinarily it runs from the date the party receives the arbitral award, but where a request has been made under Section 33 (for correction, interpretation, or an additional award), it instead runs from the date the arbitral tribunal disposes of that Section 33 request. However, courts have noted conflicting authority on what counts as a genuine Section 33 application for this purpose — a request that is, in substance, an attempt to have the tribunal review the award on its merits (rather than a limited correction) may not be treated as shifting the limitation start date. So a routine, valid correction request should move the trigger date to the disposal of that request, but a disguised merits challenge dressed up as a Section 33 application may not get you that benefit — this is an area where the specific facts of your correction request matter.

A contractor was supposed to deliver custom-made furniture to my office by a certain date, but delivered it three months late, causing me to lose a client who needed the office ready by then. Can I claim this lost business as damages under Indian contract law?

It depends on whether that loss falls within what Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 allows you to recover. Section 73 entitles the party who suffers a breach to compensation for loss or damage that either naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or that both parties knew, at the time of contracting, was likely to result from the breach — but expressly excludes any remote or indirect loss. This reflects the same principle as the English case of Hadley v. Baxendale (1845), on which Section 73 is based. If you never told the contractor that timely delivery was critical to retaining a specific client, the lost business might be treated as too remote or unforeseeable to recover. However, if the contractor knew (or you had specifically informed them) that a client's onboarding depended on the office being ready by that date, the lost business could fall within the second limb of Section 73, as a loss the parties knew was likely to result from delay. You would still need to prove the actual loss suffered, since damages under Section 73 are compensatory, not automatic.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a passport being impounded or seized?

Under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967, a passport can be impounded or revoked by the passport authority on specific statutory grounds — including where the passport was obtained by suppressing material facts or giving false information, or where a court has issued a warrant, summons, or an order prohibiting the holder's departure from India in a pending case. The passport authority is required to record its reasons in writing and, on demand, share a copy with the holder (unless doing so would harm India's security or foreign relations).
Someone in my apartment complex asked me about maintenance for a wife, child, or parent — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Maintenance claims by a wife, child, or parent are now governed by Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, which replaced CrPC Section 125 from 1 July 2024. It covers a wife (including a divorced wife who hasn't remarried), a minor child, an adult child unable to maintain itself due to disability, and parents unable to maintain themselves — payable by anyone with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to support them. There is no statutory ceiling on the amount, interim maintenance is available during the case, and failure to pay can mean imprisonment of up to one month per default. In practice, for that person, the practical route is to file the maintenance application before a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class, and to ask specifically for interim maintenance so support isn't delayed until the case concludes.
If a tenant I know is affected by an agreement or contract involving a minor, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

A contract entered into with a minor has no legal existence at all under Indian law — it's void ab initio, not simply cancellable, following the century-old Privy Council precedent in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903). Because there was never a valid agreement in the first place, Section 65 of the Contract Act (which allows restitution when an agreement is later discovered to be void) doesn't even apply, and the minor generally cannot be compelled to return anything received. In practice, in the tenant's case, even if the other party claims they were misled about the age involved, that misrepresentation doesn't revive the contract or bind the minor to it.
A cheque for ₹30,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹30,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹60,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
What is the correct legal procedure a client I'm helping should follow regarding consequence of not challenging an award in time under Indian law?
If an award is not challenged within the Section 34(3) limitation period, it attains finality under Section 35 and becomes enforceable as a decree under Section 36.
If a friend's mother is affected by an unresolved e-commerce or online shopping complaint, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The 2019 Consumer Protection Act extended consumer rights explicitly to online transactions, and the accompanying e-commerce rules require platforms to acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and resolve them within a month. Alongside this, the Act created a Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) with the power to investigate unfair trade practices, order recalls of unsafe goods, and penalise misleading advertisements. In practice, in your friend's mother's case, the right forum depends on the value of the goods or services — the District Consumer Commission can hear complaints up to Rs 1 crore, with higher-value matters going to the State or National Commission.
A tenant I know brought up whether a small business needs to register for GST recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The current GST registration thresholds — Rs 40 lakh for goods, Rs 20 lakh for services — have been in place since 1 April 2019, when they were raised from the earlier Rs 20 lakh (goods and services) limit. The Rs 40 lakh goods threshold doesn't apply unconditionally, though — certain categories like ice cream, pan masala, tobacco products, and businesses making inter-state taxable supplies of goods are excluded and must register regardless of turnover. In practice, so the tenant should check which category the business falls into — if it's goods, services, or a mix, since the two thresholds (Rs 40 lakh vs Rs 20 lakh) and the special-category-state exceptions can materially change the answer.
What are the sequential procedural steps for seeking temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC in India?

The process for seeking temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC under Court Procedures requires compliance with established steps: Step 1: Establish prima facie case in favor of claimant. Step 2: Demonstrate that balance of convenience lies in granting injunction. Step 3: Prove that irreparable injury will occur if interim protection is not granted. Step 4: Court may grant ex-parte or inter-partes temporary injunction. Formats, fee schedules, and limitation periods must be verified with the official forum rules.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment, for a friend from Chennai?

Under Section 3(2) read with the rest of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, presents given to the bride or bridegroom at the time of marriage are not treated as 'dowry' as long as they aren't demanded as a consideration for the marriage and are of a customary nature reasonable given the financial status of the person giving them — though these gifts must still be listed in a signed list with descriptions and approximate value, under the Rules made under the Act. In practice, so if your friend saw or received something like a newspaper notice offering money in exchange for marriage, that itself is a separate punishable offence under Section 4A, independent of whether any dowry was actually exchanged.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over recovering unpaid gratuity from an employer, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for recovering unpaid gratuity from an employer is determined by statutory rules under Labour and Employment Law. Initial Filing: Verify 5 years of continuous service in an establishment with 10+ employees. Followed by: Submit Form I in writing to the employer within 30 days of leaving. Adjudication Route: If unpaid or disputed, file Form N before the Controlling Authority. Concluding with: Obtain an order and recover dues with statutory simple interest. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹12,000/month residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 2 months' rent for residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹12,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹24,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
Does the Hindu Succession Act's 2005 amendment on daughters' property rights apply to Muslim or Christian families too?

No. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (and its 2005 amendment giving daughters equal coparcenary rights) applies specifically to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs, as defined under Section 2 of the Act -- it is a personal law statute, not a general civil law. Muslim inheritance in India is governed by Muslim personal law (largely uncodified, following Hanafi or Shia schools depending on the sect, with shares fixed by religious law rather than equal division), and the Christian and Parsi communities are governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which has its own distinct rules for intestate succession. So a Muslim or Christian daughter's inheritance rights need to be assessed under the specific personal law or statute that applies to her family, not under the Hindu Succession Act.
What is the correct legal procedure my elder relative should follow regarding filing against relatives of the husband under Indian law?
A proviso to the PWDV Act, 2005 lets an aggrieved wife file a complaint against a relative of the husband, not only the husband himself.
What is the correct legal procedure my cousin who works in Chennai should follow regarding the second-motion cooling-off period under Indian law?
Section 13B(2) requires the second motion to be moved between six and eighteen months after the first, so the court can confirm consent remains genuine.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding express versus implied maintenance condition?

Courts differ on whether the maintenance condition under Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 must be explicitly written into the transfer deed: the Kerala High Court's full bench has held the condition must be expressly stated, while other High Courts (including the Bombay High Court) have allowed the condition to be inferred from the relationship and surrounding circumstances even without an express clause.

I'm Sanjay. I noticed a fraudulent net-banking transfer out of my account for Rs. 150000, and I reported it to my bank about 40 hours after I got the bank's SMS alert. Will I get the full amount back?

If this transaction happened due to a third-party breach and you weren't at fault, reporting it within roughly 1.7 day(s) generally falls inside the RBI's zero-liability window. The actual rule is framed as '3 WORKING days' from the bank's alert, not a flat 72 hours -- working days exclude weekends and bank holidays, so it's worth confirming the exact working-day count with your bank rather than just counting clock hours.

If you qualify for zero liability, the bank is expected to credit the disputed Rs. 150000 back to your account within 10 working days of your complaint, without waiting for its own investigation or any insurance claim to conclude, and the complaint itself should be resolved within 90 days. Do file a written complaint with the bank (not just a phone call) and keep the acknowledgment.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of penalty on a defaulting PIO isn't handled correctly?
Section 20 of the RTI Act, 2005 empowers the Information Commission to impose a per-day penalty on a PIO for unreasonable delay, malafide denial, or destruction of information.
The consumer commission ruled against the company I complained about, and they've been ordered to pay me. But now they've filed an appeal and haven't paid anything. Is that allowed?

Yes, they're allowed to appeal -- a District Commission order can be appealed to the State Commission within 45 days. However, under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the appellant (the party against whom the amount was ordered) is required to pre-deposit 50% of that ordered amount before the appeal can even be entertained. So if they've genuinely filed a valid appeal, they should have deposited that 50% -- it's worth checking with the commission's registry whether that pre-deposit was actually made, since an appeal without it typically shouldn't be admitted.
What prerequisites and documentation are essential before initiating registering a conveyance or sale deed for immovable property?

Prerequisites & Jurisdiction: In Property Law, before undertaking registering a conveyance or sale deed for immovable property, applicants must ensure: (1) Mandatory preparation: Conduct title due diligence and verify encumbrance certificates for 13 to 30 years. (2) Initial compliance: Draft the sale deed incorporating complete property boundaries and consideration details. Subsequent procedure: Pay prescribed state stamp duty and registration fees. Present deed with two witnesses before the Sub-Registrar of Assurances. Careful preparation of documentary evidence avoids summary dismissal.
Villagers want to stop illegal sand mining along the riverbank discovered a month ago. Can this be taken to the National Green Tribunal, and is there a time limit?

Yes, illegal sand mining is a well-established category of case before the National Green Tribunal. Under Section 14 of the NGT Act, 2010, the Tribunal has jurisdiction over civil cases raising a substantial question relating to the environment, arising under the mining, water, and environment protection enactments listed in Schedule I — illegal riverbed sand mining falls squarely within this, and the NGT has passed numerous orders halting unauthorized mining and directing restoration of riverbeds in similar cases. Under Section 14(3), the application must be filed within 6 months of the cause of action arising; since the mining was discovered only a month ago, the villagers are well within this window and can act with some room to prepare their evidence, such as photographs, witness statements, and any available mining lease documentation, before filing. The Tribunal can also grant an interim order to halt the mining while the main application is pending.
How does Indian law actually treat notice must align with the tenancy cycle, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
A 15-day Section 106 notice for a month-to-month tenancy should expire with the end of a month of the tenancy, aligned with the monthly rental cycle.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over registering an FIR under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for registering an FIR under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) is determined by statutory rules under Criminal Procedure. Initial Filing: Report the cognizable offence to the police station having jurisdiction, or register a Zero FIR if urgent. Followed by: Ensure the statement is reduced to writing and read back to you. Adjudication Route: Obtain an authenticated copy of the registered FIR free of cost. Concluding with: If refused, escalate in writing to the Superintendent of Police or Magistrate. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
Does Section 55 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act allow a party to challenge an award at any time if fraud is later discovered, overriding the usual limitation period?

I can't confirm a Section 55 in the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 creating a fraud-based exception that overrides the limitation period. Please verify with a lawyer whether any narrow exception exists for fraud, since I'm not able to confirm one under this section number.
Can you explain what Indian law says about how long a trademark registration lasts, for someone I met recently?

The 10-year validity clock for an Indian trademark under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 runs from the original filing date, even if the actual registration certificate takes a couple of years to be issued due to examination or opposition — so a mark filed in 2020 that gets registered only in 2022 is still due for renewal in 2030, not 2032. In practice, so if this person registered the mark but hasn't actually been using it in business for five years since registration, that's a separate vulnerability the Registrar can act on, quite apart from the renewal question.
I heard something about wife's maintenance claim that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?

Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the successor to Section 125 CrPC, lets a wife unable to maintain herself — including a divorced wife who has not remarried — claim a monthly allowance from a husband with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain her, on application before a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
What does the law say if a client I'm helping is facing getting married under the Special Marriage Act?

Under Sections 5 to 7 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954, a couple wanting a civil marriage must first give written notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one of them has lived for the preceding 30 days. The Marriage Officer then publishes this notice for 30 days, during which anyone can object on specific statutory grounds (such as bigamy or a prohibited relationship); if no valid objection is raised, the marriage can be solemnised after that period. In practice, for your client, the residency requirement means the notice has to be filed with the Marriage Officer of a district where one of them has actually lived for the preceding 30 days — not just anywhere convenient.
I heard something about State Commission pecuniary jurisdiction that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?
Per the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules made under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a State Commission has jurisdiction where the consideration paid exceeds Rs. 50 lakh but does not exceed Rs. 2 crore.
A friend from Chennai is dealing with a situation involving a company's exposure to insolvency proceedings. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, a financial creditor can apply to the National Company Law Tribunal to start Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor only where the default is at least Rs 1 crore — a threshold that was raised from the original Rs 1 lakh by a government notification in March 2020. In practice, for your friend, the practical checkpoint is whether the outstanding default actually crosses Rs 1 crore — below that, the Section 7 route to the NCLT simply isn't available, though other recovery options may be.
What are the stamp duty and registration requirements for documents executed in Criminal Procedure?

Under the Indian Stamp Act and Registration Act, instruments in Criminal Procedure must be stamped with adequate state-specific stamp duty prior to or at execution. Failure to stamp properly renders the document inadmissible in evidence.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding maternity leave entitlement?

Eligibility for the 26-week paid maternity leave under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended in 2017) requires that the woman has worked at least 80 days for the employer in the 12 months before her expected delivery date, at an establishment employing 10 or more people. For miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy, the law separately allows 6 weeks of leave.
How should a citizen prepare to handle issuing a statutory legal notice prior to civil suit smoothly?

Practical Guide: Handling issuing a statutory legal notice prior to civil suit in Civil Law involves: Step 1: Set out facts, breach of obligations, and exact monetary or specific relief demanded. Step 2: Provide a reasonable response period (typically 15 to 30 days). Step 3: Dispatch via Registered Post with Acknowledgment Due (RPAD) and retain proof of delivery. Step 4: If unheeded, proceed with filing the civil suit. Key Tip: Retain stamped acknowledgment copies of all applications and track official correspondence closely.
Can a company legally stop a former employee from soliciting the company's clients after they resign?

Non-solicitation clauses sit in a somewhat different, more contested space than blanket non-compete clauses. Some Indian courts have distinguished a narrow restriction on directly soliciting a former employer's existing clients from a broader restriction on working in the industry, and have been more willing to enforce reasonable, narrowly drafted non-solicitation clauses -- since they don't stop the person from practising their profession or trade generally, only from targeting specific relationships built through the former employer. However, this isn't a settled bright-line rule, and other courts have struck down non-solicitation clauses as void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 when they're drafted broadly enough to effectively restrain the person's ability to work. Whether a specific non-solicitation clause survives scrutiny depends heavily on how narrowly it's drafted (client list, duration, geography) and the facts of the case, so this is genuinely an area where you'd want a lawyer to review the actual clause and the circumstances.
Can you explain what Indian law says about snatching as a standalone offence, for a startup founder I'm advising?

As of the new criminal code (BNS, 2023), snatching is dealt with under its own Section 304, separately from ordinary theft. The offence covers sudden or forceful grabbing of movable property, and the punishment is imprisonment for a term that may extend to three years, along with a fine. In practice, in practical terms this gives the founder a clearer basis to push the police to register and investigate the incident specifically as snatching rather than folding it into a generic theft complaint.
If my elder relative is affected by an agreement or contract involving a minor, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The rule from Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) still governs today — an agreement with a minor is void ab initio under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, and this holds even if the minor lied about their age to get the other party to agree. The one recognised carve-out is for contracts made by a guardian that are genuinely for the minor's benefit, such as school admission or a beneficial apprenticeship, which courts have upheld as valid. In practice, so if your elder relative's situation involves a guardian entering into the agreement specifically for the minor's benefit — like schooling or medical care — that's the one context where the agreement could still be treated as valid.
If a person I met recently is affected by waiver of a termination notice by accepting rent, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Courts have held that a landlord who serves a Section 106 termination notice under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 but then continues to accept rent from the tenant afterward risks that conduct being treated as a waiver of the notice, undermining a later eviction claim based on it.
If a colleague at work is affected by compounding a cheque dishonour offence, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes offences under Section 138, including cheque dishonour, compoundable notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure, meaning the complainant and accused can settle at any stage and the accused stands acquitted once the matter is compounded.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding bond to prevent further violence?

Under Section 19(3) of the PWDV Act, 2005, the Magistrate may require the respondent to execute a bond, with or without sureties, to prevent the commission of further domestic violence; such an order is treated as one under Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for enforcement purposes.
What is the hierarchy of appeals available to an aggrieved party in Women and Child Protection?

Appellate Hierarchy: In Women and Child Protection, initial orders from statutory tribunals or trial courts are subject to structured appeals. Statutory Appeal: First appeals generally lie on questions of fact and law to the immediate appellate authority or District/High Court. Subsequent Review: Second appeals or revisions are typically restricted to substantial questions of law, concluding with discretionary review under Article 136 of the Constitution.
If a factory worker I spoke with is affected by getting married under the Special Marriage Act, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The 30-day notice period under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 is meant to allow objections strictly on the grounds specified in Section 4 — such as either party already being married, being under the minimum marriageable age, or falling within a prohibited degree of relationship. It is not a general public consultation on the marriage itself, and objections outside these grounds cannot legally block the marriage from proceeding. In practice, so the worker needs to plan around the full 30-day notice-and-objection window before the marriage can actually be solemnised, in addition to whatever documentation the Marriage Officer requires.
I was harmed by a car airbag that failed to deploy in a collision. Can I claim compensation from the manufacturer under Indian consumer law?

Yes — this falls under the product liability provisions in Chapter VI of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Section 84 makes a product manufacturer liable in a product liability action where, among other grounds, the product has a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from its own manufacturing specifications, doesn't conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions and warnings to prevent harm — your case appears to involve manufacturing or design defect in a critical safety component. Importantly, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer can be held liable even if they weren't negligent or fraudulent in making an express warranty, which introduces a strict-liability element focused on whether the product caused harm rather than the manufacturer's intent. You can file a complaint before the relevant Consumer Commission (District, State, or National, depending on the claim value), which has the power to order removal of the defect, replacement, refund with interest, compensation including punitive damages for negligence, and even direct withdrawal of the hazardous product from the market. Keep your purchase receipt, photos or medical records of the harm, and any advertising material showing the manufacturer's claims, as this evidence strengthens a product liability claim.
What is mandatory reporting under POCSO in simple terms under Indian law?

mandatory reporting under POCSO is an established legal concept within Women and Child Protection. Explanation: In plain words, a strict statutory duty imposed on any person, medical professional, or educational institution aware of sexual offences against a minor to report the incident immediately to police or child welfare committees. For citizens, this principle provides clarity on legal rights and responsibilities, ensuring that actions are evaluated under predictable legal standards rather than arbitrary discretion.
Under Section 12A of the Hindu Succession Act, does a daughter lose her coparcenary rights if she does not file a claim within three years of her father's death?

I'm not able to verify a Section 12A in the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 imposing a three-year claim deadline on a daughter's coparcenary rights. The coparcenary right itself is governed by Section 6, and the Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) held this right accrues by birth; I'm not aware of a specific limitation provision within the Hindu Succession Act itself cutting off that right after three years (though ordinary limitation rules for filing a partition suit, under the Limitation Act, 1963, would separately govern how long she has to actually sue for partition). Please verify the exact position with a property lawyer rather than relying on this section number.

This clause appears in an agreement I was given: "The property is conveyed on an 'as-is, where-is' basis without any representation or warranty regarding encumbrances or title defects." What does it mean in practical terms?

Plain Meaning: The clause states: "The property is conveyed on an 'as-is, where-is' basis without any representation or warranty regarding encumbrances or title defects." Explanation: This is an 'as-is' disclaimer. While it puts the buyer on notice to conduct due diligence, Indian law under the Transfer of Property Act imposes a statutory duty on the seller to disclose latent material title defects of which the seller is aware and the buyer could not easily discover. Practical Advice: Read this in the context of the entire document, especially definitions, cure periods, and exception clauses.
A tenant i spoke with is dealing with a situation involving filing a domestic violence complaint. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, an aggrieved person, a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf can file an application before a Magistrate seeking relief for domestic violence.
In Gujarat, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Gujarat, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding a builder delaying possession of a flat?

RERA, 2016 makes builders directly liable under Section 18 whenever possession is delayed past the promised date. A buyer can either terminate the agreement for a full refund with interest, or continue and get compensated monthly for the delay; if the builder doesn't comply voluntarily, the complaint goes to the state Real Estate Regulatory Authority, and the builder can additionally face imprisonment or a fine of up to 10% of the project's estimated cost for non-compliance.
If my elder relative is affected by whether a small business needs to register for GST, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

GST registration becomes mandatory once a business's aggregate turnover crosses Rs 40 lakh for suppliers of goods, or Rs 20 lakh for suppliers of services, in most states — with lower thresholds of Rs 20 lakh (goods) and Rs 10 lakh (services) applying in special category states in the North East and hill regions. Below these limits, registration is optional (though it can still be done voluntarily to claim input tax credit). In practice, in your elder relative's case, if the business sells across state lines even occasionally, that can trigger mandatory registration regardless of total turnover, since inter-state taxable supply is one of the categories excluded from the higher threshold.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over incorporating a Private Limited Company in India, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for incorporating a Private Limited Company in India is determined by statutory rules under Company and Business Law. Initial Filing: Obtain DSC and DIN for proposed directors. Followed by: Apply for name reservation through SPICe+ Part A on the MCA portal. Adjudication Route: Draft MoA and AoA specifying corporate objects and regulations. Concluding with: Submit SPICe+ Part B along with AGILE-PRO-S for PAN, TAN, GST, and bank integration. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
A 16-year-old has been accused of a heinous offence. Will he automatically be tried as an adult?

No, not automatically. Under Section 15 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, when a child who has completed or is above 16 years of age is accused of a heinous offence (as defined under Section 2(33), broadly offences carrying a minimum sentence of 7 years or more), the Juvenile Justice Board must first conduct a preliminary assessment — not a trial — into the child's mental and physical capacity to have committed the offence, his ability to understand the consequences of his actions, and the circumstances in which the offence was allegedly committed. The Board may take the assistance of psychologists or psycho-social experts in making this assessment, and is expected to complete it within 3 months from the date the child was first produced before the Board. Only if the Board concludes, based on this assessment, that the child should be tried as an adult does it pass an order under Section 18(3) transferring the case to the Children's Court for trial as an adult; otherwise, the matter continues before the Board itself under the standard juvenile justice process, which focuses on rehabilitation rather than adult-style punishment.
What essential standards and statutory principles govern consent and notice under DPDP Act under Indian law?

Under Privacy and Data Protection, consent and notice under DPDP Act is governed by established statutory standards and judicial doctrines. The foundational statutory principle under digital personal data legislation requiring data fiduciaries to obtain clear, unbundled, and informed consent accompanied by an itemized privacy notice specifying processing purposes. Courts and regulatory bodies require strict adherence to procedural fairness, proper documentation, and statutory preconditions before granting relief or enforcing liabilities under this principle.
What is the correct legal procedure my neighbour should follow regarding filing a domestic violence complaint under Indian law?
Under Section 12 of the PWDV Act, 2005, an aggrieved person, a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf can file an application before a Magistrate.
How does Indian law actually treat theft after preparation to cause hurt, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Where a person makes preparation for causing death, hurt, or restraint in order to commit a theft, to escape after committing it, or to retain the stolen property, Section 307 of the BNS, 2023 applies, prescribing rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years plus a fine.
How does Indian law actually treat damages for breach of contract, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 entitles a party who suffers a breach to compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things, or that both parties knew at the time of contracting was likely to result from the breach — but excludes remote or indirect loss.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding hit-and-run accident compensation?

Section 161 of the Motor Vehicles Act, along with the 2022 hit-and-run compensation scheme, entitles victims to Rs 2 lakh (death) or Rs 50,000 (grievous injury) from a dedicated government fund, untraced-driver cases included. This is separate from the criminal side — under BNS Section 106(2), a driver who causes death by rash driving and flees without reporting can face up to 10 years' imprisonment.
I was stopped in Delhi and my breathalyser reading was above the limit for the first time. What's the penalty?

Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), driving with a blood alcohol concentration above 30 mg per 100 ml of blood is an offence regardless of which state you're in, since this is a central enactment applied uniformly, including in Delhi. For a first-time offence, the punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Your driving licence can also be suspended, and traffic police are empowered to seize the vehicle. If the case goes to court, you'll be tried in the local Traffic Court or Judicial Magistrate's court, and if an accident causing injury or death resulted, you could separately face charges under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 as well.

A retail application collects continuous background geolocation from users without displaying any privacy disclosure or obtaining consent. What legal liabilities or duties arise for the parties involved in this matter?

Direct Assessment: Under Privacy and Data Protection, this situation engages specific legal duties relating to consent and notice under DPDP Act. Applicable Rule: The foundational statutory principle under digital personal data legislation requiring data fiduciaries to obtain clear, unbundled, and informed consent accompanied by an itemized privacy notice specifying processing purposes. What prerequisites and documentation are essential before initiating filing an RTI application and first appeal?
