If a state's High Court jurisdiction doesn't yet have a graded arbitral institution, the Chief Justice of that High Court may maintain a panel of arbitrators for this purpose instead. Courts and the designated institution are required to dispose of such applications as expeditiously as possible, and case law has indicated a general expectation of around 60 days. At the Section 11 stage, courts generally take a limited, prima facie look at whether an arbitration agreement exists, leaving deeper jurisdictional or merits disputes to the arbitral tribunal itself (the 'kompetenz-kompetenz' principle). This is general information; drafting the Section 11 application correctly, and choosing the right forum, benefits from a lawyer experienced in arbitration matters.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on anticipatory bail?

The BNSS, 2023 shifted anticipatory bail from CrPC Section 438 to its own Section 482. The substance of the remedy is unchanged: someone who reasonably apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence can ask the Sessions Court or High Court to direct that they be released on bail if arrested. One statutory exception under Section 482(4) blocks this route in cases of rape of a girl under sixteen or gang rape of a woman under eighteen.
How does Indian law actually treat filing against relatives of the husband, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
A proviso to the PWDV Act, 2005 lets an aggrieved wife file a complaint against a relative of the husband, not only the husband himself.
I received an arbitral award in a real estate joint development dispute 4 months ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 4 months have passed since you received the award, you are very likely already outside both the initial 3-month window and the extra 30-day condonable period, meaning a Section 34 challenge may no longer be maintainable regardless of the merits of your objection — courts have consistently held there is no scope to condone delay beyond 3 months plus 30 days. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
Which court do I approach to file a cheque bounce case against Arjun in Coimbatore, and is there a time limit?

A Section 138 complaint is filed before the Judicial Magistrate having jurisdiction, typically where the cheque was presented for collection or where the bank branch is located, subject to the specific territorial rules that apply after the 2015 amendment to the NI Act. In practice, this usually means the court within whose jurisdiction Coimbatore's relevant bank branch falls.

On timing: you must send the demand notice within 30 days of the cheque-return memo, wait 15 days for payment, and then file the complaint within 30 days after that 15-day period ends. Missing these windows can be fatal to the complaint, so it's worth confirming the exact dates with a lawyer before filing.
What is the correct legal procedure a classmate studying law should follow regarding children are exempt from the reporting-failure penalty under Indian law?
Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 exempts a child from the penalty for failure to report under Section 21(1).
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹60,000/month non-residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 6 months' rent for non-residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹60,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹360,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
If a friend of mine is affected by children are exempt from the reporting-failure penalty, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 21(3) of the POCSO Act, 2012 explicitly states that the penalty for failure to report under Section 21(1) does not apply to a child under the Act, meaning a minor's silence or failure to report abuse (their own or another's) cannot itself be criminally punished.
I received an arbitral award in a supply contract disagreement 10 weeks ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 10 weeks have passed since you received the award, you should still be within, or close to, the permissible window, so you should file your Section 34 application without further delay to be safe, especially since if you're past the initial 3 months you would need to show sufficient cause for the extension and delay itself weakens that showing. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
My sister-in-law is dealing with a situation involving minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company. What does Indian law say about this?

The high-profile Tata Sons v. Cyrus Mistry dispute was fought under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 — illustrating that this remedy isn't limited to small family companies, but is available even in large public companies where minority (or removed) shareholders believe the majority's conduct has been unfairly prejudicial to their interests. In practice, for your sister-in-law, the first practical check is the numerical threshold under Section 244 — without holding at least 10% of shares (or meeting the 100-member/one-tenth alternative), the petition to NCLT can't even be filed.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of revoking a conditional gift for failure to maintain isn't handled correctly?

Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 provides that where a senior citizen transfers property on condition the transferee provide basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee fails to do so, the transfer can be declared void by the Maintenance Tribunal.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of notice period after cheque dishonour isn't handled correctly?

Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, once a cheque is dishonoured for insufficiency of funds against a legally enforceable debt, the payee must send a written demand notice within 30 days of learning of the dishonour.
What does Indian law currently say about how long a trademark registration lasts?

A lapsed trademark isn't necessarily gone forever — Section 25(4) allows an application for restoration within one year of expiry (after a six-month grace period from the expiry date itself), on payment of a restoration fee, though this window is strict and missing it means the mark goes back into the pool for anyone else to register.
What prerequisites and documentation are essential before initiating exercising data subject rights under the DPDP Act?

Prerequisites & Jurisdiction: In Privacy and Data Protection, before undertaking exercising data subject rights under the DPDP Act, applicants must ensure: (1) Mandatory preparation: Submit formal request to the Data Fiduciary seeking data processing summary. (2) Initial compliance: Request correction, updating, or erasure of outdated personal data. Subsequent procedure: Follow up with the designated Data Protection Grievance Officer. If unresolved, escalate the complaint to the Data Protection Board of India. Careful preparation of documentary evidence avoids summary dismissal.
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹15,000/month residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 2 months' rent for residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹15,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹30,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
Are there mandatory pre-litigation steps or notices required before approaching a court under Family Law?

In Family Law, several statutory frameworks mandate pre-litigation steps. For government bodies or statutory claims, advance notice of 30 to 60 days is frequently mandatory. Commercial disputes and certain family matters require attempting pre-litigation mediation unless urgent interim relief is claimed.
My business partner cheated me. What can I do legally?

'Cheated' could point to several different legal routes depending on exactly what happened -- was money or property misappropriated from the business (which could raise criminal breach of trust or cheating under the BNS), or is this a dispute over how partnership profits/losses were shared (which would usually be a civil/partnership-law matter), or did they violate specific terms of a partnership agreement? The remedy, the forum, and even whether this is a criminal or civil matter change significantly based on that. Could you share what specifically happened -- funds diverted, false representations made, or a breach of the partnership deed?
Is anticipatory bail available for every kind of criminal case in India?

No. Anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS, 2023 (replacing Section 438 CrPC) is available only for non-bailable offences -- for bailable offences, a person has an outright right to bail at the police station itself under Section 478 BNSS, so there's no need for anticipatory bail. Certain specific categories are also excluded or restricted by statute in some states (for example, some states' amendments bar anticipatory bail for particular serious offences), and courts have generally been more cautious in granting it for very grave offences like those attracting the death penalty or life imprisonment, though there's no absolute statutory bar unless the specific law involved (like certain provisions of the NDPS Act or UAPA) restricts it. Whether it's available and likely to be granted in a specific case depends heavily on the exact offence alleged, so this needs a lawyer's assessment of the particular FIR or complaint.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving disqualification of a wife from maintenance. What does Indian law say about this?

A wife can be disqualified from claiming maintenance under Section 144 BNSS, 2023 if she is living in adultery, if she refuses to live with her husband without sufficient reason, or if the couple are living separately by mutual consent — these operate as statutory bars on an otherwise valid maintenance claim.
A client I'm helping brought up a passport being impounded or seized recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

Before a passport can be impounded under Section 10(3), the holder is ordinarily entitled to a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to know the grounds — flowing from the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that impounding a passport without a fair hearing violates the constitutional right to personal liberty. In practice, so your client is entitled to ask for the written reasons behind the impounding order, since the passport authority is legally required to record and, in most cases, share them.
My brother wants to understand maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 initially appeared to limit a husband's maintenance obligation to just the iddat period (roughly three months), but the Supreme Court in Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001) interpreted the Act to mean the husband must make a 'reasonable and fair provision' within the iddat period that is sufficient to sustain the divorced wife for her entire future, not just those three months — effectively extending real protection well beyond the iddat window while keeping the Act's text intact. In practice, in your brother's case, if the amount offered under the 1986 Act seems inadequate, she isn't locked out of also applying under the regular maintenance provision (BNSS Section 144) as long as she hasn't remarried.
My neighbour is dealing with a situation involving maintenance for elderly parents. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023, a father or mother unable to maintain themselves can claim a monthly allowance from a child who has sufficient means but neglects or refuses to maintain them, decided by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class through a summary proceeding meant for quick relief.
What does the law say if a relative going through a difficult time is facing a passport being impounded or seized?

An order impounding a passport under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967 can be appealed to the Central Passport Organisation (or, depending on which authority passed the order, a designated appellate authority) within 30 days of the order being communicated to the holder. In practice, for your relative, the key question is which authority actually impounded the passport — if it was just the police holding onto it (as opposed to a formal impounding order from the passport office), that itself may be legally questionable.
How does Indian law actually treat liquidated damages versus proving actual loss, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs liquidated damages where a contract itself fixes a sum payable on breach; courts can award reasonable compensation up to that stipulated amount, and unlike a claim under Section 73, strict proof of actual loss is not required to invoke Section 74.
An artist friend of mine brought up being laid off or retrenched from a job recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The Industrial Disputes Act's retrenchment compensation under Section 25F is calculated the same way as gratuity — 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service (or part thereof exceeding six months) — but it's a separate entitlement from gratuity, payable in addition to it where both apply, and gratuity payable on retrenchment is specifically excluded from the retrenchment compensation calculation itself. In practice, so if your artist friend's job ended because the whole business was sold or transferred, the same notice-and-compensation protection applies unless the new employer kept your artist friend on with no less favourable terms.
What is the correct legal procedure a person I met recently should follow regarding theft after preparation to cause hurt under Indian law?

Where a person makes preparation for causing death, hurt, or restraint in order to commit a theft, to escape after committing it, or to retain the stolen property, Section 307 of the BNS, 2023 applies, prescribing rigorous imprisonment of up to ten years plus a fine.
If my neighbour is affected by drawer's payment window after notice, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

After receiving a Section 138 demand notice under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the drawer of a dishonoured cheque has 15 days to pay the cheque amount; only if payment is not made within that window does the cause of action to file a criminal complaint arise, on the 16th day.
Are there mandatory pre-litigation steps or notices required before approaching a court under Alternative Dispute Resolution?

In Alternative Dispute Resolution, several statutory frameworks mandate pre-litigation steps. For government bodies or statutory claims, advance notice of 30 to 60 days is frequently mandatory. Commercial disputes and certain family matters require attempting pre-litigation mediation unless urgent interim relief is claimed.
Someone I met recently is dealing with a situation involving a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan. What does Indian law say about this?

Once a loan account is classified as a non-performing asset, Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 requires the secured creditor (usually a bank or NBFC) to issue a demand notice giving the borrower 60 days to repay the outstanding dues before the lender can move to take possession of the mortgaged property under Section 13(4). In practice, for this person, the 60-day period isn't just a waiting period — it's the window to either repay, negotiate a settlement, or file a written objection under Section 13(3A) challenging the notice.
I'm Pooja. As a elderly mother, my father moved out and doesn't pay for the children's school fees or food. Can I claim maintenance, and how does that work?

Yes -- under Section 144 of the BNSS (the successor to the old Section 125 CrPC, in force since 1 July 2024), a Magistrate can order a person with sufficient means to pay monthly maintenance if they've neglected or refused to maintain a wife, minor child, a major child unable to maintain itself due to disability, or a parent unable to maintain themselves.

To succeed, you'd generally need to show three things: the other person has sufficient means, they've neglected or refused to maintain you, and you're unable to maintain yourself. This provision applies regardless of religion. If you file an application, both sides are usually required to submit affidavits disclosing their income and assets, and courts are expected to decide interim maintenance applications within 60 days of the notice being served.
How does Indian law actually treat notice period for agricultural or manufacturing leases, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 106 treats agricultural or manufacturing leases as year-to-year tenancies, terminable by six months' notice, longer than the 15-day period for other leases.
Someone in my apartment complex asked me about maternity leave entitlement — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 raised paid maternity leave under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children, of which up to 8 weeks can be taken before the expected delivery date. For a third or subsequent child, the entitlement drops to 12 weeks, and adoptive or commissioning mothers get 12 weeks from the date of adoption or the child's birth. The Act applies to establishments with 10 or more employees. In practice, for that person, the key eligibility check is the 80-days-worked-in-12-months requirement — if that's satisfied, the 26-week entitlement applies regardless of whether she's on a permanent or contract role.
A factory worker I spoke with asked me about how long a trademark registration lasts — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

A lapsed trademark isn't necessarily gone forever — Section 25(4) allows an application for restoration within one year of expiry (after a six-month grace period from the expiry date itself), on payment of a restoration fee, though this window is strict and missing it means the mark goes back into the pool for anyone else to register. In practice, this means the worker should file the renewal well before expiry — Form TM-R with the fee — since the process is described as far less involved than the original registration itself.
My sister-in-law is dealing with a situation involving a passport being impounded or seized. What does Indian law say about this?

Before a passport can be impounded under Section 10(3), the holder is ordinarily entitled to a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to know the grounds — flowing from the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that impounding a passport without a fair hearing violates the constitutional right to personal liberty. In practice, so your sister-in-law is entitled to ask for the written reasons behind the impounding order, since the passport authority is legally required to record and, in most cases, share them.
If someone in my apartment complex is affected by setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 4 of the POSH Act, 2013, the 10-employee threshold that triggers a mandatory Internal Committee counts everyone — permanent staff, contract workers, interns, and daily-wage employees combined. Where the workplace is below that threshold, the complaint is instead handled by the district-level Local Committee. Section 26 of the Act penalises an employer's failure to constitute the IC, with fines starting at Rs 50,000. In practice, so that person's complaint, once filed with a properly constituted Internal Committee, is legally required to be concluded within 90 days of receipt.
A friend from Chennai wants to understand snatching as a standalone offence. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The BNS, which came into force on 1 July 2024 and replaced the IPC, created a new, separate offence of snatching under Section 304. Earlier, a chain- or phone-snatching incident would just be charged as ordinary theft; now it has its own provision, punishable with up to three years' imprisonment and a fine. In practice, for your friend, this means the police should register the FIR specifically under BNS Section 304 rather than the general theft provision, since snatching now has its own separate charge.
A cheque for ₹75,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹75,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹150,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
If my cousin who works in Chennai is affected by punishment for cheque dishonour, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes cheque dishonour for insufficient funds (against an existing debt or liability) punishable with imprisonment of up to two years, a fine that may extend to twice the cheque amount, or both.
If a tenant I know is affected by a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The 60-day window in a SARFAESI demand notice under Section 13(2) is not a formality — the Supreme Court has held that a bank's failure to properly respond to a borrower's written objection during this period is a fatal procedural flaw that can void the entire subsequent possession or sale action. The borrower can also approach the Debt Recovery Tribunal to challenge steps taken under Section 13(4). In practice, so the tenant should treat the 60-day notice as the real deadline to act, since after that the bank can move straight to taking possession of the secured asset.
How does Indian law actually treat filing a second appeal, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
A Second Appeal to the Central or State Information Commission can be filed under Section 19(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, within 90 days of the FAA's order or the expiry of its decision period.
My brother is dealing with a situation involving a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking, or abetting the giving or taking of dowry is punishable with a minimum of five years' imprisonment and a fine of at least Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is higher (courts can impose a lesser sentence only for adequate and special reasons recorded in writing). Section 4 separately punishes merely demanding dowry, directly or indirectly, from the bride's or groom's family, with imprisonment of six months to two years and/or a fine. In practice, in your brother's case, if dowry was given only because of pressure or coercion from the other side, the law has been read to shield the giver from being treated as equally culpable as an abettor.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a company's exposure to insolvency proceedings?

A financial creditor's right to file under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016 doesn't guarantee automatic admission — the Supreme Court has held that the NCLT retains discretion (the section uses "may," not "shall") and must apply its mind to relevant factors beyond just the existence of the Rs 1 crore default before starting the insolvency process.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding filing an RTI application?

The standard application fee for filing an RTI request with a central government public authority is Rs 10, and applicants who are Below Poverty Line (BPL), with proof, don't have to pay any fee at all. States can set their own fee under their respective RTI rules — most match the Rs 10 central figure, though a few charge more.
A friend of mine is dealing with a situation involving consequence of not challenging an award in time. What does Indian law say about this?

If an arbitral award is not challenged within the limitation period under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (three months plus the 30-day condonable extension), it attains finality under Section 35 and becomes enforceable as a decree of the court under Section 36.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding duty to report child sexual abuse?

Section 19 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 places a duty on any person who has knowledge of, or apprehends, an offence under the Act to report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police.
What are the stamp duty and registration requirements for documents executed in Senior Citizen-related law?

Under the Indian Stamp Act and Registration Act, instruments in Senior Citizen-related law must be stamped with adequate state-specific stamp duty prior to or at execution. Failure to stamp properly renders the document inadmissible in evidence.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of 60-day timeline for interim maintenance isn't handled correctly?

Once a maintenance application is made under Section 144 BNSS, 2023, the Magistrate is expected, as far as possible, to dispose of the application for interim maintenance within sixty days from the date of service of notice.
A client i'm helping is dealing with a situation involving waiver of the cooling-off period. What does Indian law say about this?

In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, the Supreme Court held that the six-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is directory, not mandatory, and family courts have discretion to waive it where reconciliation is impossible and disputes such as alimony and custody are genuinely settled.
If a client I'm helping is affected by filing a second appeal, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

A Second Appeal against the First Appellate Authority's decision (or its failure to decide) can be filed with the Central or State Information Commission under Section 19(3) of the RTI Act, 2005, within 90 days of receiving the FAA's order or of the expiry of the FAA's decision period.
How does Indian law actually treat cheating by personation online, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 66D of the IT Act, 2000 punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource, with the same punishment as Section 66C: up to three years imprisonment and a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of damages for breach of contract isn't handled correctly?

Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 entitles a party who suffers a breach to compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things, or that both parties knew at the time of contracting was likely to result from the breach — but excludes remote or indirect loss.
I bought a induction stove that short-circuited and damaged other appliances on the same line, though I wasn't hurt. Can I still claim under product liability even though there's no personal injury?

Yes. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines 'harm' under product liability broadly to include not just personal injury but also damage to property, including consequential commercial loss in certain cases, arising from a defective product. Since your induction stove's defect damaged other appliances, you can bring a product liability action under Section 84 against the manufacturer for a manufacturing or design defect, seeking compensation for the damaged appliances, the cost of replacing the defective stove, and any related losses. File your complaint with the appropriate Consumer Commission based on the value of your claim, and keep your purchase invoice, the damaged appliances or repair estimates, and any evidence of the stove's malfunction as documentation.
A relative going through a difficult time is dealing with a situation involving setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment. What does Indian law say about this?

The POSH Act, 2013 requires an Internal Committee wherever an employer has 10 or more employees (Section 4), and where an organisation doesn't cross that threshold, complaints instead go to the Local Committee set up by the District Officer. The Internal Committee's inquiry into a complaint must conclude within 90 days, and non-constitution of the committee is penalised under Section 26. In practice, this means your relative can point the employer to Section 4 of the POSH Act as the legal basis for demanding the committee be set up, rather than this being a discretionary HR policy.
If my cousin in Pune is affected by gratuity owed after leaving a job, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to any factory, shop, or establishment with 10 or more employees — and once it applies, it keeps applying even if headcount later drops below 10. Gratuity is payable at 15 days' wages for every completed year of service (or any part of a year beyond six months), calculated on the last drawn basic salary plus dearness allowance, with a statutory ceiling of Rs 20 lakh. In practice, so if your cousin's employer is delaying payment, the law doesn't require your cousin to wait passively — an application in Form I to the employer, and if unresolved, to the Controlling Authority, can push the payment along, with interest accruing on delayed amounts.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime, for a startup founder I'm advising?

The 2015 Juvenile Justice Act was the first Indian law to allow trying a 16-18 year old as an adult, but this isn't automatic — the Juvenile Justice Board must first assess, within three months of the child being produced before it, whether the child had the capacity to understand the offence and its consequences, before referring the matter to the Children's Court for a final decision on adult trial. In practice, in the founder's case, it's worth confirming through the JJ Board process that a lawyer and child psychologist are actually involved in the preliminary assessment, since the law specifically requires that support.
A classmate studying law is dealing with a situation involving the 3-month limitation to challenge an award. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an application to set aside an arbitral award must be made within three months from the date the party received the award, or, if a Section 33 correction request was made, from the date that request was disposed of.
I'm Sanjay. Deepa's cheque for Rs. 42000 bounced, and I sent the legal notice 5 days ago. Deepa hasn't responded. What happens now?

Since Deepa received the notice 5 days ago, they still have until the 15-day mark to make the payment. If that period passes with no payment, the offence under Section 138 NI Act is treated as complete, and you get 30 days from the end of the 15-day period to file a criminal complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court.

Keep your proof of notice delivery (courier/postal receipt, or acknowledgment) safe, as you'll need it to show the notice was validly served. If payment does come in during the remaining days, that would resolve the matter without needing to go to court.
A friend from Chennai brought up challenging an arbitration award recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

Unlike ordinary civil suits, where the general Limitation Act's provisions for condoning delay can sometimes apply more flexibly, the Supreme Court has held that the extra 30-day condonable period in Section 34(3) of the Arbitration Act is rigid — a challenge filed even one day late, beyond three months and 30 days, will be dismissed as time-barred, regardless of the reason for the delay. In practice, so your friend's lawyer needs to build the substantive challenge — jurisdiction, procedure, or public policy grounds — but none of that matters if the filing itself is even a day late.
My neighbour wants to understand filing an RTI application. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The standard application fee for filing an RTI request with a central government public authority is Rs 10, and applicants who are Below Poverty Line (BPL), with proof, don't have to pay any fee at all. States can set their own fee under their respective RTI rules — most match the Rs 10 central figure, though a few charge more. In practice, in your neighbour's case, if there's a genuine BPL certificate to attach, the entire application fee (and the fee for receiving the information) can be waived altogether.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding withdrawing consent before the decree?

Under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, either spouse can withdraw their consent to a mutual consent divorce at any point before the decree is actually passed; if consent is withdrawn, the court cannot grant the mutual consent divorce and the case cannot proceed on that basis.
A former employee I used to manage is dealing with a situation involving a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment. What does Indian law say about this?

Any offer or advertisement in a newspaper or other media of money or property as consideration for a person's marriage is itself a punishable offence under Section 4A of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, carrying imprisonment of six months to five years, or a fine, or both — separate from and in addition to the offences of actually giving, taking, or demanding dowry. In practice, for the former employee, it matters whether what happened was an actual exchange of dowry (Section 3) or just a demand for it (Section 4) — both are offences, but they carry different minimum and maximum punishments.
Is there a Section 40 in the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 that lets a Magistrate evict the aggrieved woman if the respondent proves the household was inherited?

I'm not able to verify a Section 40 in the PWDV Act, 2005 that allows such an eviction. In fact, Section 19 of the Act (residence orders) is designed to protect the aggrieved person's right to remain in the shared household and explicitly says this applies regardless of whether the respondent has a legal or equitable interest in that household — so inheritance status of the household would not, on its own, be a basis under Section 19 to evict the aggrieved person. Please have this checked against the current bare act.
A group of farmers wants to challenge a pesticide manufacturing unit that has been contaminating their irrigation canal for about 6 months now. Is it too late to approach the NGT?

They're right at the edge of the window and should file immediately. Under Section 14(3) of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, an application must be made within 6 months from when the cause of action first arose. At roughly 6 months, they are at or very near the statutory limit, though the Tribunal has power to condone a further delay of up to 60 days if satisfied there is sufficient cause for the delay — but that extension isn't guaranteed, so they shouldn't rely on it. If the contamination is ongoing rather than a single past event, they may also be able to argue a continuing cause of action, but the safest course is to file without any further delay rather than count on either the condonation or the continuing-harm argument.
A client i'm helping is dealing with a situation involving punishment for cheque dishonour. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes cheque dishonour for insufficient funds (against an existing debt or liability) punishable with imprisonment of up to two years, a fine that may extend to twice the cheque amount, or both.
My cousin in Pune wants to understand maintenance for a wife, child, or parent. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Under BNSS Section 144 (the successor to CrPC Section 125), a Magistrate can order a person with sufficient income to pay maintenance to a wife, children, or parents who cannot support themselves. This is a secular remedy, applicable regardless of religion, and courts can also grant interim maintenance while the case is pending; if the payer defaults, the law allows for imprisonment of up to a month for each unpaid instalment. In practice, in your cousin's situation, it helps to know the amount isn't capped by law — the Magistrate decides it based on the paying party's income and the claimant's needs, so it's worth documenting both carefully.
Under Section 200 of the Hindu Marriage Act, can a court grant a mutual consent divorce immediately, with no minimum separation period, if both spouses are under financial hardship?

I'm not able to verify a Section 200 in the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 creating a financial-hardship exception. The mutual consent divorce provision is Section 13B, which requires the spouses to have lived separately for at least one year under Section 13B(1) before the first motion can even be filed; courts have discretion under Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) to waive the six-month gap between the first and second motions in appropriate cases, but that is different from waiving the initial one-year separation requirement, and I'm not aware of a financial-hardship exception to it.
How does Indian law actually treat waiver of a termination notice by accepting rent, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
A landlord who serves a Section 106 notice but then accepts rent afterward risks that conduct being treated as a waiver of the notice.
What does Indian law currently say about minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company?

The NCLT's powers once it finds oppression or mismanagement under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are broad — it can order the majority to buy out the minority's shares, set aside prejudicial agreements, remove directors, order forensic audits, or even restructure how the company is managed going forward, though courts have clarified that a director's removal, an isolated bad decision, or simply a breakdown of trust between shareholders doesn't by itself amount to oppression.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over exercising data subject rights under the DPDP Act, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for exercising data subject rights under the DPDP Act is determined by statutory rules under Privacy and Data Protection. Initial Filing: Submit formal request to the Data Fiduciary seeking data processing summary. Followed by: Request correction, updating, or erasure of outdated personal data. Adjudication Route: Follow up with the designated Data Protection Grievance Officer. Concluding with: If unresolved, escalate the complaint to the Data Protection Board of India. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
My brother is dealing with a situation involving filing an RTI application. What does Indian law say about this?

Beyond the initial Rs 10 application fee, additional charges apply once information is actually supplied — commonly around Rs 2 per photocopied page under the central RTI Rules, with different rates for information provided on CD or in other formats — but these copying charges are separate from, and cannot exceed, what the Rules actually prescribe. In practice, so your brother can expect to pay a small additional amount per page once the information is actually supplied — that's normal and separate from the original Rs 10 filing fee, not a sign of overcharging.
A startup founder I'm advising wants to understand being laid off or retrenched from a job. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 requires an employer to satisfy three conditions before retrenching a workman who has completed at least one year of continuous service: one month's written notice (or wages in lieu of notice), retrenchment compensation equal to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service, and notice served on the appropriate government authority. In practice, in the founder's case, it's worth checking the average pay calculation carefully, since retrenchment compensation is meant to be 15 days per completed year, not a token lump sum the employer sets unilaterally.
A stranger used screenshots of my ID card to open a fake trading account and is soliciting funds from my social circle. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers identity theft using your identification documents to commit fraud, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
In West Bengal, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in West Bengal, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
A friend from Chennai asked me about an agreement or contract involving a minor — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, minority is treated as an absolute bar to contractual capacity, not just a factor courts weigh. There's a narrow exception: under Section 68, someone who supplies a minor with genuine necessaries (food, education, medical care) can be reimbursed out of the minor's property — but the minor is never personally liable, and can never ratify the void agreement upon turning 18. In practice, this means your friend can't be compelled to repay money or goods received under such an agreement, since a void contract doesn't attract the restitution rules that apply to otherwise-valid ones.
I run a small consulting business in Karnataka with annual turnover around ₹2,050,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of services in Karnataka, the threshold is ₹40 lakh for goods or ₹20 lakh for services, since Karnataka follows the higher normal-category limit that applies in most Indian states. Since your turnover of ₹2,050,000 is at or above this ₹2,000,000 threshold, you are required to register for GST.
Is there a Section 61 in the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 that lets a District Commission hear complaints of any value if both parties consent?

I'm not able to verify that Section 61 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction by party consent. Pecuniary jurisdiction under the Act is fixed by the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021 — District Commissions up to Rs. 50 lakh, State Commissions between Rs. 50 lakh and Rs. 2 crore, and the National Commission above Rs. 2 crore — and I'm not aware of a consent-based exception to these limits. Please verify this against the current Rules or with a consumer law practitioner before relying on it.
If a shopkeeper in Coimbatore is affected by PIO's ordinary reply deadline, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?
Under Section 7(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, a Public Information Officer must respond to an RTI application within 30 days of receipt.
Someone I met recently asked me about whether a small business needs to register for GST — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The current GST registration thresholds — Rs 40 lakh for goods, Rs 20 lakh for services — have been in place since 1 April 2019, when they were raised from the earlier Rs 20 lakh (goods and services) limit. The Rs 40 lakh goods threshold doesn't apply unconditionally, though — certain categories like ice cream, pan masala, tobacco products, and businesses making inter-state taxable supplies of goods are excluded and must register regardless of turnover. In practice, so this person should check which category the business falls into — if it's goods, services, or a mix, since the two thresholds (Rs 40 lakh vs Rs 20 lakh) and the special-category-state exceptions can materially change the answer.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on an agreement or contract involving a minor?

The rule from Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) still governs today — an agreement with a minor is void ab initio under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, and this holds even if the minor lied about their age to get the other party to agree. The one recognised carve-out is for contracts made by a guardian that are genuinely for the minor's benefit, such as school admission or a beneficial apprenticeship, which courts have upheld as valid.
Can you explain what Indian law says about how long you have to file a civil suit, for a small business owner I know?

The Limitation Act, 1963 doesn't erase the underlying right — it only bars going to court to enforce it after the deadline. So a debt that's become time-barred (typically after three years) still technically exists, and if the debtor voluntarily repays it later, that payment is valid; the debtor just can't be dragged to court to force that repayment. In practice, in the business owner's case, if there's any written acknowledgment of the debt — even something informal like an email — that can reset the limitation period under Section 18, so it's worth checking for that before assuming the claim is time-barred.
If my brother is affected by how long copyright protection lasts, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended), copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work generally lasts for the lifetime of the author plus 60 years, counted from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death. For works of joint authorship, the 60-year period runs from the death of whichever author dies last. In practice, in your brother's case, if the work was written by more than one author, the 60-year clock only starts running once the last surviving co-author has passed away, not the first.
What is the correct legal procedure a distant relative should follow regarding civil liability for unauthorized computer access under Indian law?
Beyond criminal liability under Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000, unauthorized computer access can separately attract civil liability for damages under Section 43.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of who can file a consumer complaint isn't handled correctly?

Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows a complaint before a District Commission to be filed by the affected consumer, a recognised consumer association on their behalf, consumers representing numerous others with the same interest, or the Central/State Government.
A woman I'm helping wants to know if she needs a lawyer to file this application or can do it herself. What does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provide?

She doesn't strictly need a lawyer — Section 12 is designed to be accessible, and a woman can approach the Magistrate herself, through a Protection Officer, or through any person acting on her behalf. In practice, having legal assistance helps in drafting the application and presenting evidence effectively, and she can seek free legal aid through the District Legal Services Authority if she cannot afford a lawyer.
Someone I met recently asked me about snatching as a standalone offence — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Section 304 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines snatching as theft committed by suddenly, quickly, or forcibly grabbing movable property from a person or their possession. It is a new addition — the IPC had no equivalent section — and the punishment prescribed is imprisonment up to three years, plus a fine. In practice, if the case is still pending investigation, this person should check whether the chargesheet correctly cites Section 304 BNS rather than an old IPC theft section, since the two carry different maximum punishments.
What does the law say if my neighbour is facing whether a small business needs to register for GST?

GST registration becomes mandatory once a business's aggregate turnover crosses Rs 40 lakh for suppliers of goods, or Rs 20 lakh for suppliers of services, in most states — with lower thresholds of Rs 20 lakh (goods) and Rs 10 lakh (services) applying in special category states in the North East and hill regions. Below these limits, registration is optional (though it can still be done voluntarily to claim input tax credit). In practice, in your neighbour's case, if the business sells across state lines even occasionally, that can trigger mandatory registration regardless of total turnover, since inter-state taxable supply is one of the categories excluded from the higher threshold.
I lent money to a client for services rendered and the ₹3,200,000 repayment cheque they gave bounced with 'funds insufficient' as the reason. Does the reason for bounce matter legally?

Not much, as long as the cheque was issued toward a legally enforceable debt or liability. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 applies when a cheque is dishonoured because the account has insufficient funds, or because the amount exceeds what's arranged to be paid from that account under an agreement with the bank — 'funds insufficient' is the classic and most common trigger for this section. Your process is the same regardless: send a legal demand notice within 30 days of learning of the bounce, asking for the ₹3,200,000; if a client for services rendered doesn't pay within 15 days of receiving it, you can file a criminal complaint within about a month after that. On conviction, the punishment is imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹6,400,000), or both, and courts frequently use the fine or compensation route to make you whole rather than imposing jail time, especially if a client for services rendered is willing to settle.
Can a husband claim maintenance from his wife under Indian law, or is this only a right for wives?

A husband can claim maintenance in limited circumstances. Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) -- the successor to Section 125 CrPC, in force from 1 July 2024 -- is drafted in secular, largely gender-neutral terms allowing a Magistrate to order maintenance for a wife, child, or parent who cannot maintain themselves, from a person with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to provide for them. While the classic and far more common use is a wife or ex-wife claiming from her husband, courts have in principle recognised that a husband who is unable to maintain himself (for instance due to disability) and whose wife has sufficient means could also seek maintenance under this framework, since the provision doesn't restrict claimants by gender in that specific sub-clause the way older laws sometimes did. That said, a financially capable husband generally cannot claim maintenance from his wife just because she earns more -- the core requirement of being unable to maintain oneself still applies. This is a developing and fact-specific area, so specific advice from a family lawyer is important.
If a relative going through a difficult time is affected by a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking, or abetting the giving or taking of dowry is punishable with a minimum of five years' imprisonment and a fine of at least Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is higher (courts can impose a lesser sentence only for adequate and special reasons recorded in writing). Section 4 separately punishes merely demanding dowry, directly or indirectly, from the bride's or groom's family, with imprisonment of six months to two years and/or a fine. In practice, in your relative's case, if dowry was given only because of pressure or coercion from the other side, the law has been read to shield the giver from being treated as equally culpable as an abettor.
How does Indian law actually treat identity theft using stolen credentials, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000 punishes fraudulently using another's electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature, with imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding the 3-month limitation to challenge an award?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an application to set aside an arbitral award must be made within three months from the date the party received the award, or, if a Section 33 correction request was made, from the date that request was disposed of.
An artist friend of mine asked me about maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Despite the existence of the 1986 Act specific to Muslim women, courts (including the Allahabad High Court in several recent rulings) have reaffirmed that a divorced Muslim woman retains the right to seek ongoing maintenance under the secular maintenance provision (now BNSS Section 144, earlier CrPC Section 125) as long as she hasn't remarried — the 1986 Act doesn't bar her from that route, since Parliament never explicitly excluded it. In practice, this means your artist friend should know that if her former husband genuinely cannot pay, the law does provide a further fallback — first to relatives who'd inherit from her, and only then to the State Waqf Board.
How does Indian law actually treat the 30-day condonable extension, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

The proviso to Section 34(3) allows courts to condone delay by a further 30 days for sufficient cause, but the words "not thereafter" make this an absolute outer limit, strictly applied by the Supreme Court.
How does Indian law actually treat express versus implied maintenance condition, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Courts differ on whether the maintenance condition under Section 23(1) must be expressly written into the deed: the Kerala High Court's full bench requires an express clause, while other High Courts allow the condition to be implied from circumstances.
If a small business owner I know is affected by filing a first appeal, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

If a Public Information Officer fails to respond within the time limit under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, or gives an unsatisfactory decision, the applicant can file a First Appeal to the First Appellate Authority within the same public authority under Section 19(1).
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company?

The high-profile Tata Sons v. Cyrus Mistry dispute was fought under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 — illustrating that this remedy isn't limited to small family companies, but is available even in large public companies where minority (or removed) shareholders believe the majority's conduct has been unfairly prejudicial to their interests.
What does the law say if someone I met recently is facing a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime?

Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a child aged 16 to 18 accused of a "heinous offence" — defined under Section 2(33) as one carrying a minimum sentence of seven years or more — can be tried as an adult, but only after the Juvenile Justice Board conducts a preliminary assessment of the child's mental and physical capacity to commit the offence and their ability to understand its consequences, under Section 15. In practice, for this person, the age at the time of the alleged offence is critical — if the child was under 16, this adult-trial provision simply doesn't apply regardless of how serious the offence was.
A friend of mine is dealing with a situation involving jurisdiction to file a cheque bounce complaint. What does Indian law say about this?

A Section 138 cheque dishonour case is not filed as a police FIR; it is a private criminal complaint before a Magistrate. Following the 2015 amendment to the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, jurisdiction lies with the court within whose local limits the bank branch of the payee (where the cheque was presented for collection) is situated.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding cheating by personation online?

Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device — pretending to be someone else online to deceive a third party — with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine of up to Rs. 1 lakh, the same punishment prescribed under Section 66C.
How does Indian law actually treat punishment for an ordinary person's failure to report, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Failure to report under Section 19 or Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012 is punishable under Section 21(1) with imprisonment up to six months, a fine, or both.
What prerequisites and documentation are essential before initiating seeking protection orders under the Domestic Violence Act?

Prerequisites & Jurisdiction: In Women and Child Protection, before undertaking seeking protection orders under the Domestic Violence Act, applicants must ensure: (1) Mandatory preparation: Approach Protection Officer, service provider, or Magistrate directly. (2) Initial compliance: Prepare Domestic Incident Report (DIR) detailing domestic violence and relationship. Subsequent procedure: Magistrate issues notice and conducts hearing within prescribed statutory timelines. Obtain protection, residence, monetary relief, or custody orders. Careful preparation of documentary evidence avoids summary dismissal.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on hit-and-run accident compensation?

Where the driver in an accident can't be traced, Indian law still provides for compensation: the 2022 scheme under the Motor Vehicles Act sets Rs 2 lakh for a death and Rs 50,000 for grievous injury, paid from the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund. If the vehicle and driver are traced, the compensation figures are different and higher, and the victim can alternatively pursue a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal.
What does Indian law currently say about a passport being impounded or seized?

The Supreme Court has clarified that only the passport authority under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967 has the power to impound a passport — the police, by contrast, can only seize a passport as a document or property under general criminal procedure powers, but cannot themselves impound it, since the Passports Act is a specific law that overrides the general provision.
What is the correct legal procedure a small business owner I know should follow regarding enhanced punishment for institutional heads under Indian law?
Section 21(2) of the POCSO Act, 2012 prescribes imprisonment up to one year and a fine for a person in charge of an institution who fails to report a subordinate's offence.
I'm Pooja. Sunita's cheque for Rs. 500000 bounced, and I sent the legal notice 10 days ago. Sunita hasn't responded. What happens now?

Since Sunita received the notice 10 days ago, they still have until the 15-day mark to make the payment. If that period passes with no payment, the offence under Section 138 NI Act is treated as complete, and you get 30 days from the end of the 15-day period to file a criminal complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court.

Keep your proof of notice delivery (courier/postal receipt, or acknowledgment) safe, as you'll need it to show the notice was validly served. If payment does come in during the remaining days, that would resolve the matter without needing to go to court.
What does the law say if a relative going through a difficult time is facing minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company?

Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 let a member (or members) of a company approach the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for relief where the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner oppressive to some members or prejudicial to the company's or public interest. To even file the petition, Section 244 requires either at least 100 members (or one-tenth of the total membership, whichever is less) or members holding at least one-tenth of the issued share capital, with all calls on their shares paid up. In practice, in your relative's case, it's worth documenting the specific conduct carefully, since courts have made clear that mere loss of confidence between shareholders or a single bad business decision doesn't, on its own, count as oppression.
What does Indian law currently say about being laid off or retrenched from a job?

The Industrial Disputes Act's retrenchment compensation under Section 25F is calculated the same way as gratuity — 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service (or part thereof exceeding six months) — but it's a separate entitlement from gratuity, payable in addition to it where both apply, and gratuity payable on retrenchment is specifically excluded from the retrenchment compensation calculation itself.

A retail application collects continuous background geolocation from users without displaying any privacy disclosure or obtaining consent. What legal remedies and options are available under Indian law?

Collecting continuous background location data without a clear notice or valid consent conflicts with the consent and notice requirements under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. A data fiduciary must give data principals an itemised notice describing what personal data is collected and for what purpose, and must obtain free, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent before or at the time of collection; consent cannot be inferred merely from continued use of the app. Collecting geolocation silently, in the background, without such notice and consent would not meet this standard and could expose the company to enforcement action and penalties under the Act. The company's freedom to design its product as it wishes does not override these statutory consent obligations.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding theft by a servant or employee?

Theft committed by a clerk or servant in respect of property in the possession of their employer is punished under Section 306 of the BNS, 2023 with imprisonment of up to seven years and a fine, an enhancement over ordinary theft under Section 303.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of express versus implied maintenance condition isn't handled correctly?

Courts differ on whether the maintenance condition under Section 23(1) must be expressly written into the deed: the Kerala High Court's full bench requires an express clause, while other High Courts allow the condition to be implied from circumstances.
A tenant I know asked me about setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Section 4 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) makes it mandatory for every employer with 10 or more employees to constitute an Internal Committee (IC) at each office or branch to receive and inquire into complaints. Failing to set one up attracts a penalty under Section 26 starting at Rs 50,000, doubled for a repeat offence, and can even lead to cancellation of the business's licence or registration. In practice, for the tenant, if the organisation has 10 or more people counting everyone (not just permanent staff), the absence of an Internal Committee is itself a compliance failure the employer can be penalised for under Section 26.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding PIO's ordinary reply deadline?
Under Section 7(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, a Public Information Officer must respond to an RTI application within 30 days of receipt.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of waiver of a termination notice by accepting rent isn't handled correctly?
A landlord who serves a Section 106 notice but then accepts rent afterward risks that conduct being treated as a waiver of the notice.
How does Indian law actually treat transfers other than gifts covered by Section 23, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 23(1) covers transfers "by way of gift or otherwise," which courts have read to include release deeds, settlements, and sales made on the understanding that the senior citizen would be looked after.
If my neighbour is affected by the 3-month limitation to challenge an award, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an application to set aside an arbitral award must be made within three months from the date the party received the award, or, if a Section 33 correction request was made, from the date that request was disposed of.
What does the law say if a small business owner I know is facing anticipatory bail?

Anticipatory bail is now governed by Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, which replaced Section 438 of the old CrPC from 1 July 2024. It lets a person who reasonably fears arrest for a non-bailable offence apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for a direction that, if arrested, they be released on bail. Under Section 482(4), this remedy is barred for anyone accused of raping a woman under sixteen, or of gang rape of a woman under eighteen. In practice, for the business owner, the first thing to confirm is which offence is alleged — if it falls under the Section 482(4) exception, anticipatory bail simply isn't available and a different strategy is needed.
Under which statutory framework is the notion that 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.' specifically refuted?

Statutory Refutation: The assumption that 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.' is refuted under Company and Business Law. Substantive Provision: Director immunity is not absolute. Directors face personal liability for statutory tax defaults, bouncing company cheques under the NI Act, fraud, and situations where courts pierce the corporate veil. Legal Principle: Indian statutes require formal compliance and do not sanction informal evasions.
A 16-year-old has disclosed being sexually assaulted by their coach at a sports academy. What punishment applies to the accused?

Since the victim has completed 16 years but POCSO defines a 'child' as anyone below 18, she or he is still fully covered. Under Section 4 of the POCSO Act, 2012 (as amended in 2019), penetrative sexual assault carries a minimum of 10 years' rigorous imprisonment, extendable to life, along with a mandatory fine. Because the accused is a coach — someone in a position of trust and authority over the child in a sports academy setting — the offence is very likely to qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Sections 5 and 6, which carries a higher minimum of 20 years, extendable to life imprisonment or the death penalty in the gravest cases. Consent is legally irrelevant since the victim is under 18, and the case will be tried before a Special POCSO Court.
I heard something about theft in a dwelling house or place of worship that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?

Theft committed inside a dwelling house, place of worship, or means of transport is punished more severely under Section 305 of the BNS, 2023, carrying imprisonment of up to seven years plus a fine, rather than the up-to-three-year term under ordinary Section 303 theft.
A shopkeeper in coimbatore is dealing with a situation involving penalty on a defaulting PIO. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 20 of the RTI Act, 2005 empowers the Information Commission to impose a penalty on a Public Information Officer for unreasonable delay, malafide denial, or destruction of information, calculated per day of delay, subject to a prescribed maximum.
I am Kiran from Indore. I paid Lata Rs. 42000 by cheque towards rent dues, but the cheque bounced due to insufficient funds. What should I do next?

Since the cheque bounced for insufficient funds, this falls under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Your first step is to send Lata a written legal (demand) notice, and you must do this within 30 days of receiving the bank's cheque-return memo -- don't let that window lapse, as it can affect your ability to prosecute later.

After the notice is served, Lata gets 15 days to pay the Rs. 42000 back. Only if that 15-day period passes without payment does the cause of action for a criminal complaint arise, and you'd then have 30 days from the end of that period to file the complaint in court. The trial procedure itself is now governed by the BNSS rather than the old CrPC.

I'd suggest consulting a local advocate to draft the notice correctly, since defects in the notice (wrong amount, wrong dates) are a common reason these cases get dismissed.
What does the law say if a friend's mother is facing a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan?

Once a loan account is classified as a non-performing asset, Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 requires the secured creditor (usually a bank or NBFC) to issue a demand notice giving the borrower 60 days to repay the outstanding dues before the lender can move to take possession of the mortgaged property under Section 13(4). In practice, for your friend's mother, the 60-day period isn't just a waiting period — it's the window to either repay, negotiate a settlement, or file a written objection under Section 13(3A) challenging the notice.
How do the missing details in 'I want a divorce and maintenance from my spouse immediately.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Family Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) Which personal law applies to the marriage (e.g., Hindu Marriage Act, Special Marriage Act, Muslim personal law); (2) Whether the divorce is by mutual consent or contested; (3) Whether there are minor children and existing interim maintenance orders. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
I run a small trading business in Tamil Nadu with annual turnover around ₹4,200,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of goods in Tamil Nadu, the threshold is ₹40 lakh for goods or ₹20 lakh for services, since Tamil Nadu follows the higher normal-category limit that applies in most Indian states. Since your turnover of ₹4,200,000 is at or above this ₹4,000,000 threshold, you are required to register for GST.
If the Sessions Court rejects my anticipatory bail application, is that the end of the road?

No. Under Section 482 BNSS, both the Court of Session and the High Court have concurrent jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail -- they aren't a strict hierarchy you must exhaust in order, but in practice most applicants approach the Sessions Court first and go to the High Court if that's refused, if the case involves complex legal questions, or if there's a genuine concern about a fair hearing at the lower level. If the Sessions Court rejects the application, you can file a fresh application before the High Court; this isn't technically an 'appeal' against the Sessions Court order but a fresh invocation of the High Court's own jurisdiction under the same section. Courts do expect the applicant to disclose that an earlier application was rejected and why, rather than concealing it.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding notice must align with the tenancy cycle?

A 15-day termination notice for a month-to-month tenancy under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 should be structured to expire with the end of a month of the tenancy — aligned with the monthly rental cycle — rather than being calculated as an arbitrary count of 15 calendar days from any date.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding how a correction request affects the limitation clock?

Where a party makes a genuine request under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (for correction, interpretation, or an additional award), the three-month limitation under Section 34(3) to challenge the award runs from the date the tribunal disposes of that request rather than from the date of the original award — though a request that is, in substance, a disguised attempt to have the tribunal review the award's merits may not get this benefit.
A person cloned my WhatsApp profile picture and number-adjacent account and is asking my friends for a loan. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers impersonation for financial fraud over a messaging app, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
