Can a government department refuse my RTI application just by saying the information is 'confidential'?

Not just by asserting the word 'confidential' -- the department has to bring the refusal within one of the specific exemption categories listed in Section 8(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, such as information affecting the sovereignty and integrity of India, security or strategic interests, information forbidden by a court, commercial confidence or trade secrets (unless larger public interest favours disclosure), or information held in a fiduciary relationship (again, subject to the public-interest override). A vague claim of 'confidentiality' without pointing to a specific clause and reasoning generally doesn't meet this bar, and you can challenge it in a first appeal. There's also an important time-based limitation on most of these exemptions under Section 8(3): with a few exceptions (like information affecting sovereignty/security, breach of legislative privilege, or Cabinet papers), most Section 8(1) exemptions stop applying once the information is more than 20 years old, and such older records generally have to be disclosed.
How does Indian law actually treat charging both identity theft and online cheating together, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Where stolen credentials (Section 66C) are used to impersonate the victim and deceive a third party, both Section 66C and Section 66D of the IT Act, 2000 can be invoked together for the same conduct.
My elder relative wants to understand how long a trademark registration lasts. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a trademark registration is valid for 10 years from the date of the original application (not the date the certificate is actually issued), and can be renewed indefinitely for further 10-year periods by filing Form TM-R and paying the prescribed fee before expiry. In practice, in your elder relative's case, if the renewal deadline has already passed, there's still a one-year window (six months grace plus a further six months) to apply for restoration, but after that the mark can be picked up by someone else.
Review this contract clause: "Goods once sold will not be returned, exchanged, or refunded under any circumstances." Is this enforceable under Indian law, and what are its boundaries?

Regarding the clause "Goods once sold will not be returned, exchanged, or refunded under any circumstances.": This is a common retail boilerplate disclaimer. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, such unilateral disclaimers cannot override consumer statutory rights against defective goods, deficiency in service, or unfair trade practices, and are classified as unfair contract terms. Enforceability depends on statutory compliance, public policy, and whether the restriction is unconscionable or penal.
A client i'm helping is dealing with a situation involving enforcing a maintenance charge against a transferee. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 23(2) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 allows a senior citizen with a right to receive maintenance out of an estate to enforce that right against a transferee of the estate who had notice of the right, or where the transfer was gratuitous — though not against a transferee for consideration without notice of the right.
A hotel employee found what looked like evidence of child sexual abuse involving a guest but didn't report it because it wasn't 'their business.' Is there a specific legal duty on hotel staff here?

Yes -- Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012 places a specific, heightened reporting obligation on media personnel, hotel and lodge staff, hospital staff, and photographic facility/studio staff: if they come across any material or object that is sexually exploitative of a child (such as images, recordings, or similar evidence) through the establishment or facility they work at, they must report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police. This is on top of the general duty on 'any person' under Section 19. Failing to report under Section 20, like failing to report under Section 19, attracts penalties under Section 21 POCSO -- imprisonment up to six months, a fine, or both, and up to one year plus a fine if the person is in a supervisory or in-charge role over the person who should have reported. 'Not my business' is not a defence the statute recognises.
What does Indian law currently say about whether a small business needs to register for GST?

The turnover figure that matters for GST registration is 'aggregate turnover' — which is broader than just taxable sales, and includes exempt supplies, exports, and inter-state supplies too, all computed PAN-India across every branch of the business, not per state. So a business might look like it's under the Rs 40 lakh goods threshold on taxable sales alone but actually be over it once exempt and export turnover is added in.
What does the law say if my neighbour is facing setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment?

Section 4 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) makes it mandatory for every employer with 10 or more employees to constitute an Internal Committee (IC) at each office or branch to receive and inquire into complaints. Failing to set one up attracts a penalty under Section 26 starting at Rs 50,000, doubled for a repeat offence, and can even lead to cancellation of the business's licence or registration. In practice, for your neighbour, if the organisation has 10 or more people counting everyone (not just permanent staff), the absence of an Internal Committee is itself a compliance failure the employer can be penalised for under Section 26.
Under which statutory framework is the notion that 'Signing an 'as-is' purchase receipt waives all consumer protection rights against defective products.' specifically refuted?

Statutory Refutation: The assumption that 'Signing an 'as-is' purchase receipt waives all consumer protection rights against defective products.' is refuted under Consumer Protection. Substantive Provision: Boilerplate waivers and disclaimers cannot override statutory consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Sellers remain liable for manufacturing defects, misleading advertisements, and unfair trade practices. Legal Principle: Indian statutes require formal compliance and do not sanction informal evasions.
How does Indian law actually treat bond to prevent further violence, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Under Section 19(3) of the PWDV Act, 2005, the Magistrate may require the respondent to execute a bond to prevent further domestic violence, treated as an order under Chapter VIII CrPC.
What risks arise if legal action is commenced on the basis of 'A commercial client withheld cloud access keys after an invoice dispute.' without clarifying the missing facts?

Litigation Risk: Initiating legal action on incomplete facts in Information Technology Law carries severe risks: (1) The ownership clauses governing proprietary data hosted on the servers; (2) Whether the withholding constitutes unauthorized denial of access under the IT Act; (3) The dispute resolution and suspension clauses in the master services agreement. Consequences: The suit may face summary rejection, liability for costs, or irreparable damage to the client's position.
I'm Arjun. As a disabled adult daughter, my husband has a good government job but says he owes me nothing since we're separated. Can I claim maintenance, and how does that work?

This would fall under Section 144 BNSS, which replaced Section 125 CrPC from 1 July 2024, and lets a Magistrate order maintenance for a wife, child, or parent who is neglected despite the other person having sufficient means. Courts treat this as a summary, welfare-oriented remedy meant to prevent destitution, not to punish anyone.

You'd need to file an application before the appropriate Magistrate, along with an affidavit of your income and needs. Maintenance is usually payable from the date you filed the application, not just from the date of the final order, so filing promptly matters. I'd recommend consulting a family-law advocate to help calculate a realistic amount based on the other side's income.
Can you explain what Indian law says about being laid off or retrenched from a job, for someone in my apartment complex?

The Industrial Disputes Act's retrenchment compensation under Section 25F is calculated the same way as gratuity — 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service (or part thereof exceeding six months) — but it's a separate entitlement from gratuity, payable in addition to it where both apply, and gratuity payable on retrenchment is specifically excluded from the retrenchment compensation calculation itself. In practice, so if that person's job ended because the whole business was sold or transferred, the same notice-and-compensation protection applies unless the new employer kept that person on with no less favourable terms.
Explain the legal position regarding the common misconception that 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.'

Legal Position: The premise that 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.' is contrary to established statutory principles in Company and Business Law. Director immunity is not absolute. Directors face personal liability for statutory tax defaults, bouncing company cheques under the NI Act, fraud, and situations where courts pierce the corporate veil. Judicial View: Courts consistently refuse to recognize such informal claims, holding parties strictly to statutory standards.
What is the correct legal procedure a person I met recently should follow regarding identity theft using stolen credentials under Indian law?

Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000 punishes fraudulently using another's electronic signature, password, or unique identification feature, with imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding how long copyright protection lasts?

Once a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work's copyright term expires — 60 years after the author's death under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — the work enters the public domain and can be freely copied, adapted, or republished without permission, unlike a trademark, which can in principle be renewed forever.
In Bihar, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Bihar, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of the 30-day condonable extension isn't handled correctly?

The proviso to Section 34(3) allows courts to condone delay by a further 30 days for sufficient cause, but the words "not thereafter" make this an absolute outer limit, strictly applied by the Supreme Court.
What does the law say if my elder relative is facing being laid off or retrenched from a job?

Where a business is transferred (Section 25FF) or an undertaking closes down (Section 25FFF), workmen who've completed at least a year of continuous service are entitled to the same notice-and-compensation protection as under Section 25F, treated as if they had been retrenched — unless, in the case of a transfer, the new employer offers continued service on terms no less favourable than before. In practice, for your elder relative, the first thing to verify is whether all three Section 25F conditions were actually met — a retrenchment missing even the government notice can be challenged as legally invalid, separate from any dispute about the reason for the layoff.
My brother asked me about a passport being impounded or seized — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The Supreme Court has clarified that only the passport authority under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967 has the power to impound a passport — the police, by contrast, can only seize a passport as a document or property under general criminal procedure powers, but cannot themselves impound it, since the Passports Act is a specific law that overrides the general provision. In practice, this means your brother has a 30-day window to appeal the impounding order to the appropriate appellate authority, so that deadline shouldn't be missed while gathering other paperwork.
I received an arbitral award in a franchise agreement dispute 3 months and 25 days ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 3 months and 25 days have passed since you received the award, you should still be within, or close to, the permissible window, so you should file your Section 34 application without further delay to be safe, especially since if you're past the initial 3 months you would need to show sufficient cause for the extension and delay itself weakens that showing. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
What is the correct legal procedure a small business owner I know should follow regarding jurisdiction to file a cheque bounce complaint under Indian law?

A Section 138 case is a private criminal complaint before a Magistrate, not a police FIR. Following the 2015 amendment, jurisdiction lies with the court where the payee's bank branch (where the cheque was presented) is situated.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of filing against relatives of the husband isn't handled correctly?
A proviso to the PWDV Act, 2005 lets an aggrieved wife file a complaint against a relative of the husband, not only the husband himself.
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹40,000/month residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 2 months' rent for residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹40,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹80,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
Under which statutory framework is the notion that 'A domestic violence complaint can only be filed against the husband, not in-laws or other relatives.' specifically refuted?

Statutory Refutation: The assumption that 'A domestic violence complaint can only be filed against the husband, not in-laws or other relatives.' is refuted under Women and Child Protection. Substantive Provision: Under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, a domestic incident can be filed against any adult male or female relative who has lived in a shared household with the aggrieved woman. Legal Principle: Indian statutes require formal compliance and do not sanction informal evasions.
Under Section 250 of the Transfer of Property Act, is a landlord required to give six months' notice even for a purely residential month-to-month tenancy?

I'm not able to verify a Section 250 in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 imposing that requirement. In fact, Section 106 of the Act specifically treats a residential (or other non-agricultural, non-manufacturing) tenancy as month-to-month, requiring only 15 days' notice for termination by either party — the six-month notice period applies to agricultural or manufacturing leases, not residential ones. Please verify the correct section before relying on any six-month figure for a residential tenancy.
A woman wants to know if she can still file under Section 12 even though she and her husband have been legally separated for the past year, if past abuse is what she wants addressed.

Yes, legal separation does not automatically bar her from filing. What matters for a Section 12 application is that a 'domestic relationship' existed at some point between her and the respondent, as defined under the Act — it isn't strictly limited to currently cohabiting couples. There's no fixed limitation period tied to when the abuse occurred, so she can seek reliefs like monetary compensation or protection orders addressing the impact of past abuse even after separation. The Magistrate, once the application is filed, is required to try to dispose of it within 60 days of the first hearing under Section 12(5).
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over issuing a statutory legal notice prior to civil suit, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for issuing a statutory legal notice prior to civil suit is determined by statutory rules under Civil Law. Initial Filing: Set out facts, breach of obligations, and exact monetary or specific relief demanded. Followed by: Provide a reasonable response period (typically 15 to 30 days). Adjudication Route: Dispatch via Registered Post with Acknowledgment Due (RPAD) and retain proof of delivery. Concluding with: If unheeded, proceed with filing the civil suit. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
What is the correct legal procedure someone from my hometown should follow regarding compulsory registration of property transfer documents under Indian law?

Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires compulsory registration of non-testamentary instruments creating, assigning, limiting, or extinguishing a right, title, or interest of Rs. 100 or more in immovable property.
Can you explain what Indian law says about maternity leave entitlement, for a shopkeeper in Coimbatore?

Since the 2017 amendment to the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, paid leave for the first two children stands at 26 weeks, not the earlier 12 — making India's entitlement one of the more generous globally. Employers who knowingly ask a woman to work in the six weeks immediately following delivery or miscarriage can face up to 3 months' imprisonment, with or without a fine, under the Act. In practice, so the shopkeeper can also ask about the work-from-home option once the 26-week leave ends, since the amendment specifically enables that where the job allows it.
What is the correct legal procedure a tenant I spoke with should follow regarding obtaining a protection order under Indian law?

Once satisfied domestic violence occurred, a Magistrate can pass a protection order under Section 18 of the PWDV Act, 2005, restraining the respondent from further violence, aiding it, or contacting the aggrieved person.
What legal traps or risks arise if someone relies on the assumption that 'Parents who gifted property to children can never revoke the gift even if children abandon them.'?

Risk Overview: Relying on 'Parents who gifted property to children can never revoke the gift even if children abandon them.' exposes individuals to serious legal vulnerabilities in Senior Citizen-related law. Correct Principle: Under Section 23 of the Senior Citizens Act, if property was transferred on condition of providing basic care, failure to do so allows the Maintenance Tribunal to declare the transfer void. Next Step: Consult an advocate and rely exclusively on formal registered documentation and statutory procedures. Note: Courts are not fully aligned on whether the maintenance condition must be expressly recorded in the transfer document (Madras High Court) or can be inferred (Bombay High Court, 2026) -- so document the maintenance condition explicitly wherever possible to avoid this dispute.
I think the terms in a service contract I signed are deeply one-sided and unfair. Can I challenge just the contract itself under consumer law?

Yes -- the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 specifically allows a consumer to challenge a contract as an 'unfair contract' and seek its annulment, not just claim compensation for a specific defective good or service. For this category, jurisdiction is based purely on the value of the goods/services involved: the State Commission handles it if the value is up to Rs. 10 crore, and the National Commission if it exceeds that. This is a useful route if your real objection is to how the contract itself was drafted -- for example, one-sided penalty clauses or clauses that let the company escape all liability -- rather than to a single transaction going wrong.
My neighbour is dealing with a situation involving filing against relatives of the husband. What does Indian law say about this?

While the PWDV Act, 2005 primarily defines a "respondent" as an adult male in a domestic relationship with the aggrieved person, a specific proviso allows an aggrieved wife or a woman in a relationship in the nature of marriage to also file a complaint against a relative of the husband or male partner, so female in-laws can be named as respondents alongside the husband.
I'm Pooja. I was in a road accident 10 year(s) ago that caused months of hospitalisation, and I never filed for compensation. Is it too late to approach the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal?

You're likely not barred by time. Unlike many other claims, there's no fixed limitation period for filing a compensation claim before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) -- an older six-month bar under a earlier provision was removed by amendment. That said, a delay of 10 year(s) is fairly long, and the Tribunal can still ask you to explain the delay even though there's no statutory deadline forcing rejection.

Practical point: gather whatever records you still have -- the FIR, medical/post-mortem records, hospital bills, and any accident report -- since after this much time, evidence becomes harder to establish. I'd recommend approaching a lawyer soon to file the claim rather than delaying further, given how documentation degrades over time.

This clause appears in an agreement I was given: "The security deposit shall be forfeited in full in case of early termination of this agreement by the tenant before the lock-in period." What does it mean in practical terms?

Plain Meaning: The clause states: "The security deposit shall be forfeited in full in case of early termination of this agreement by the tenant before the lock-in period." Explanation: This is a forfeiture and lock-in stipulation in a lease agreement. Under Indian contract law, forfeiture of security deposits must represent a genuine pre-estimate of loss rather than an unconscionable penalty under Section 74 of the Contract Act. Reasonable lock-in terms are enforceable, but outright forfeiture without reference to actual vacant period loss may be contested. Practical Advice: Read this in the context of the entire document, especially definitions, cure periods, and exception clauses.
What is the correct legal procedure a client I'm helping should follow regarding compulsory registration of leases exceeding one year under Indian law?
Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires compulsory registration of leases of immovable property from year to year, for a term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent.
I was harmed by a two-wheeler helmet that cracked on a minor fall, offering no real protection. Can I claim compensation from the manufacturer under Indian consumer law?

Yes — this falls under the product liability provisions in Chapter VI of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Section 84 makes a product manufacturer liable in a product liability action where, among other grounds, the product has a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from its own manufacturing specifications, doesn't conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions and warnings to prevent harm — your case appears to involve design defect making the product inherently unsafe. Importantly, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer can be held liable even if they weren't negligent or fraudulent in making an express warranty, which introduces a strict-liability element focused on whether the product caused harm rather than the manufacturer's intent. You can file a complaint before the relevant Consumer Commission (District, State, or National, depending on the claim value), which has the power to order removal of the defect, replacement, refund with interest, compensation including punitive damages for negligence, and even direct withdrawal of the hazardous product from the market. Keep your purchase receipt, photos or medical records of the harm, and any advertising material showing the manufacturer's claims, as this evidence strengthens a product liability claim.
Can you explain what Indian law says about an agreement or contract involving a minor, for a factory worker I spoke with?

A contract entered into with a minor has no legal existence at all under Indian law — it's void ab initio, not simply cancellable, following the century-old Privy Council precedent in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903). Because there was never a valid agreement in the first place, Section 65 of the Contract Act (which allows restitution when an agreement is later discovered to be void) doesn't even apply, and the minor generally cannot be compelled to return anything received. In practice, in the worker's case, even if the other party claims they were misled about the age involved, that misrepresentation doesn't revive the contract or bind the minor to it.
A cheque for ₹3,500,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹3,500,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹7,000,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on gratuity owed after leaving a job?

Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employee becomes eligible for gratuity after completing five years of continuous service (courts have accepted 240 days worked in the fifth year as satisfying this), except where employment ends due to death or disablement, in which case the five-year requirement doesn't apply at all. Gratuity is calculated as (last drawn salary × 15 × number of years of service) ÷ 26, and the maximum payable under the Act is capped at Rs 20 lakh, following the 2018 amendment that raised it from Rs 10 lakh.
If my neighbour is affected by a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The 2015 Juvenile Justice Act was the first Indian law to allow trying a 16-18 year old as an adult, but this isn't automatic — the Juvenile Justice Board must first assess, within three months of the child being produced before it, whether the child had the capacity to understand the offence and its consequences, before referring the matter to the Children's Court for a final decision on adult trial. In practice, in your neighbour's case, it's worth confirming through the JJ Board process that a lawyer and child psychologist are actually involved in the preliminary assessment, since the law specifically requires that support.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a dowry demand or dowry-related harassment?

Under Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, giving, taking, or abetting the giving or taking of dowry is punishable with a minimum of five years' imprisonment and a fine of at least Rs 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is higher (courts can impose a lesser sentence only for adequate and special reasons recorded in writing). Section 4 separately punishes merely demanding dowry, directly or indirectly, from the bride's or groom's family, with imprisonment of six months to two years and/or a fine.
If a colleague at work is affected by anticipatory bail in a case under the SC/ST Atrocities Act, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The SC/ST Act's Section 18 bar on anticipatory bail exists to protect complainants from intimidation, but courts scrutinise whether the alleged conduct was actually connected to the victim's caste or tribal identity — knowing someone's SC/ST status while insulting them isn't, by itself, enough; the insult has to be intended to humiliate them because of that identity for the Act's offences, and its bail bar, to apply. In practice, this gives your colleague's lawyer a specific legal argument to raise at the first hearing: that the alleged remarks or conduct weren't shown to be linked to the complainant's caste identity, which is a requirement for the Act to apply.
I run a small trading business in Telangana with annual turnover around ₹1,950,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of goods in Telangana, the threshold is ₹20 lakh, since Telangana is a special category state (or notified as such) with a lower limit than most other states. Since your turnover of ₹1,950,000 is below this ₹2,000,000 threshold, registration isn't mandatory yet, though you can opt for voluntary registration under Section 25(3) if you want to claim input tax credit or issue GST invoices. Note that certain categories — like inter-state suppliers, e-commerce sellers, or those under compulsory registration in Section 24 — must register regardless of turnover.
A child aged 10 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, penetrative sexual assault on a child below 16 years of age — which covers a 10-year-old victim — carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 20 years, extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's natural life, along with a mandatory fine. The 2019 amendment specifically raised this minimum from 10 to 20 years for victims under 16 to reflect the heightened severity. Since the accused is described as a relative, the offence may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5/6 if the relative was in a position of trust or authority, in which case the minimum sentence rises further to 20 years up to life, or even the death penalty in the most extreme cases where the court considers it warranted. Since a child under 18 is involved, consent is legally irrelevant, and the case will be tried by a Special POCSO Court, with the trial conducted in a manner sensitive to the child.
Before the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act, what rights did a daughter have in her father's ancestral property, and how is that different from today?

Before the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, only male descendants — sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons — were coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family governed by Mitakshara law, meaning they acquired an interest in ancestral property by birth. A daughter was treated merely as a "member" of the family without any inherent birthright to that property; she could inherit only a limited share after her father's death, and even then subject to restrictions, and she could not demand partition or claim survivorship rights during her father's lifetime. The 2005 amendment to Section 6 changed this entirely by making the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth in her own right, with the same rights and liabilities as a son — and the Supreme Court has since clarified in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) that this operates retrospectively based on the daughter's birth, not on whether her father was alive when the amendment took effect.
If a friend from Chennai is affected by the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The RTE Act's Section 12(1)(c) reservation applies to private unaided non-minority schools, requiring 25% of Class 1 (or equivalent entry-level) seats to go to children from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups. Implementation has varied significantly by state, and courts have repeatedly had to direct governments to frame clearer rules to ensure the quota is actually filled rather than left as seats on paper. In practice, so if your friend's application is refused without valid reason despite meeting the eligibility criteria, that refusal can be challenged, since the Supreme Court has upheld this reservation as a constitutionally valid, enforceable right.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding the 25% quota for weaker-section children in private schools?

Under Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009, admission under the 25% EWS quota is meant to be free of cost to the family — the school cannot charge tuition or other fees for these seats, and instead claims reimbursement from the government at the rate specified under the rules.
My sister-in-law wants to understand maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Despite the existence of the 1986 Act specific to Muslim women, courts (including the Allahabad High Court in several recent rulings) have reaffirmed that a divorced Muslim woman retains the right to seek ongoing maintenance under the secular maintenance provision (now BNSS Section 144, earlier CrPC Section 125) as long as she hasn't remarried — the 1986 Act doesn't bar her from that route, since Parliament never explicitly excluded it. In practice, this means your sister-in-law should know that if her former husband genuinely cannot pay, the law does provide a further fallback — first to relatives who'd inherit from her, and only then to the State Waqf Board.
Is it true that a cheque bounce case under Section 138 of the NI Act can be filed at any police station in India, since it's a criminal offence?

No, that is not correct. A Section 138 NI Act case is not initiated through a police FIR at a local police station in the way an offence like theft might be; it proceeds by way of a private criminal complaint filed by the payee or holder in due course before a Magistrate having jurisdiction. Following the 2015 amendment to the Negotiable Instruments Act, jurisdiction lies with the court within whose local limits the bank branch of the payee (where the cheque was presented for collection) is situated. Filing at an unrelated police station or an incorrect court would not satisfy the procedural requirements of Section 138, and the complainant must still first send the mandatory 30-day demand notice and wait for the drawer's 15-day payment window before the complaint can be filed at all.
Someone in my family is dealing with a situation involving notice period for a month-to-month tenancy. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contrary contract, local law, or usage, a lease for any purpose other than agriculture or manufacturing (such as residential or commercial use) is deemed a month-to-month tenancy, terminable by either party giving 15 days' notice.
Are there mandatory pre-litigation steps or notices required before approaching a court under Criminal Law?

In Criminal Law, several statutory frameworks mandate pre-litigation steps. For government bodies or statutory claims, advance notice of 30 to 60 days is frequently mandatory. Commercial disputes and certain family matters require attempting pre-litigation mediation unless urgent interim relief is claimed.
If a client I'm helping is affected by punishment for an ordinary person's failure to report, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Failure to report an offence under Section 19 or Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012 (or failure to record such an offence) is punishable under Section 21(1) with imprisonment of either description for up to six months, a fine, or both.

A small business owner receives a sixty-day formal possession notice from a secured lender under recovery statutes after three unpaid loan installments. On whom does the burden of proof lie in this situation, and what legal presumptions apply?

Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023, the general rule on burden of proof is that whoever desires a court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability depending on the existence of certain facts must prove that those facts exist -- this general burden lies on the party who asserts the fact. The BSA also contains separate, more specific provisions on burden of proof: one dealing with which party bears the burden as the case proceeds, and another dealing with the burden of proving particular facts that are especially within a person's own knowledge. These are distinct provisions and should not be treated as identical or automatically equated with the corresponding provisions of the earlier Indian Evidence Act, 1872, without checking the exact text and numbering currently in force, since the renumbering between the two enactments is not a simple one-to-one mapping in every case.

My cousin's college classmate created a fake LinkedIn account with his details and is scamming his professional contacts. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
A client i'm helping is dealing with a situation involving the 30-day condonable extension. What does Indian law say about this?

Someone I met recently brought up filing an RTI application recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

What is the key difference between right to shared household and mandatory reporting under POCSO under Indian law?

right to shared household and mandatory reporting under POCSO are distinct legal concepts in Women and Child Protection. right to shared household: The legal right of an aggrieved woman to reside in the shared household irrespective of whether she holds legal title, joint ownership, or proprietary rights in the dwelling. mandatory reporting under POCSO: A strict statutory duty imposed on any person, medical professional, or educational institution aware of sexual offences against a minor to report the incident immediately to police or Child Welfare Committees. My sister-in-law is dealing with a situation involving a daughter's coparcenary rights. What does Indian law say about this?

Prior to 2005, daughters had no birthright share in ancestral Mitakshara property; the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 changed that by rewriting Section 6 so daughters become coparceners by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as sons. This is not retrospective in the sense of unwinding partitions completed before 20 December 2004, but the Supreme Court's 2020 ruling in Vineeta Sharma confirmed the right doesn't depend on the father being alive in 2005. In practice, so your sister-in-law isn't automatically excluded just because her father may have passed away — the Supreme Court's 2020 ruling clarified she can still claim coparcenary rights as long as she herself was alive on 9 September 2005.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of punishment for an ordinary person's failure to report isn't handled correctly?
Failure to report under Section 19 or Section 20 of the POCSO Act, 2012 is punishable under Section 21(1) with imprisonment up to six months, a fine, or both.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan, for my elder relative?

The 60-day window in a SARFAESI demand notice under Section 13(2) is not a formality — the Supreme Court has held that a bank's failure to properly respond to a borrower's written objection during this period is a fatal procedural flaw that can void the entire subsequent possession or sale action. The borrower can also approach the Debt Recovery Tribunal to challenge steps taken under Section 13(4). In practice, so your elder relative should treat the 60-day notice as the real deadline to act, since after that the bank can move straight to taking possession of the secured asset.
If a chemical spill's groundwater contamination is still actively spreading 9 months after the original leak, does the 6-month NGT deadline still block a fresh complaint?

Not necessarily. The National Green Tribunal has held, in cases like Amit Maru v. Secretary, MoEF, that where harm is ongoing or a fresh injury continues to occur (such as contamination that keeps spreading rather than being a single completed event), each continuing instance can be treated as giving rise to an independent, fresh cause of action — meaning the 6-month limitation under Section 14(3) of the NGT Act, 2010 would run from the most recent continuing harm, not solely from the original leak 9 months ago. A small business owner I know is dealing with a situation involving how long a trademark registration lasts. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a trademark registration is valid for 10 years from the date of the original application (not the date the certificate is actually issued), and can be renewed indefinitely for further 10-year periods by filing Form TM-R and paying the prescribed fee before expiry. If a PIO fails to respond in time under Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, or gives an unsatisfactory decision, the applicant can file a First Appeal under Section 19(1).
My elder relative is dealing with a situation involving a passport being impounded or seized. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967, a passport can be impounded or revoked by the passport authority on specific statutory grounds — including where the passport was obtained by suppressing material facts or giving false information, or where a court has issued a warrant, summons, or an order prohibiting the holder's departure from India in a pending case. An artist friend of mine wants to understand challenging an arbitration award. Could you walk through what applies to them?

In practice, in your artist friend's case, given how strictly courts have enforced the 3-month-plus-30-day cap, it's worth treating that deadline as truly final rather than assuming a court will show flexibility for a good reason.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding obtaining a protection order?

Once a Magistrate is satisfied that domestic violence has taken place under Section 12 of the PWDV Act, 2005, a protection order can be passed under Section 18, restraining the respondent from committing further acts of violence, aiding or abetting violence, or contacting the aggrieved person.
I run a small trading business in Meghalaya with annual turnover around ₹1,850,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. If a shopkeeper in Coimbatore is affected by notice period for agricultural or manufacturing leases, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 treats a lease for agricultural or manufacturing purposes as a year-to-year tenancy, terminable by either the lessor or lessee giving six months' notice — a longer period than the 15 days that applies to other kinds of leases.
If someone in my apartment complex is affected by how long a trademark registration lasts, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

First, the allottee may withdraw from the project and claim a full refund of the amount paid, along with interest. Second, the allottee may choose to remain in the project, in which case the promoter must pay interest for every month of delay until possession is handed over. The exact rate of interest is not fixed by Section 18 itself -- it is prescribed by the rules framed by the relevant State's Real Estate Regulatory Authority, so the applicable state rules should be checked for the precise figure. This is separate from Section 31, which deals with the filing of complaints before the Authority or the Adjudicating Officer, not with penalties or imprisonment.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a bank's recovery notice on a defaulted loan, for a small business owner I know?

Under the SARFAESI Act, a bank cannot simply seize mortgaged property the moment a loan goes into default — Section 13(2) requires a formal 60-day demand notice first, and only if the borrower fails to pay within that window can the lender proceed to symbolic or physical possession under Section 13(4). Within those 60 days, the borrower can also file a written objection under Section 13(3A), which the bank is legally required to consider and respond to with reasons. In practice, in the business owner's case, it's worth checking whether the bank actually responded in writing to any objection raised, since courts have voided possession actions where the bank simply ignored the borrower's reply.

Review this contract clause: "The lessee shall not assign, sublet, or part with possession of the premises without the prior written consent of the lessor." Is this enforceable under Indian law, and what are its boundaries?

Regarding the clause "The lessee shall not assign, sublet, or part with possession of the premises without the prior written consent of the lessor.": This is a covenant against unauthorized subletting. Under the Transfer of Property Act, subletting in violation of an express restrictive covenant constitutes a ground for determination of lease and eviction. Enforceability depends on statutory compliance, public policy, and whether the restriction is unconscionable or penal.
Regarding 'A client gave me a cheque that bounced, and I want to recover the money.', how do the legal consequences differ depending on the underlying facts?

Branching Legal Outcomes: In Banking and Financial Law, the legal path diverges significantly based on key variables: (1) The date on the bank return memo; (2) Whether statutory demand notice was dispatched within 30 days of receiving the memo; (3) Whether 15 days elapsed without payment. Comparative Scenarios: If formal documentation and statutory notice exist, summary or expedited remedies may be available. Conversely, if transactions were informal or dispute arises over core facts, comprehensive evidentiary trials are required.
My father was injured in a road accident four months ago and we're only now getting ready to file a compensation claim with the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. Are we already too late?

You are likely still within time, but this is an area of law currently in flux, so it's worth double-checking the latest position before filing. The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted Section 166(3), which states that no application for compensation shall be entertained unless made within six months of the accident; this provision was notified and came into force only from 1 April 2022. Since four months have passed, you would still be within that six-month window. However, this six-month limitation itself is currently being challenged before the Supreme Court as arbitrary and unconstitutional, and courts have at times directed that claim petitions should not be dismissed as time-barred while that challenge remains pending. Given the case-by-case and evolving nature of this issue, it would be prudent to file as soon as possible rather than relying on any extended timeline, and to have a lawyer confirm the current status of the Supreme Court proceedings before you finalize your filing strategy.

What risks or one-sided obligations does this clause impose: "Any dispute arising out of this agreement shall be referred to and finally resolved by arbitration seated in New Delhi under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996."?

The clause "Any dispute arising out of this agreement shall be referred to and finally resolved by arbitration seated in New Delhi under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996." presents specific commercial and legal risks: This is a seat selection and arbitration clause. Designating New Delhi as the seat confers exclusive supervisory jurisdiction on courts in New Delhi for supervisory remedies including appointment of arbitrators, interim relief, and challenges to arbitral awards, irrespective of hearing venues. The signing party should seek mutual obligations, reasonable liability caps, or specific carve-outs.
I lent money to a tenant for rent and the ₹28,000 repayment cheque they gave bounced with 'funds insufficient' as the reason. Does the reason for bounce matter legally?

Not much, as long as the cheque was issued toward a legally enforceable debt or liability. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 applies when a cheque is dishonoured because the account has insufficient funds, or because the amount exceeds what's arranged to be paid from that account under an agreement with the bank — 'funds insufficient' is the classic and most common trigger for this section. Your process is the same regardless: send a legal demand notice within 30 days of learning of the bounce, asking for the ₹28,000; if a tenant for rent doesn't pay within 15 days of receiving it, you can file a criminal complaint within about a month after that. On conviction, the punishment is imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹56,000), or both, and courts frequently use the fine or compensation route to make you whole rather than imposing jail time, especially if a tenant for rent is willing to settle.
What is the difference between the damages available under Section 73 versus Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, and does a party always need to prove actual loss to claim damages for breach?

Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs unliquidated damages — compensation the court assesses for loss naturally arising from a breach or foreseeable at the time of contracting — and here the claimant generally does need to prove the actual loss or damage suffered. Section 74, by contrast, deals with liquidated damages: where the contract itself specifies a sum payable as compensation or a penalty in the event of breach, courts can award reasonable compensation not exceeding that stipulated amount, and proof of actual loss is not necessary to claim under Section 74 in the way it is under Section 73 — though courts still assess reasonableness rather than mechanically awarding the full stipulated sum. So which section applies significantly changes what you need to prove: a contract without a pre-agreed compensation clause is decided under the general compensatory principles of Section 73, requiring proof of natural or foreseeable loss, while a contract with a pre-agreed damages or penalty clause falls under Section 74.
How do the missing details in 'A neighbor has constructed a wall that partially blocks light and access to my driveway.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Civil Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) Whether a registered easement deed or prescriptive easement exists over the access path; (2) Whether the construction violates municipal building bylaws or local setback rules; (3) The historical duration of uninterrupted enjoyment of the right. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
A client I'm helping is dealing with a situation involving setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 4 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) makes it mandatory for every employer with 10 or more employees to constitute an Internal Committee (IC) at each office or branch to receive and inquire into complaints. Failing to set one up attracts a penalty under Section 26 starting at Rs 50,000, doubled for a repeat offence, and can even lead to cancellation of the business's licence or registration. In practice, for your client, if the organisation has 10 or more people counting everyone (not just permanent staff), the absence of an Internal Committee is itself a compliance failure the employer can be penalised for under Section 26.
Why have Indian courts consistently rejected the premise that 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.'?

Judicial Rationale: Courts reject this premise because it undermines public policy and statutory intent in Company and Business Law. Legal Reasoning: Director immunity is not absolute. Directors face personal liability for statutory tax defaults, bouncing company cheques under the NI Act, fraud, and situations where courts pierce the corporate veil. Precedent: Judicial orders hold that statutory mandates cannot be bypassed by customary assumptions.
Under Section 512 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, what is the punishment for repeat theft offenders?

I'm not able to verify that Section 512 of the BNS covers repeat theft offenders. The BNS's substantive provisions run only up to Section 358 (Chapter XX, Repeal and Savings), so Section 512 does not correspond to an existing provision. Repeat theft convictions are actually addressed under Section 303(2) of the BNS, 2023, which prescribes rigorous imprisonment of one to five years plus a fine for a second or subsequent conviction. Please verify any specific section number against the current bare act before relying on it.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of wife's maintenance claim isn't handled correctly?

Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the successor to Section 125 CrPC, lets a wife unable to maintain herself — including a divorced wife who has not remarried — claim a monthly allowance from a husband with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain her.
My old employment contract has a clause saying I can't work for any competitor anywhere in India for 2 years after I resign. Is that enforceable?

Very likely not, as a blanket restriction. Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 states that 'every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void' -- and Indian courts have consistently held that, unlike English law, this rule doesn't distinguish between 'reasonable' and 'unreasonable' restraints once employment has ended: post-employment non-compete clauses restraining you from working in your field after you leave are generally void, whether the restriction is total or partial, nationwide or local. This was established as far back as Madhub Chander v. Raj Coomar (1874) and has been repeatedly reaffirmed, including in cases like Superintendence Company of India v. Krishan Murgai. The main exception the Act carves out is for a person who sells the goodwill of a business, who can agree not to compete with the buyer within specified local limits, provided the restriction is reasonable. Note the important distinction, though: restrictions that operate DURING your employment (like an exclusivity clause while you're still working there), and reasonable confidentiality or trade-secret protection clauses that survive employment, are generally enforceable and aren't hit by Section 27 in the same way, because they aren't restraining you from practising your profession as such. This is general information, and the specific wording of your clause matters, so a lawyer should review it before you rely on this.
What does the law say if someone I met recently is facing minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company?

The high-profile Tata Sons v. Cyrus Mistry dispute was fought under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 — illustrating that this remedy isn't limited to small family companies, but is available even in large public companies where minority (or removed) shareholders believe the majority's conduct has been unfairly prejudicial to their interests. In practice, for this person, the first practical check is the numerical threshold under Section 244 — without holding at least 10% of shares (or meeting the 100-member/one-tenth alternative), the petition to NCLT can't even be filed.
A colleague at work asked me about challenging an arbitration award — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The three-month clock under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration Act starts from the date of receipt of the signed award, not from when it was merely delivered or dispatched — a distinction that has actually decided cases, since 'receipt' and 'delivery' aren't treated as automatically the same thing under the Act. In practice, this means your colleague should file the Section 34 application well within the window rather than waiting close to the deadline, since even administrative delays (like a court being on vacation) haven't been accepted as grounds for extension beyond the cap.
What does the law say if a startup founder I'm advising is facing filing an RTI application?

The standard application fee for filing an RTI request with a central government public authority is Rs 10, and applicants who are Below Poverty Line (BPL), with proof, don't have to pay any fee at all. States can set their own fee under their respective RTI rules — most match the Rs 10 central figure, though a few charge more. In practice, in the founder's case, if there's a genuine BPL certificate to attach, the entire application fee (and the fee for receiving the information) can be waived altogether.
Can you explain what Indian law says about an unresolved e-commerce or online shopping complaint, for a factory worker I spoke with?

The 2019 Consumer Protection Act extended consumer rights explicitly to online transactions, and the accompanying e-commerce rules require platforms to acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and resolve them within a month. Alongside this, the Act created a Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) with the power to investigate unfair trade practices, order recalls of unsafe goods, and penalise misleading advertisements. In practice, in the worker's case, the right forum depends on the value of the goods or services — the District Consumer Commission can hear complaints up to Rs 1 crore, with higher-value matters going to the State or National Commission.
A child aged 17 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, since the POCSO Act defines a 'child' as anyone below 18 years, a 17-year-old victim is fully covered. Penetrative sexual assault carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 10 years, extendable to imprisonment for life, along with a mandatory fine to be used for the victim's medical treatment and rehabilitation. Because the accused is described as a relative, the case may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Sections 5 and 6 if the relative held a position of trust, which raises the minimum sentence to 20 years. Consent is legally immaterial for a child under 18, the offence is non-bailable and cognizable, and the trial takes place before a designated Special Court under the Act.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of the pre-2022 position on claim timelines isn't handled correctly?

Before Section 166(3) came into force on 1 April 2022, the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 did not itself prescribe a strict limitation period for compensation claims, and courts generally took a liberal, claimant-friendly approach to delayed filings given the beneficial nature of the provision.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding waiver of the cooling-off period?

In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, the Supreme Court held that the six-month cooling-off period under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is directory, not mandatory, and family courts have discretion to waive it where reconciliation is impossible and disputes such as alimony and custody are genuinely settled.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding the 30-day condonable extension?

The proviso to Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 allows the court to entertain a delayed challenge to an arbitral award for a further 30 days beyond the three-month limitation period if sufficient cause is shown — but the words "not thereafter" make this an absolute outer limit that courts, including the Supreme Court, have applied strictly.
A friend's mother wants to understand being laid off or retrenched from a job. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Before an employer can lawfully retrench a workman under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, three things have to happen together — notice or pay in lieu of notice, compensation at 15 days' average pay per completed year of service, and intimation to the government. Skipping any of these makes the retrenchment procedurally invalid, giving the workman grounds to challenge it, quite apart from whether the underlying reason for the layoff was itself justified. In practice, this means your friend's mother is entitled to this compensation regardless of why the retrenchment happened, as long as it isn't because of misconduct or a voluntary retirement scheme.
My colleague's UPI ID was used by someone who created a similar-looking fake payment QR code claiming to be him. What can I do under Indian cyber law?

This falls under Sections 66C and 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66C punishes identity theft — fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or any unique identification feature — with imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Section 66D specifically punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device, which directly covers impersonation for payment fraud using a computer resource, and carries the same punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years and/or a fine up to ₹1 lakh. Both sections can apply together if both the credential misuse and the deceptive impersonation are present. Preserve screenshots, URLs, and message logs as digital evidence, then file a complaint at your nearest cybercrime cell or via the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); you can also lodge an FIR with local police citing Sections 66C/66D alongside relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for cheating.
A child aged 13 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, penetrative sexual assault on a child below 16 years of age — which covers a 13-year-old victim — carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 20 years, extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's natural life, along with a mandatory fine. The 2019 amendment specifically raised this minimum from 10 to 20 years for victims under 16 to reflect the heightened severity. Since the accused is described as a relative, the offence may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5/6 if the relative was in a position of trust or authority, in which case the minimum sentence rises further to 20 years up to life, or even the death penalty in the most extreme cases where the court considers it warranted. Since a child under 18 is involved, consent is legally irrelevant, and the case will be tried by a Special POCSO Court, with the trial conducted in a manner sensitive to the child.
If a friend of mine is affected by first conviction for simple theft, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

This is theft under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, the successor to Section 378 IPC. For a first conviction, Section 303(2) prescribes imprisonment of either description for up to three years, a fine, or both.
What does Indian law currently say about how long copyright protection lasts?

The Copyright Act, 1957's 60-year term (extended from the original 50 years by a 1992 amendment, to bring it in line with international norms) applies to the individual work itself, not to the author's entire body of work as a unit — each work has its own copyright term running from that author's death (or the last surviving joint author's death).
A supplier issued a cheque of Rs. 2 lakh to settle a business debt, but it bounced due to insufficient funds. What is the legal procedure and punishment under Indian law for cheque dishonour?

This falls under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Since the cheque was dishonoured for insufficiency of funds against an existing debt or liability, the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the bank's dishonour memo, demanding payment of the cheque amount. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay. If payment is not made within those 15 days, a criminal complaint can be filed, and the cause of action arises on the 16th day. The offence carries imprisonment of up to two years, a fine that may extend to twice the cheque amount, or both. Under Section 147 of the Act, the offence is compoundable, so the parties can settle at any stage and the accused would then stand acquitted.
Can a woman file a domestic violence case against her sister-in-law, or only against her husband?

Yes, she can, and this is a point that's often misunderstood. Under Section 2(q) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, the definition of 'respondent' originally said 'adult male person' -- but in Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora (2016), the Supreme Court struck down the words 'adult male' from that definition, holding that restricting the law to male respondents only had no rational basis and violated Article 14 of the Constitution. So today, a domestic violence complaint under the Act can be filed against any adult person -- male or female -- who is or has been in a domestic relationship with the aggrieved woman, which includes a husband's female relatives such as a sister-in-law or mother-in-law, not just the husband himself. The complaint would need to describe the specific acts of abuse (physical, verbal, emotional, sexual, or economic) attributable to that person.
In Kerala, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Kerala, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
How do the missing details in 'An elderly parent was made to sign transfer papers while hospitalized and now wishes to revoke them.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Senior Citizen-related law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) Whether the document was a registered gift deed, will, or general power of attorney; (2) The medical mental competency records at the time of execution; (3) Whether conditions of providing maintenance were stipulated in the instrument. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
A friend's mother wants to understand gratuity owed after leaving a job. Could you walk through what applies to them?

Under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, an employee becomes eligible for gratuity after completing five years of continuous service (courts have accepted 240 days worked in the fifth year as satisfying this), except where employment ends due to death or disablement, in which case the five-year requirement doesn't apply at all. Gratuity is calculated as (last drawn salary × 15 × number of years of service) ÷ 26, and the maximum payable under the Act is capped at Rs 20 lakh, following the 2018 amendment that raised it from Rs 10 lakh. In practice, in your friend's mother's case, since gratuity is calculated on the *last drawn* salary, any recent increment actually raises the gratuity amount, so it's worth confirming the employer used the most recent basic + DA figure.

I'm Suresh. I noticed an online purchase made using my debit card details without my knowledge for Rs. 90000, and I reported it to my bank about 60 hours after I got the bank's SMS alert. Will I get the full amount back?

If this transaction happened due to a third-party breach and you weren't at fault, reporting it within roughly 2.5 day(s) generally falls inside the RBI's zero-liability window. The actual rule is framed as '3 WORKING days' from the bank's alert, not a flat 72 hours -- working days exclude weekends and bank holidays, so it's worth confirming the exact working-day count with your bank rather than just counting clock hours.

If you qualify for zero liability, the bank is expected to credit the disputed Rs. 90000 back to your account within 10 working days of your complaint, without waiting for its own investigation or any insurance claim to conclude, and the complaint itself should be resolved within 90 days. Do file a written complaint with the bank (not just a phone call) and keep the acknowledgment.
I received an arbitral award in an insurance claim arbitration 7 weeks ago and I disagree with it. Can I still challenge it in court?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you have 3 months from the date you received the arbitral award to file an application to set it aside in the relevant court, and the court can extend this by a further 30 days — but only if you show sufficient cause for the delay, and not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances (courts have treated this outer limit as absolute). Given that 7 weeks have passed since you received the award, you should still be within, or close to, the permissible window, so you should file your Section 34 application without further delay to be safe, especially since if you're past the initial 3 months you would need to show sufficient cause for the extension and delay itself weakens that showing. Note that Section 34 challenges are limited to specific grounds — such as incapacity of a party, invalid arbitration agreement, lack of proper notice, the award dealing with matters beyond the scope of arbitration, improper composition of the tribunal, patent illegality (for domestic awards), or conflict with public policy — it is not an appeal on the merits, so you cannot simply argue the arbitrator got the facts wrong.
How does Indian law actually treat revoking a conditional gift for failure to maintain, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 provides that where a senior citizen transfers property on condition the transferee provide basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee fails to do so, the transfer can be declared void by the Maintenance Tribunal.

The foundational statutory principle under digital personal data legislation requiring data fiduciaries to obtain clear, unbundled, and informed consent accompanied by an itemized privacy notice specifying processing purposes. A Section 138 case is a private criminal complaint before a Magistrate, not a police FIR. Following the 2015 amendment, jurisdiction lies with the court where the payee's bank branch (where the cheque was presented) is situated.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime?

The Children's Court, not the Juvenile Justice Board, makes the final call on whether a 16-18 year old accused of a heinous offence should be tried as an adult, based on the Board's preliminary assessment under Section 15 of the JJ Act, 2015. Courts have also clarified that an offence only counts as "heinous" if the relevant law prescribes an actual minimum sentence of seven years — an offence with only a maximum punishment above seven years but no specified minimum does not qualify.
My cousin is worried he might be arrested over a business dispute that's been made into a criminal complaint. Can he get bail before he's even arrested?

Yes, if the offence alleged against him is non-bailable, he can apply for anticipatory (pre-arrest) bail under Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 -- the successor to Section 438 CrPC, in force from 1 July 2024. He doesn't need to wait for an FIR to be registered; a reasonable apprehension of arrest (based on a complaint, summons, or credible information) is enough, as long as it isn't merely speculative. The application can be filed in the Court of Session or the High Court -- most lawyers file first in the Sessions Court and go to the High Court only if that's refused or the matter is urgent/complex. Courts typically weigh the nature and gravity of the accusation, his prior antecedents, flight risk, and whether the complaint looks like it's meant to harass or pressure him. Per the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench ruling in Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020), anticipatory bail, once granted, doesn't have to be time-limited and can continue until the end of trial unless the court itself restricts it. This is general information -- he should consult a criminal lawyer promptly since anticipatory bail is very fact-specific.
How do the missing facts in 'I want a divorce and maintenance from my spouse immediately.' impact which court or forum has jurisdiction?

Jurisdictional Thresholds: The missing facts directly determine forum competency in Family Law: (1) Which personal law applies to the marriage (e.g., Hindu Marriage Act, Special Marriage Act, Muslim personal law); (2) Whether the divorce is by mutual consent or contested; (3) Whether there are minor children and existing interim maintenance orders. Legal Danger: Filing in an improper forum due to unverified facts leads to rejection of plaint and loss of limitation period.

How does Indian law actually treat the second-motion cooling-off period, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 13B(2) requires the second motion to be moved between six and eighteen months after the first, so the court can confirm consent remains genuine.

In Telangana, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Telangana, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law.
